title: Panthers vs Cardinals: Offensive Preview
summary: The preseason is upon us, and if you’re like me, it snuck up on you pretty quick. I guess that’s what happens when your team is playing in the Hall of Fame game and gets the honor of playing an early and extra preseason game that nobody wants. The opponent in this game that no […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - DECEMBER 08: Carolina Panthers offensive coordinator Brad Idzik looks on during the game between the Philadelphia Eagles and the Carolina Panthers on December 08, 2024 at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Andy Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The preseason is upon us, and if you’re like me, it snuck up on you pretty quick. I guess that’s what happens when your team is playing in the Hall of Fame game and gets the honor of playing an early and extra preseason game that nobody wants. The opponent in this game that no one wants to play in is the Arizona Cardinals, who have the lowest win total over/under you’ll ever see at 3.5 games. All that’s good for is making people freak out if the Panthers struggle in this game. You’ll see takes along the lines of “it might be a long season for us if our backups are worse than the Cardinals backups” and things of that nature. I’m here to remind you that the result of this game means absolutely nothing knowing full well people are going to ignore this and try to read into it either way. Anyway, there are some things we can pay attention to as we scratch our itch to watch football on our TVs. Whether or not the Carolina Panthers win or not isn’t worth analyzing, but there are some more micro-level things we can watch for. Kenny Pickett’s viability as a backup quarterback This is going to be more of an eye test thing than a stats thing. Given the context of the game and the players that are going to be on the field, Pickett might not have great protection or windows to throw through. More important will be how decisive and poised he looks operating the offense and how accurate he is when he gets a chance to deliver the football. Pickett has a lot of real NFL games under his belt, so he should be fine, but a strong performance can quiet some concerns Panthers fans have about him as the team’s backup. Can the backup tackles block people? The Panthers got dealt a rough bit of news with Taylor Moton missing time with a blood clot in his lung. That means both of last season’s starters are on the shelf for the foreseeable future, which pushes free agent signing Rasheed Walker and rookie first round pick Monroe Freeling to the starting spots. After them is anyone’s guess. The Panthers are walking a dangerous line at that position group right now. They need one of their inordinately tall depth guys to be better than expected to make the depth at that position look a little less scary. The mechanics of Brad Idzik as a play caller There isn’t going to be a whole lot in terms of scheme for the preseason, but we’ll get our first look at Brad Idzik calling plays. We’re not going to worry about play design, but it will be interesting to see some of his tendencies start to show in different situations. Like what does he call in 3rd and short, or how often does he run or pass the ball on first down. And perhaps most importantly for this setting, is he quick at getting the personnel groupings and play calls down to the field. It’s not the end of the world if it’s a little choppy given this is a new gig, but it’ll be interesting to see how the debut goes. Jonathon Brooks? We’ve hardly seen Brooks since the Panthers picked him in the second round of the 2024 NFL Draft. He’s been a full go throughout training camp, and with the starters not getting the call for the Hall of Fame game, I’d expect Brooks to get at least a few looks. We’ll see how well he’s bounced back from multiple ACL tears, and the game reps will be paramount to get him back in a rhythm going into the regular season.
author: Jonathan DeLong

title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 40 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: 8 Dec 1996: Linebacker Lamar Lathon of the Carolina Panthers celebrates during a game against the San Francisco 49ers at 3Com Park in San Francisco, California. The Panthers won the game, 30-24. | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #40. Lamar Lathon Lamar Lathon started his career as an off-ball linebacker out of the University of Houston. The hometown Houston Oilers selected Lathon 15th overall in the 1990 NFL Draft. After a rookie season that saw mostly backup and special teams duties, he took the starting role at strong side linebacker in his second season. That year just so happened to be his best year in Houston, logging 116 tackles, two sacks, three interceptions, and six forced fumbles. A couple years later, an injury and a coaching change cost him that starting role. During training camp in 1993, Lathon suffered a broken forearm. Newly hired defensive coordinator Buddy Ryan kept Joe Bowden as the starter even after Lathon was healthy. Lathon moved to more of an edge rusher role the following season, notching 8.5 sacks. Despite showing some pass rush promise, Houston released Lathon after the season. The Carolina Panthers had just come into existence in 1995 as Lathon hit the open market. Defensive coordinator Vic Fangio liked Lathon’s fit in his 3-4 as an outside linebacker, and the team signed Lathon. The team was rewarded with one of Lathon’s best seasons to that point. He then followed up that campaign with a 1996 season full of accolades. He combined with fellow edge rusher Kevin Greene to terrorize opposing quarterbacks. Lathon alone logged 77 tackles and 13.5 sacks (still good for fifth most in franchise history for a single season), leading to him being named to the Pro Bowl and All Pro Second Team. He even got seventh place in the Defensive Player of the Year voting, proving how dominant he truly was. After Kevin Greene left for San Francisco the following year, Lathon’s production took a huge hit, as did his health. He started the year with foot and ankle injuries and suffered a major knee injury in Week 3. Though he played through the injury for most of the rest of the season, the knee would need major reconstructive surgery during the offseason. Lathon tried to return the following season, but being 31 years old and coming off a major knee injury ultimately ended his career. Lamar Lathon showed incredible ability as both an off ball linebacker and edge rusher, essentially being a Micah Parsons or Abdul Carter before they were even born. His true home, like Parsons and Carter, was at edge. The “Salt and Pepper” combination of Greene and Lathon drove the Panthers defense to be second in points allowed, leading the team to a 12-4 record and a NFC Championship Game appearance. Though his time in Carolina was cut short, his dominance for the then expansion franchise helped catapult the Panthers into the hearts of the people of Charlotte. For this contribution, Lamar Lathon earned the No. 40 spot on our countdown.
author: Daniel Belton

title: Chicago Bears roster 2026: Kyle Monangai, Devin Bush, and Malik Muhammad are underrated
summary: If you want to feel better about the fact that the Chicago Bears are the only NFL team without a 4,000-yard passer in its history, consider that 12 other teams hadn’t seen it happen for them until the new millennium turned around. And some of the league’s best current teams — the Houston Texans, Philadelphia […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - JANUARY 18: Kyle Monangai #25 of the Chicago Bears completes a catch and carries the ball during the second quarter of an NFL divisional playoff game against the Los Angeles Rams at Soldier Field on January 18, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images If you want to feel better about the fact that the Chicago Bears are the only NFL team without a 4,000-yard passer in its history, consider that 12 other teams hadn’t seen it happen for them until the new millennium turned around. And some of the league’s best current teams — the Houston Texans, Philadelphia Eagles, Tampa Bay Buccaneers, Buffalo Bills, and Seattle Seahawks — didn’t see it for their franchises until the last few years . The larger point, of course, is that Caleb Williams, who threw for 3,942 yards in the 2025 regular season — and 4,560 if you include the postseason — is on the verge of getting the Bears off the schneid. Williams is also the man to finally break the Bears’ epic quarterback curse , which started after Sid Luckman and World War II. How far can the 2026 Bears go with a quarterback of Williams’ caliber? This will be Williams’ second season with Ben Johnson as his head coach and offensive mastermind, and everybody’s pretty psyched about that. “He’s had two offseasons and one training camp so far, and a full season to where he’s had a lot of the similar concepts repeat for him,” Johnson said of Williams a few days ago . “Now, we’re at the point where he’s not thinking about the play call, he’s not thinking about the cadence, the motion and all the rigmarole before the snap. “Things are starting to slow down. So, what we need to see here in camp is that anticipation. Take it up a notch. I think with that, the coverage recognition gets taken up another notch. There are other ways we’re going to continue to challenge and push him, more of which are going to happen post-snap. Last year we talked about that pre-snap operation quite a bit. [We] feel a lot better about that this time of year than we did [last summer], so now we’re just moving onto the next stage.” Williams agrees. “Plays get more detailed,” the quarterback said of his current work with Johnson. “He’s adding more on my plate of figuring out the coverage before, and having an idea of where I can go with the ball faster and sooner. I haven’t thrown a lot of picks in my career, because I can see the coverage and feel the coverage. It’s a little more detailed from play to play, and specifics within the play, towards the coverage that we are attacking. Then, adding more plays in there so that we can kill, alert and check to these different man checks, Cover-2 checks, single-high or whatever the case may be. “We are excited about that. I’m excited. The challenge that he’s giving me to be able to take the next step and progress is what I’m most excited about. It’s going to be hard. It’s going to be tough like it is every year. That’s what you embrace, that’s what you enjoy. Because when it shows up on game days and Sundays or whatever day we play on, it’s really rewarding.” Last season, the 11-6 Bears got as far as the Divisional Round of the playoffs for the first time since 2010, and there’s no reason to assume that they can’t do it again — or go even further in the tournament. If that’s the case, of course, it can’t just be about Johnson and Williams. Everyone on the roster must be at their best, including the lesser-known names. To that end, I’ve identified three Hidden Gems for the Bears’ new season — one underrated veteran, one underrated free agent, and one underrated draft pick. Underrated veteran: RB Kyle Monangai There are times when you watch a draft prospect’s tape, and you then see how the NFL values him, and you tend to wonder what the hell the NFL is thinking. When I saw that the Bears were able to lift Rutgers running back Kyle Monangai with the 235th overall pick in the seventh round of the 2025 draft, I must admit that I thought a lot of pro personnel people had lost their damned minds. Because what I saw from the 5′ 8¼, 211-pound Monangai made it pretty clear in my mind: Forget about the height. Forget about the 4.6-second 40-yard dash at the combine . This guy is a football player , and I don’t care what anybody says in any other direction. Rutgers RB Kyle Monangai is a one-cut-and-go Pocket Hercules with serious lateral juice, hatred in his heart for anybody trying to tackle him, and a SERIOUS stiff-arm. Probably a third-day guy who could turn himself into more. pic.twitter.com/qG9Mpvuuue — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) April 24, 2025 Monangai proved the point in a rookie season that had him gain 846 yards and score five rushing touchdowns on 190 carries, adding 23 catches on 34 targets for 222 yards. His first start came in Week 9 against the Cincinnati Bengals when D’Andre Swift was out with a groin injury. All Monangai did in that game was to blow up Cincy’s defense to the tune of 176 yards on 26 carries. “When you come into the building like he does, and have his approach every single day, and it doesn’t matter whether it’s in the meetings or in walkthroughs or practices, you know what you’re going to get,” Johnson said of Monangai last November . “He is a very consistent player. He ran hard; he lowered his pads. I thought that he played some inspiring football for anybody that was watching it, whether you were on the field or on the sidelines. No one was surprised.” Swift was more succinct, but equally complimentary. “He doesn’t carry himself like a rookie, and he [darn] sure doesn’t play like one.” Kyle Monangai was ignored by the NFL until the seventh round of the 2025 draft. Monangai responded by taking it out on the rest of the league throughout his rookie season. @ChicagoBears pic.twitter.com/cyFMStXX5h — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) August 2, 2026 Monangai’s high-contact playing style does come with some danger — he’s been dealing with a soft tissue injury in training camp — but when he’s healthy, he will undoubtedly be proving the doubters wrong yet again. Underrated free agent: LB Devin Bush Just because you don’t succeed in the NFL right away doesn’t mean that you can’t do so over time. Some players have everything it takes to create legitimate careers, but the growth takes a while. Or, they’re in the wrong systems. Or, trends haven’t quite caught up to what they can do. Or, on and off-field issues get to them for a while. Take the example of linebacker Devin Bush. The Pittsburgh Steelers selected the 5’11, 234-pound Bush with the 10th overall pick in the 2019 draft out of Michigan, and it never quite worked out. Bush had his moments in Pittsburgh’s defense, but not nearly enough for such a high pick — especially a high pick that the team had to trade first- and second-round picks in 2019, and a third-round pick in 2020, just to take in the first place. The Steelers refused to exercise Bush’s fifth-year option, so he was out after the 2022 season. Bush signed with the Seattle Seahawks for a nondescript 2023 season, and then, the turnaround started to happen when Bush signed a one-year, $1.5 million contract with the Cleveland Browns in 2024 and had his best season to date under Jim Schwartz. That led to a one-year, $3.25 million contract with the Browns in 2025, whereupon Bush had his best season to date under Schwartz once again. Last year, Bush totaled 50 solo tackles, 24 stops, seven tackles for loss, a forced fumble, three interceptions, and five pass breakups. He had three more picks than he allowed, and with his two pick-sixes and 164 return yards, Bush was as dangerous an interceptor as you could get in the NFL. Very quietly, Devin Bush was a DUDE for the @Browns last season. Led the NFL in pick-sixes (two) and interception return yards (164). Now, the @ChicagoBears can benefit from his skill set. pic.twitter.com/e74yHS3z04 — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) August 3, 2026 “I’m going into Year 8,” Bush said after the…
author: Doug Farrar

title: Injuries put more pressure on Dennis Allen, Bears defense to simply survive in 2026
summary: It can happen to anyone, any team, at any time. Right now, unfortunately, the Chicago Bears are going through it. Safety Coby Bryant, arguably the centerpiece of this year’s free-agent haul, will reportedly miss 8-10 weeks after suffering a knee injury in yesterday’s practice—better than the alternative, as it won’t require surgery, but not ideal […]
full_text: It can happen to anyone, any team, at any time. Right now, unfortunately, the Chicago Bears are going through it. Safety Coby Bryant, arguably the centerpiece of this year’s free-agent haul, will reportedly miss 8-10 weeks after suffering a knee injury in yesterday’s practice—better than the alternative, as it won’t require surgery, but not ideal for the Bears. He’ll now join fellow safety Elijah Hicks (shin) and cornerback Kyler Gordon (calf) on the PUP list, putting additional strain on the defensive back room. When you take into account that edge Dayo Odeyingbo is coming off of an Achilles injury and second-year defensive lineman Shemar Turner (knee) is also on the PUP list from the injury he suffered last year, this defense has a lot of question marks heading into a critical 2026 season. That’s especially concerning given that Chicago largely kept their defensive core the same—aside from adding quality starters like Bryant and linebacker Devin Bush and rookies like first-round pick Dillion Thieneman—rather than making a high-upside splash move this offseason. And Ryan Poles likely doesn’t have a major move up his sleeve to change the calculus, with adding veteran secondary depth probably his only consideration right now. In the end, all of that points toward the same thing: all the pressure is on Dennis Allen to make this defensive roster work. Bears defensive coordinator Dennis Allen on leading a group dealing with injuries: “I want to see 11 fricken dudes on the field competing their ass off.” pic.twitter.com/vrwlzOrmup — Chris Emma (@CEmma670) August 4, 2026 Despite ranking poorly in most advanced metrics and missing true blue-chip talent last season, the Bears’ defense broke even, more or less, by generating a league-leading 33 takeaways (including 23 interceptions) in 2025. Moreover, players like Nahshon Wright (now with the New York Jets) stepped up when called upon and turned in strong seasons, suggesting the Bears can likewise get big plays out of backups and young players in 2026 as well. Is it wise to count on the whole of the Bears’ defense being greater than the sum of its parts again? Probably not. Turnovers are famously finicky, as many rely on good luck. Just take the drop-off between the Bears’ record-setting 2018 season (36 takeaways) and their underwhelming 2019 campaign (19 takeaways) as evidence. History would suggest Chicago is in for a similar regression to the mean this season when it’s all said and done. For those interested, Allen’s teams (as either a DC or head coach) have had eight seasons ranked in the bottom half of the league in takeaways against seven in the top half of the NFL. Do they have the talent to withstand that variance? I’m not sure they do. But they seem ready to roll the dice. Allen’s defenses, aside from a few peak years in New Orleans from 2022-2024, have rarely been among the league’s best in terms of points per game and yards allowed . Some units, like last year’s, were basically turnstiles. But the trick is that they’re usually good enough to survive even without top talent, adhering to the old “bend, don’t break” philosophy and using mind games and simulated pressure as much as possible to disrupt an offense’s thought process. They don’t usually dominate; they keep the bleeding to a minimum and try to get key stops/takeaways in big moments. That’s a tough way to live, but last year was proof it can be done. And with Ben Johnson seemingly trying to score 40 points a game with his stacked offensive unit, Allen and the Bears defense just have to allow no more than 39 on their end. As the San Francisco 49ers game last year demonstrates, that approach can get you burned. But, as seen in the playoffs against the Packers and Rams, Allen’s squad proved it could step up when the chips are down. Without the assurance of Bryant, Gordon, and several other players being available or as effective as they could be, that’s what Allen and this defense must do: enough.
author: Khari Thompson

title: Chicago Bears sign safety Marlen Sewell
summary: With safety Coby Bryant’s injury sidelining him for eight to ten weeks, and with safety Elijah Hicks still on the PUP list, the Chicago Bears signed safety Marlen Sewell today. Sewell (6′, 199), a 2026 undrafted free agent from Vanderbilt, was originally signed by the Kansas City Chiefs after a May tryout, but was released […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - OCTOBER 18: Marlen Sewell #7 of the Vanderbilt Commodores reacts during the first half of the game against the LSU Tigers at FirstBank Stadium on October 18, 2025 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty Images) | Getty Images With safety Coby Bryant’s injury sidelining him for eight to ten weeks, and with safety Elijah Hicks still on the PUP list, the Chicago Bears signed safety Marlen Sewell today. Sewell (6′, 199), a 2026 undrafted free agent from Vanderbilt, was originally signed by the Kansas City Chiefs after a May tryout, but was released in June. During his five years in college with the Commodores, he had 102 tackles, 2.5 tackles for loss, .5 sack, 3 passes defended, a forced fumble, and a fumble recovery. He has a lot of special teams experience while a reserve early in his collegiate career, but last year he emerged as a leader for their defense. At his Pro Day, he ran a 4.48 forty, had a 36′ vertical, and a 10’6″ broad jump. He’s no relation to the Sewell brothers currently on the Bears, and he goes by Marlo. He’ll compete with Anthony Johnson Jr., Gervarrius Owens, and Skyler Thomas to win a backup safety spot or a place on the practice squad. To make room for Sewell on the roster, the Bears placed defensive end Jonathan Garvin on injured reserve.
author: Lester A. Wiltfong Jr.

title: Chicago Bears Question of the Day: What offseason narrative is most tired?
summary: It’s been a long offseason, but real football is back. In less than two weeks time the Bears will be taking the field against the Cleveland Browns to open the preseason. Already a handful of days into training camp and some players are already trying to reset narratives that have occurred throughout the summer break. […]
full_text: It’s been a long offseason, but real football is back. In less than two weeks time the Bears will be taking the field against the Cleveland Browns to open the preseason. Already a handful of days into training camp and some players are already trying to reset narratives that have occurred throughout the summer break. A few that I have seen pop up consistently since season’s end: Luther Burden will be the Bears #1 WR in 2026 and beyond Subtext, Rome Odunze will not be Dayo Odeyingbo and Grady Jarrett were flops Subtext, these two players will be minimal contributors in 2026 and will get cut next offseason Kyler Gordon’s soft tissue injuries are a major problem Subtext, the Bears are assessing replacements for him after the 2026 season at NB The Bears have problems at LT and C Subtext, Braxton Jones, Jedrick Wills, Garrett Bradbury, and Logan Jones will be worse than their 2025 starting counterparts The Bears will regress in 2026 Subtext, their defense, turnover differential, and 4th quarter comebacks are unsustainable and will lead to a regression to the mean There might be others, but these were some that I consistently gleaned from the media, other blogs, and even here at WCG. So which of these are the most tired? Which do we need to set straight and pull out of the offseason echo chamber? This is the basis of this week’s question: Which offseason Bears narrative is most tired? For me, it’s the conversation around Grady Jarrett and Dayo Odeyingbo. I get it — these two failed to live up to their lofty contracts in 2025. A reminder of each contract below: Grady Jarrett signed a 3 year, $42.75 million deal including cap hits of $18.9 and $16.8 million in 2026 and 2027 (but only $4 million in dead money in 2027) His annual average salary of $14.5 million ranks 24th in the NFL amongst IDL. Dayo Odeyingbo signed a 3 year, $48 million deal including cap hits of $20.5 and $19.5 million in 2026 and 2027 (but only $4.5 million in dead money in 2027) His average annual salary of $16 million ranks 29th in the NFL among Edge rushers. Neither of these are small cap hits, and one might argue that they kept the Bears from pursuing other defensive upgrades this offseason. I get it. But I think we are confusing sunken cost with a player that is no longer on the team. In case the offseason narrative has convinced you otherwise, Grady Jarrett and Dayo Odeyingbo are still members of the 2026 Chicago Bears — and I think they are both severely underrated for what they can do for the 2026 defense. Let’s start with the veteran, Grady Jarrett. Jarrett came in with a pedigree and something to prove after his long tenure with the Atlanta Falcons came to a close following a cut in March of 2025. Ryan Poles viewed him as the interior rusher and veteran presence that the Bears DL desperately needed. Unfortunately, in 14 games last season, Jarrett only tallied 1.5 sacks, 39 tackles, 1 TFL, 8 QB hits, and 3 PDs. Those numbers aren’t enough to justify his cost. But that’s not to say that Jarrett doesn’t have anything left in the tank. Jarrett himself has owned up to his 2025 season by saying: No, so we hear it, man. But it also comes with the job, you know, it comes with the job. And at the end of the day, we gotta really take it personal and get back to work. Even if sometimes your best ain’t good enough. So you gotta find out ‘Where can I be better at? Jarrett isn’t a stranger to down years, either. He also isn’t a stranger to bounce backs. In 2021, his age 28 season, Jarrett had a down year following two Pro Bowl seasons, where he only notched 1 sack, and 3 TFLs in 17 games. The next season, Jarrett responded with 6 sacks and 12 TFLs — a massive improvement that shows his ability to right the course. Additionally, he has noted being in better shape this offseason, after working through a knee injury that sidelined him for portions of 2025. So it should not be outlandish to expect a better Grady Jarrett in 2026, something that I have seen consistently discounted this offseason. As for Dayo Odeyingbo. It’s safe to say that Dayo has become the newest punching bag for Bears fans. Reports of a “Motivated Dayo” has become a sarcastic refrain for fans that expect him to be a non contributor in 2026. While I understand why people are questioning his impact, I think it is far too premature to write him off at this stage in his career. Dayo was but 26 years old with 3.5 seasons under his belt when he joined the Bears last offseason. Odeyingbo has draft pedigree and prototypical size for the position as a 2nd round pick that measures at 6’-5” and 282 lbs. While he still hasn’t put together a spectacular season in his career, he mustered 11 sacks, 16 TFLs, and 34 QB hits in his age 24 and 25 seasons combined — numbers that suggest a jump still may be warranted. Still, in his 8 starts in 2026, Odeyinbo struggled to string together strong performances and eventually ended with 1 sack and 2 TFLs — disappointing numbers that have led many to write him off. I think that’s a mistake. Odeyingbo had seen steady improvement under the tutelage of Gus Bradley, and found himself under a new defensive scheme for the first time in his career in 2025. When revisiting tape, I saw a player that frequently looked indecisive — which often led to him playing slower. I see an extra year under Allen, an offseason of good health, and more “motivation” as being key to a turnaround for Dayo. Will he ever be a 10 sack player? Unlikely. But to write him off would be a mistake. I think there is a very good chance of him tallying 6+ sacks and being a powerful counterpunch to Austin Booker’s speed/length. In total — I suppose my primary gripe is that we simply cannot write off two players after one season on a team and defense that feature a lot of new. I’ll eat my words if we continue to see the same issues 4-5 games into 2026. But until then, let’s give these two a chance to change the narrative. Now it’s your turn! Which offseason Bears narrative is most tired? Sound off in the comments!

title: From starters through depth, are you confident in the Chicago Bears’ offensive line?
summary: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bears fans and fans across the country. Heading into the offseason, three-fifths of the Chicago Bears’ offensive line were locked in. Left guard Joe Thuney, a 2025 Pro Bowler, All-Pro, and winner of […]
full_text: Jul 31, 2026; Lake Forest, IL, USA; Chicago Bears players practice during Training Camp at Halas Hall. Mandatory Credit: Kamil Krzaczynski-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bears fans and fans across the country. Heading into the offseason, three-fifths of the Chicago Bears’ offensive line were locked in. Left guard Joe Thuney, a 2025 Pro Bowler, All-Pro, and winner of the Protecter of the Year award, was recently named the best guard in the NFL by Pro Football Focus . Right tackle Darnell Wright is one of the best young tackles in the game and is coming off a second-team All-Pro nod. And right guard Jonah Jackson, a former Pro Bowler, bounced back in a huge way as he was reunited with Ben Johnson and was just named PFF’s 18th-best guard in the league. We’re now a week into training camp, and Chicago’s starting five is coming into focus. With Drew Dalamn retiring, center was up in the air, and after trading for Garrett Bradbury and drafting Logan Jones, it seemed like a camp battle was set up, but recent comments from Ben Johnson could allude to the battle being settled. On Saturday, tight end Cole Kmet said the transition from Dalman to Bradbury has been “flawless,” and Johnson was asked his take on that earlier today. “Yeah, he’s extremely impressive,” Johnson said . “He’s super smart. H’s played high-level football in a couple of places now, and he’s brought that here. I think what stands out the most is he’s got an elite level of communication. He is loud. He is decisive. He does a great job with seeing the defense… We’re cooking right now with him out there, so, really pleased.” But while Bradbury has received all the number one reps, left tackle has had a bit of a rotation during training camp. Braxton Jones got just about all the first-string left tackle reps in the offseason, but last week, the Bears gave Kiran Amegadjie and Jedrick Wills Jr. each a day with the ones. Jones was back with the starters today, but with pads finally on this week, I would not be surprised to see Amegadjie and Wills get some more work with the starting offense. Ben Johnson discussed what he wants to see from his left tackles this week. “It’s consistency for me,” he said. “We’re judging the ability to block these defensive ends one-on-one. And the ability to cut off on the backside of our wide zone scheme is huge for us. I think each one of those guys is probably a little bit stronger in certain areas than the other guy. And I think when we look at it, it’s who’s the most consistent player that we feel like is going to help us on a weekly basis.” Johnson was asked about Wills, who sat out last season, and he said that Wills has had a “good start” to camp. “Like I said, Braxton’s been great,” Ben continued. “Jed’s firmly in the mix. Kiran got some reps with the ones. I think Theo’s [Benedet] worth mentioning as well. I mean, I think we got a really good group of guys that continue to ascend and get better, so hopefully it’s a really difficult decision for us.” The Bears open their preseason slate on August 15 against the Cleveland Browns, and while Johnson was noncommittal on playing starters, those three preseason games and two joint practices will be a factor in who wins the left tackle job. title: Cash, Stash, or Slash: Rome Odunze
summary: As we continue our series of Cash, Stash, or Slash, we are going to look at Rome Odunze next, who I think you could argue is one of the most fascinating cases on the team. Odunze has had two good seasons at this point of his career, but there have been factors keeping him from […]
full_text: LAKE FOREST, ILLINOIS - JULY 29: Rome Odunze #15 of the Chicago Bears looks on during Chicago Bears Training Camp at Halas Hall on July 29, 2026 in Lake Forest, Illinois. (Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images As we continue our series of Cash, Stash, or Slash, we are going to look at Rome Odunze next, who I think you could argue is one of the most fascinating cases on the team. Odunze has had two good seasons at this point of his career, but there have been factors keeping him from reaching the heights that the Bears fans thought he could reach when they drafted him in the top ten of the 210 NFL Draft. With Odunze, we know Slash isn’t one of the options to consider, but is this a man that the Bears should hammer down next offseason and make sure he’s locked into a contract? Let’s take a look at Odunze. Rome Odunze: Stash I think “wait and see” is a key aspect here for Odunze due to so many factors. Let’s look at all of them. One, if we are being honest, he hasn’t been as good as we all hoped. That doesn’t mean he’s been bad; he’s been a solid WR and one that Caleb Williams looks to often, but he hasn’t been an elite catcher of the football that can change a game. That’s what the Bears drafted, and he hasn’t been that. The injuries are also something to keep in mind. I know Odunze tried to clarify the situation with his foot and that it’s not some chronic disaster, but it did cost him 5 games last year, and he was compromised in other games he played. Will this be a lingering problem for him or will it be completely behind him? The Bears definitely would like to see a clean, fairly healthy season from Odunze. Three, how good does Luther Burden look this year? If Burden breaks out like many people think he could be, if he’s a true WR1 and an elite player, that’s going to impact how you want to treat Odunze moving forward. If Burden is inconsistent and shows flashes but doesn’t put it all together, that’s going to make Odunze more valuable to the franchise. Right now, there are simply too many factors to consider before the Bears can make a decision on what to do with Odunze. If Odunze breaks out and has a massive season with 1500 yards receiving and 15 touchdowns, then yes, sure, pay him next year and be excited he’s become the player you thought he could be. There are plenty of NFL analytic nerds that say that all the numbers are there for Odunze to break out and take several steps forward in 2026. Personally, I don’t see it. I think Odunze is a good player. I think Odunze is going to settle in as an excellent WR2, but I just don’t know if he has shown that he is going to step into that WR1 role. As always, I hope I’m wrong. I hope Odunze proves that he’s an elite receiver. I think he’s good to very good and makes him a great WR2 for the Bears or another team if the Bears do move on down the road. If I’m right and Odunze has another good season, but it isn’t an elite season, I think he’s still a “stash” a year from now. If I’m the Bears, and Odunze has a good year, I would pick up the 5th year option next year and let the 2027 season play out as well, and then you can decide if you want ot extend Odunze after the 2027 season before he heads into his 5th year in Chicago. A fifth-year option for Odunze in Chicago should fall somewhere between $18 and $24 million for that season. Right now, the range that Odunze could get paid is massive. If he breaks out and becomes an elite receiver, the value of his contract is going to be at least $30 million a year, if not $35 million. If Odunze continues to look like the solid, but not spectacular receiver he has looked like the first two seasons of his career and the Bears do want to keep him around as part of the team, Odunze’s salary should be somewhere between $15 and $20 million a year. That’s a $20 million gap in average yearly salary depending on how Odunze plays. With that kind of difference, I would like to have two more years of data before I decide what kind of contract to offer him. It’s also possible that if you wait two more seasons, Burden and Colston Loveland become an incredible duo and maybe even Jahdae Walker or Savion Thomas become reliable targets where Odunze becomes expendable. There are so many factors surrounding Odunze that trying to figure out his contract at this point is nearly impossible. Don’t just wait one season; wait two seasons. Get as much data on this offense with Burden, Loveland, Odunze, and the others, and figure out who the key pieces are that have to be around for years to come. Odunze is the most clear “Stash” on the team right now.

(Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images ESPN’s Adam Schefter is reporting that the knee injury that Chicago Bears safety Coby Bryant sustained today at practice would keep him sidelined for about eight to ten weeks with no surgery required. Schefter reports that Bryant hyperextended his knee, has a bone bruise, and a small fracture. All things considered, things could have been much worse, so I’m chalking this one up as good news for the Bears’ defense. With Bryant out and Elijah Hicks on the PUP list, it’ll likely be Cam Lewis getting first-string reps alongside rookie safety Dillon Thieneman. Lewis signed a free agent deal this March with Chicago after playing with the Buffalo Bills since 2019. He’s appeared in 76 games with 14 starts in his career, with reps at both safety and nickel. Other safeties on the roster are Gervarrius Owens, Anthony Johnson Jr., and Skyler Thomas. Owens spent last year on the Bears’ practice squad, and he has 5 games under his belt from 2023 to 2024 with just 1 snap on defense. Johnson missed the 2025 season due to injury, but in 2023 and 2024, he played in 21 total games with 4 starts (all in’ 23). Thomas is a 2026 UDFA from Oregon State. title: Cincinnati Bengals roster 2026: Dax Hill, Jonathan Allen, Connor Lew are Hidden Gems
summary: It was not too long ago that the Cincinnati Bengals were right up top in the AFC pecking order. In 2021 and 2022, they got as close as you can get to winning a Super Bowl without actually winning it. There was the 23-20 loss to the Los Angeles Rams in Super Bowl LVI at […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals cornerback Dax Hill (23) catches a pass during the Cincinnati Bengals Training Camp 2026 at Kettering Practice Field in Cincinnati on Thursday, July 30, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co It was not too long ago that the Cincinnati Bengals were right up top in the AFC pecking order. In 2021 and 2022, they got as close as you can get to winning a Super Bowl without actually winning it. There was the 23-20 loss to the Los Angeles Rams in Super Bowl LVI at the end of the 2021 season and the 23-20 loss to the Kansas City Chiefs in the 2022 AFC Championship game. Of course, after those two 23-20 games in a span of less than a year, things started to come apart. Joe Burrow’s health became more of a concern in 2023 and 2025, and when Burrow played at a thermonuclear level in 2024, he did so with a Lou Anarumo defense that ranked 25th in points allowed and 27th in DVOA . Last season, Burrow played in just eight games, and in the first half of the season, Al Golden’s defense was one of the worst… like, ever. According to FTN’s data, Cincinnati’s defensive DVOA of 30.1% in Weeks 1-9 was the worst in the history of the metric, which currently goes back to 1977. Running back Chase Brown and receiver Ja’Marr Chase were yowling about said defense in October , and for good reason. Then, it all turned around. From Week 10 through the end of the season, the Bengals improved their Defensive DVOA to -2.2% (Defensive DVOA is better when it’s negative), up from 32nd to 13th. And though the sins of the season’s first half would not be erased by that improvement — the 2025 Bengals finished 30th in Defensive DVOA behind only the Dallas Cowboys and the New York Jets — there was enough on the bone for management to spend in both draft capital and actual dollars to improve things on that side of the ball. Hence, the trade for ex-New York Giants game-wrecker Dexter Lawrence, as well as the signings of former Seattle Seahawks edge-rusher Boye Mafe, veteran defensive lineman Jonathan Allen, former Kansas City Chiefs safety Bryan Cook, and veteran defensive back Kyle Dugger. Adding Texas A&M edge-rusher Cashius Howell and Washington cornerback Tacario Davis in the second and third rounds of the 2026 draft should provide even more enforcement potential. So, here’s what the plan for the Bengals this season seems to be: Bank on a healthy Joe Burrow and all of his weapons, and give the defense enough juice to be league average or better after that historical awfulness. It worked not too long ago, and it could work again. For that to happen, of course, the Bengals will need the best possible performance from everybody on the roster. To that end, I’ve identified three Hidden Gems for the 2026 team — one underrated veteran, one underrated free agent, and one underrated draft pick. Here are the Hidden Gems for your 2026 Cincinnati Bengals. Underrated veteran: DB Dax Hill A primary reason for the aforementioned defensive improvement in the second half of the 2025 season was the decision to move Dax Hill outside from the slot more often. Since the Bengals took the Michigan alum with the 31st overall pick in the 2022 draft, Hill has alternated between the two spots, with varying degrees of distinction. 2024 was a complicated season for Hill: he missed all but the first five games with a knee injury, but he came back strong, especially when the team needed someone to bookend the estimable DJ Turner II. From Weeks 1-11 last season, Hill took just 20% of his 666 ( Iron Maiden riff here ) snaps outside; the rest of the time, he was either a slot defender or a box guy. But starting in Week 12 against the New England Patriots, Hill’s outside reps increased exponentially. 76% of his 366 reps in that time period came on the outside, and when targeted there, Hill allowed 12 catches on 19 targets for 6.7 yards per catch, no touchdowns, no interceptions, four pass breakups, and an opponent passer rating of 76.2. Most importantly. Hill’s outside deployment told opponents that they couldn’t just avoid Turner and get away with THAT all day long. If you blinked or looked away for a second, you probably missed the @Bengals ' massive uptick in defensive efficiency in the second half of the 2025 season. Moving Dax Hill from slot to outside had a lot to do with it. pic.twitter.com/kMtGnSQuiV — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) July 30, 2026 After the season, the Bengals named Hill their winner of the NFL’s Ed Block Courage Award , which credits players who show “professionalism, great strength and dedication” in the face of adversity. “I want to thank the entire organization and my teammates for thinking highly of me in coming back from my injury,” Hill said. “Representing the team well, coming back, and making an impact was my big focus. I thank everybody for being in my corner, and I’m happy being back with the guys.” “There is not a more deserving player than Dax Hill for the Ed Block Courage Award,” said Bengals Director of Sports Medicine/Head Athletic Trainer Matt Summers. “Dax is a very consistent ‘everyday’ guy. His unwavering work ethic and trust in the rehab plan allowed him to return to the field in 2025 without hesitation. Dax is also very gracious with the time he commits to community service, and his humility further reflects the values he poses for his teammates to vote him as this year’s recipient.” If Hill’s on-field community service continues to be the ability to shut receivers down as that outside guy, that’s one more box for the team to check off as they fight for relevance again. Underrated free agent: IDL Jonathan Allen Dexter Lawrence was obviously the big move the Bengals made this offseason, but it wasn’t the only contract signed to bolster the defensive line. Getting nine-year veteran Jonathan Allen on a two-year, $25 million contract with $7.5 million guaranteed should provide some sneaky dividends. Last season in Brian Flores’ crazy-quilt defense for the Minnesota Vikings, Allen had four sacks, 34 pressures, 44 solo tackles, 34 stops, and seven tackles for loss. That was Allen’s first season in Minnesota after eight with the Washington (YOUR NAME HERE) franchise, which selected him with the 17th overall pick in the 2017 draft out of Alabama. At his peak, Allen lived up to all that draft capital spent, and while he may not be the pressure machine he was in 2021 and 2022, he’s not that far off. At 6’3” and 300 pounds, he brings all the movement skills and a surprising amount of power to displace double teams for his size. As long as Sexy Dexy is on the field, Allen won’t see as many doubles as he did in 2025 — 190— and 17 of his 34 pressures came when he had more than one guy on him. So, there could be a bump in the numbers for the veteran. And the run defense is already *chef’s kiss.* Jonathan Allen spending time in yo' backfield. Moving Allen around with Sexy Dexy as the epicenter should be fun. @Bengals pic.twitter.com/7rh2meKKGk — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) July 30, 2026 Allen is certainly happy about the prospects for that interior line. “I don’t think there’s ever been a guy to play like Dexter,” Allen said in June. “Dexter is a unique guy, and I’m just excited for the opportunity. “It’s funny. After I left Minnesota (last season), I just sat down and had to really think what I wanted. I’d be lying if I said I didn’t want to come up here and put up great numbers. That proves your worth and why they brought you in. But, honestly, I just want to play meaningful football in December, and I want to help the team any way I can. I believe if I do that, the numbers will come. “At this point in my career, it’s all about winning, man.” It’s been a while since anybody voiced that reason for signing with the Bengals, but here we are, and it could happen more quickly with Allen’s contributions. Underrated draft pick: Center Connor Lew You obviously don’t know how NFL teams feel about your draft binkies until one actually selects one of them. In the case of…

title: Tee Higgins and Dexter Lawrence snubbed from NFL Top 100 Players ranking
summary: When I was in middle school and high school, my springs and summers were spent anticipating the weekly episodes of the NFL Top 100 Players going into the upcoming season. Ten players per week were revealed on NFL Network, and there were reaction shows right after each episode. The list was voted exclusively by the […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - JULY 29: Tee Higgins #5 of the Cincinnati Bengals performs during the Cincinnati Bengals Training Camp at Kettering Health Practice Fields on July 29, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) | Getty Images When I was in middle school and high school, my springs and summers were spent anticipating the weekly episodes of the NFL Top 100 Players going into the upcoming season. Ten players per week were revealed on NFL Network, and there were reaction shows right after each episode. The list was voted exclusively by the players, and they were usually spot on with the rankings every year. But this year, the list is drawing major criticism on Twitter. Lamar Jackson is ranked No. 69. Okay, yes, Jackson missed four games last year and wasn’t as dynamic as he was in 2023 or 2024, but the players are saying there are 68 players better than Jackson? Going into this season, they think there are nearly 70 players better than two-time NFL MVP Lamar Jackson? Look, availability is the best ability, and players do pay attention to production. A player’s whole career, though, should be taken into account when compiling this annual list. From a Bengals’ perspective, Joe Burrow checked in at No. 44 last week. So, there are 43 players better than Joe Burrow? Yeah, sure. But the ridiculousness doesn’t stop there. Tee Higgins and Dexter Lawrence didn’t even make the list. They were ranked just outside the top 100, as revealed early this week. Players who just missed the NFL Top 100… 110: Tyler Warren 109: Tee Higgins 108: Brian Branch 107: Devon Witherspoon 106: Jameson Williams 105: Dexter Lawrence 104: Chris Lindstrom 103: CJ Stroud 102: Lane Johnson 101: Mike Evans pic.twitter.com/bjfSYLDg0V — NFL (@NFL) August 3, 2026 Hold on… so the players who voted think there are 100 players better than BOTH Higgins and Lawrence? Humor me, a little bit. Tee Higgins absolutely justified the Bengals paying him with a terrific 2025 season. All he did, playing with three different starting quarterbacks, was score 11 receiving touchdowns on 59 receptions for 846 yards. Lawrence may have only had a half-sack last season. But as we have talked about at length this offseason, a change of scenery could be exactly what he needs to get back to his beast-like production from the middle of the defensive line. Let’s not forget he had nine sacks in 2024, and that was only in 12 games. Look, players and coaches know the NFL game better than anybody. That’s why the NFL Top 100 Players list used to matter significantly. It was a refreshing concept to have the players be the only ones voting. But this year, the list is coming into serious question and is being heavily criticized. For the players who voted, thinking there are 100 better players than Tee Higgins and Dexter Lawrence is lunacy. And 43 better players than Joe Burrow? Come on.

title: Bengals training camp Day 6 News and discussion
summary: The news from Monday’s training camp session was once again about the Cincinnati Bengals’ defense making plays. After an offseason of additions, this is music to fan’s ears. As the pads came on, the impact of free agent signing Jonathan Allen and the blockbuster trade for Dexter Lawrence II was felt all over the practice […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - JULY 29: Joe Burrow #9 of the Cincinnati Bengals performs during the Cincinnati Bengals Training Camp at Kettering Health Practice Fields on July 29, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) | Getty Images The news from Monday’s training camp session was once again about the Cincinnati Bengals’ defense making plays. After an offseason of additions, this is music to fan’s ears. As the pads came on, the impact of free agent signing Jonathan Allen and the blockbuster trade for Dexter Lawrence II was felt all over the practice fields outside of Paycor Stadium. While the performance of the defense has been applauded, some are wondering if concern for the offense is warranted. Reports state that Zac Taylor’s offense has been operating from under center more than we’ve seen in any training camp, but the results seem mixed. While the run game had success Monday, the defense appeared to win more of the passing situations. We’re in early August, so it isn’t time to panic about the offense, but coming out of training camp with confidence and momentum could do wonders for a defense that ranked at or near the bottom of the NFL in 2025. Bengals News Dexter Lawrence making instant impact at Bengals camp: ‘Honestly, he’s been terrorizing practice’ “A maligned Bengals defense loaded up on offseason upgrades to the tune of a practice group that offensive players say is more intense and competitive than Cincinnati’s defense flashed last training camp.“ Could one player make that big of a difference on a defense? It appears that it could. Add that to the other offseason additions and it is easy to see why the offense can see a difference in the 2026 defense as training camp ramps up. Joe Burrow, Bengals find camaraderie on unusual battlefield “Cincinnati’s first week of training camp has featured a few spirited practices, a noted practice scuffle and an intense edge from a team sick of missing the playoffs. But as it has looked to put the rest of the AFC North in check in 2026, the first days of the season have also featured a chessboard.“ Plenty of work takes place on the field during training camp, but connections are made in the locker room just as much, if not more. Players are spending tons of time with one another and finding ways to connect beyond the game are crucial. This year, the thing that is bringing them together appears to be a chessboard. Training Camp Report | A Dax Hill Vignette As Bengals Put On The Pads “I feel like we can play a lot faster, be more confident and play faster knowing the ball has to come out. Simple as that,” Monday was reportedly a great day for Dax Hill. With all the talk about DJ Turner II’s contract, Hill is entering a contract year as well. Hill has battled injuries and played several different positions in his time in Cincinnati, but that experience and versatility were on full display for the first day in pads. Bengals experience false alarm in first padded practice of training camp, Joe Burrow and the offense struggle in specific area “The 25 year-old is eligible for a big-time payday before the regular season begins, which is when Cincinnati traditionally finalize its biggest internal contracts. He’s been completely locked in despite the potential distraction and it’s great to see him push through what appeared to be a cramp.” A scare at training camp to say the least. For DJ Turner II, it comes while contract negotiations are presumably going on behind the scenes. Thankfully, Hill was able to get back on the field quickly. Meanwhile, the Bengals’ offense struggled in an area it would really benefit them to succeed at.

Young spoke with the media after practice. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images Training camp is all about evaluation for teams, especially the Cleveland Browns, who are trying to decide who their starting quarterback will be . Whether it is underrated players , impressive NFL draft picks , or the bottom of the roster, Browns GM Andrew Berry and HC Todd Monken have a lot of people to keep their eyes on. Interestingly, Monken noted that he isn’t fully evaluating the quarterbacks right now due to the install process the team is going through . Other players, on the other hand, are having decisions made after evaluation. On Monday, Cleveland waived UDFA RB TJ Harden to make room for DT Travis Bell . On Tuesday, the Browns waived OT Jack Conley to make room for signing former Seattle Seahawks CB Tyler Hall . An undrafted free agent in 2020, Hall has played for four teams, including one game last season for the Super Bowl champions. With the Las Vegas Raiders, Hall had his most playing time in 2022 and 2023 when he combined to play 18 games with six starts. All but six of his defensive snaps came during those two seasons, while he has also contributed 253 snaps on special teams. Conley was an undrafted free agent in 2025 and spent time on three practice squads, including the Browns, last season, but did not see any regular-season action.

title: Browns roster 2026: Dillon Gabriel, Quincy Williams, Emmanuel McNeil-Warren are underrated
summary: Okay, so. We don’t need to torture avid Cleveland Browns fans with the quarterback jokes, because they’ve all been told. We don’t need to bag on Deshaun Watson or Jimmy Haslam, as much as those two individuals have presented legit reasons for mockery and scorn. And we don’t really need to go over all the […]
full_text: Okay, so. We don’t need to torture avid Cleveland Browns fans with the quarterback jokes , because they’ve all been told. We don’t need to bag on Deshaun Watson or Jimmy Haslam, as much as those two individuals have presented legit reasons for mockery and scorn. And we don’t really need to go over all the changes that happened with the coaching staff per se — everyone visiting this fine site likely already knows that Kevin Stefanski was replaced by Todd Monken as head coach and offensive shot-caller, while Jim Schwartz was replaced by Mike Rutenberg as the man in charge of the defense. Instead, let’s dive into reasons for optimism that have very little to do with the quarterback thing because we’ll go there in a minute. The 2026 Browns can benefit from EVP/general manager Andrew Berry’s recent personnel moves, including a 2025 draft that appears to be long-term great. The defense under Schwartz was generally anywhere from pretty good to really good, and outside of Myles Garrett, most of the key pieces are returning. It’s not as if Jared Verse, who came to Cleveland in the Garrett trade, is chopped liver, either — he’s just not a lead-pipe first-ballot Hall of Famer lock like No. 95. At least not yet. The 2026 draft brought two estimable weapons in receivers KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston, and the offensive line underwent a neat transformation this offseason with first-round tackle Spencer Fano and free agents Zion Johnson, Elgton Jenkins, and Tytus Howard. 2025 Hidden Gem Teven Jenkins announced his presence with authority last season, so the front five should be very solid over time. Rookie running back Quinshon Judkins was an absolute boss when healthy. Basically, the 2026 Browns appear to be one of those teams that are just a quarterback away from contention. Which is a bit like saying that you’re one Eddie Van Halen away from being Van Halen, but one does the best one can with what one has. Wherever the Browns are headed this season, they’ll need the best possible from everyone on the roster — not just the big names. To that end, I’ve identified three Hidden Gems — one underrated veteran, one underrated free agent, and one underrated draft pick. And I’m sure the underrated veteran won’t inspire some agita in the comments. All I ask is that you hear me out on this one. Underrated veteran: QB Dillon Gabriel The Browns should not expect top-tier quarterback play in the 2026 season. We’re pretty sure about that. Once you’ve lowered the bar accordingly in that regard, what’s the next most crucial thing for the game’s most important position? For the Browns, situational consistency could be it. And that’s why Dillon Gabriel could be the team’s best option this season . You can always share your Browns-related thoughts, as JohnW81 did, in DBN’s Feed by clicking here! It started in 2024, when Gabriel was Bo Nix’s replacement at Oregon. Overall in that season, Gabriel completed 326 of 451 passes for 3,854 yards, 30 touchdowns, six interceptions, and a passer rating of 114.6. Good numbers, but it’s how Gabriel got to those numbers that impressed me. When under pressure: 56 of 104 for 892 yards, eight touchdowns, one interception, and a passer rating of 104.3. When blitzed: 103 of 142 for 1,286 yards, 15 touchdowns, one interception, and a passer rating of 132.5. On passes of 20+ air yards: 27 of 49 for 960 yards, eight touchdowns, one interception, and a passer rating of 131.9. Throwing from the pocket: 275 of 361 for 3,137 yards, 22 touchdowns, three interceptions, and a passer rating of 118.6. Throwing outside the pocket: 51 of 86 for 720 yards, eight touchdowns, three interceptions, and a passer rating of 102.9. Gabriel had to wait for his shots with the Browns in 2025, but when he got them, he did deliver. Overall, he completed 110 of 185 passes for 937 yards, seven touchdowns, two interceptions, and a passer rating of 80.8. Again, it was how Gabriel got to those numbers that stood out in a quarterback room that couldn’t get out of its own way most of the time. When under pressure: 32 of 63 for 320 yards, four touchdowns, one interception, and a passer rating of 80.1. When blitzed: 37 of 63 for 313 yards, two touchdowns, one interception, and a passer rating of 75.7. On passes of 20+ air yards: 2 of 8 for 44 yards, one touchdown, one interception, and a passer rating of 50.0 (okay, this needs some improvement). Throwing from the pocket: 97 of 157 for 767 yards, six touchdowns, one interception, and a passer rating of 84.0. Throwing outside the pocket: 13 of 28 for 170 yards, one touchdown, one interception, and a passer rating of 63.1. Does this bring to mind Tua Tagovailoa as a point guard-style quarterback who’s pretty good at distributing the ball all over the place, as long as you don’t ask him to scald defenses with deep balls, and rely too much on functional mobility? Before you laugh at any Tua comps, think about how much Tagovailoa at his best would have presented a marked improvement over what Shedeur Sanders or Joe Flacco did with the Browns last season, and certainly what Deshaun Watson would have forced us to watch had he been healthy. It’s not that Dillon Gabriel is the guy to break the Browns’ ridiculous quarterback curse. For the 2026 season, that’s not the point. The point is that if you ask Gabriel to limit his deeper shots to the intermediate level (on throws of 10-19 yards last season, he completed 19 of 44 for 305 yards, four touchdowns, no interceptions, and a passer rating of 97.3), and let him cook under center ( where he did see a relatively nice uptick in EPA/Play )… well, maybe the Browns could make enough of that to avoid stranding their defense again, and actually win some ballgames in successive order. explain to my why and how dillon gabriel isn't the browns' best quarterback yes, i know the bar is buried underground pic.twitter.com/1iu6Rvn41g — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) August 1, 2026 Underrated free agent: LB Quincy Williams New coaches love to bring players with whom they’re familiar to their new stops, and new Browns defensive coordinator Mike Rutenberg happily brought linebacker Quincy Williams to Cleveland once he had signed on as Jim Schwartz’s replacement. Williams, the brother of former New York Jets and current Dallas Cowboys interior defensive lineman Quinnen Williams, was selected in the third round of the 2019 draft by the Jacksonville Jaguars out of Murray State, and Rutenberg was the Jags’ assistant linebackers coach at the time. When Rutenberg became the Jets’ linebackers coach in 2021, he brought Williams onto the roster after Williams failed to make final cuts with Jacksonville in August of that year. This reunion should not come as a surprise. “That’s my dog. He’s like my brother,” Williams said of Rutenberg once Williams had signed his two-year, $13 million contract with $9.5 million guaranteed. “First thing before we talk about football, the biggest thing is Rudy cares about the heart. What I do off the field affects what I do on the field. So, he wanted to tackle both things as far as what I do on the field, so I can show up as myself — show up as this personality always smiling as me, show up every single day at work like that. So, he cares about that a lot. And then on the field, as long as we take care off the field, on the field should be easy. He taught me every single thing I know as far as the linebacker positions in the league. He was with me the two teams I’ve been on, so we have a good relationship.” Williams has never been what you would call a star in coverage, but when it comes to facing forward, blowing up run fits, and going after the quarterback, he’s got it all on point. Last season for a Jets defense that was generally quite abysmal, Williams racked up four sacks, 12 pressures, eight tackles for loss, 61 solo tackles, and 42 stops. For a Browns defense that will be looking to place pressure players around Jared Verse as it once tried to do for Myles Garrett, Williams’ blitz…

There is more hope connected to Sanders from the 50 coaches and executives, but he is also ranked at the bottom of the list of 35 quarterbacks. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images Is the above comment about Cleveland Browns QB Shedeur Sanders a strong one to title this piece? Of course it is. Is it accurate? At least it is what one defensive coordinator believes. The Browns QB competition is off and running. All we know, according to HC Todd Monken, is that a lot of things still have to be installed in Week 2’s schedule and QB Dillon Gabriel has earned more reps . Day 5 was a lot like the previous days at Cleveland’s training camp , with a few exciting plays and a lot of concern about the quarterback play . From the outside looking in, the Browns quarterback room does not have a lot of believers. In Mike Sando’s annual QB tiers article , with 50 executives and coaches ranking 35 veteran quarterbacks, Deshaun Watson was ranked 31st, with Sanders a few slots behind at 35th, last overall. Both were in the lowest tier of the rankings. The comment that jumped out about Watson was about as negative as the one on Sanders that we titled this piece with: “I don’t think he can come back,” an offensive coach said. “You do not all of a sudden get drive and desire and processing skills. He showed he had none of that with what he put on film. He’s a 5 (lowest tier ranking) at this point.” Important to note that one voter believes so much in Monken that he put Watson in Tier 2, at least that is the assumption Sando noted. The Sanders write-up is a bit longer for NY Times subscribers, but is led by the above quote from a defensive coordinator. It wasn’t all negative, however, as there are notes of hope: “If Shedeur has really invested in himself to be a professional quarterback, studying the playbook and knowing his assignments and being able to get the offense in and out of the huddle at an efficient clip, which he could not do last year, then there might be some upside,” the voter said. With one head coach actually adding praise, not just hope: “I thought he was all right, better than expected,” this coach said. “They did a good job with him of making the game simple. And I thought Shedeur played with a chip on his shoulder.” In the end, the rankings are about what the quarterbacks have done. Now, under Monken with a new offensive system, line, and set of weapons, Watson and Sanders have a chance to change the narrative about their talents. If not, 17 weeks of good sleep are coming for different defensive coordinators. What do you think about the quotes related to Watson and Sanders? Do you think they are fair or go over the top? title: Browns: Stadium updates are a bit light on substance
summary: The Cleveland Browns entered the second week of training camp by enjoying their first padded practice of the summer. So far, camp has included the first injury scare of the summer, a big-name free agent passing on a Cleveland reunion, and the annual quarterback battle that is not exactly inspiring anyone involved.  While head coach […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - DECEMBER 15: Cleveland Browns mascot Chomps performs prior to a game against the Kansas City Chiefs at Huntington Bank Field on December 15, 2024 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images The Cleveland Browns entered the second week of training camp by enjoying their first padded practice of the summer. So far, camp has included the first injury scare of the summer , a big-name free agent passing on a Cleveland reunion , and the annual quarterback battle that is not exactly inspiring anyone involved . While head coach Todd Monken and the coaching staff work to build the roster for 2026, the business side of the organization is busy building the team’s new stadium in the Cleveland suburb of Brook Park. Things have been mostly quiet in recent weeks on the stadium front, outside of the occasional nonsensical question about who the quarterback will be when the facility opens in 2029. But two items have recently come out that are of particular interest. The first is a report from Front Office Sports that, for the first time in franchise history, the Browns are expected to play their home games on an artificial turf field rather than grass. If that turns out to be true, 17 of the league’s 32 teams will be playing on artificial turf: The news comes as the long-simmering grass vs. turf debate is as active as ever thanks to the 2026 World Cup, which saw eight NFL teams temporarily replace artificial turf playing surfaces with natural grass to comply with FIFA’s requirements. The NFL Players Association used the tournament as an opportunity to advocate for more grass usage across the league. Its efforts included a coordinated social media campaign, dubbed #WorthTheCost, timed to the World Cup Final; alongside the union itself, dozens of players shared the hashtag across platforms to express their preference for grass fields. The Browns new stadium will have the “ability to accommodate grass,” … but that will likely only happen if and when the venue hosts soccer matches. Except the Browns haven’t actually announced a decision yet on the playing surface of the new stadium. Turns out the story from Front Office Sports is based on a standard Pro Football Talk post that doesn’t really say anything substantial or new. And the PFT report appears to be based on a May 5 article from cleveland.com that cites an unnamed club spokesperson who says artificial turf is “very likely.” Got all that? Good, let’s move on. The second item involves just how much fans will pay for the privilege of watching the Browns in Brook Park. During last week’s media session at training camp, owner Jimmy Haslam was asked about the possibility of fans experiencing “sticker shock” over the cost of Personal Seat Licenses, but Haslam said the pricing structure is still a work in progress : “I’m not sure who said that. We actually had a meeting on it today, and I can unequivocally say this: we have made no decisions on pricing for PSLs or tickets. We have a lot of work to do. I can tell you this — probably our number one overarching goal is to have as many affordable tickets as we can, because we’ve got great fans and they deserve it.” So what have we learned today? The Brook Park stadium might have artificial turf for football games and might have the “ability to accommodate grass,” unless it does not. In which case, the Browns will be playing indoors but on natural grass. There has been no decision made on how much tickets will be to watch the Browns, but the “goal” is to make sure an unknown will be affordable. We now return you to the training camp quarterback battle, already in progress.

title: Cowboys safety group making a name for itself beyond Caleb Downs
summary: Keeping with the theme of 2026 Dallas Cowboys training camp having a different look and feel to it from the start, we are back to discuss players that are starting to string together early consistency – now including the team’s first padded practice that happened on Monday. Yesterday, we mentioned the importance of using multiple […]
full_text: OXNARD, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 14: Julius Wood #33 of the Dallas Cowboys defends during a joint practice against the Los Angeles Rams at River Ridge Playing Fields on August 14, 2024 in Oxnard, California. (Photo by Ric Tapia/Getty Images) | Getty Images Keeping with the theme of 2026 Dallas Cowboys training camp having a different look and feel to it from the start, we are back to discuss players that are starting to string together early consistency – now including the team’s first padded practice that happened on Monday. Yesterday, we mentioned the importance of using multiple reps and days of practice trending in the right direction for a player to truly feel good about their projection. With only unpadded practices through this point, the consistency tag was handed to two skill position players and QB Dak Prescott maestro-ing it all. Christian Parker’s defense seem to have taken that personally, as it took just one padded practice for them to start flipping the narrative strongly in their favor. You’ve likely already seen by now how the Cowboys cornerbacks stole the show at Monday’s more physical practice . Cobie Durant had an interception, Shavon Revel strung together more flash plays in coverage, and DaRon Bland got in on the action as well. The cornerback versus wide receiver battles have taken up alot of the attention from Cowboys camp as a whole, and allowed other important things to go under the radar. One such thing that we are here to talk about now, which does tie into cornerback and secondary play at large, is the play the Cowboys are getting at safety. The Cowboys depth chart at safety shows a side to Parker’s coaching excellence that hasn’t been discussed as much as his eye for player acquisition specific to the scheme, and how the front office has supported that, or the way he’s utilizing the current rookie class. The arrow-pointing-up reports about safeties Malik Hooker, Markquese Bell, even Julius Wood and Alijah Clark, and, of course, even through the most recent practice, 11th overall pick Caleb Downs . Throw in the fact that P.J. Locke and Jalen Thompson are expected to see plenty of snaps once the regular season begins, and this is a very interesting, versatile safety group budding for the Cowboys. The update on Wood came from Nick Eatman of the team’s official website , and Clark flashed in a similar way as well: Bringin’ the Wood – On the first day of pads, you wouldn’t expect anything other than someone named “Julius Wood” to have a physical practice. Just an hour before, his head coach Brian Schottenheimer mentioned Wood as being active and making the safety position rather deep. And then in practice, he had several big pops, jarring the ball loose on a pass during the team drills and he also wasn’t afraid to come up in run support. Also, Caleb Downs had a few run stops as well. But Wood is a guy trying to get noticed – and he did that Monday. – (Nick Eatman) Cowboys S Alijah Clark with a nice run stuff pic.twitter.com/7GoFX1aTe9 — Sebastian Sanchez (@Sanchez_Reports) August 3, 2026 Downs was also mentioned for his run support, meaning the Cowboys are starting to have a stacked list of safeties comfortable coming down to defend in the box. Paired with how well the cornerbacks are playing in coverage, and linebackers are being used in disguise as well, and the Cowboys defense is on a whole new level of scheming in an attempt to confuse offenses this season. Safeties are the ultimate chess piece of a defense that can unlock so much of this, and the Cowboys are learning that pretty quickly in Oxnard. One key way to forecast how good a team may or may not be in the NFL for any given season is to look at where they can make the most difference in their play versus the opponent, and how much those things often weigh on the outcome of games. For example, the Cowboys have likely the best duo of wide receivers in the league, with Ryan Flournoy rising as a third option. If this trio continues doing what they’re capable of, and the Cowboys cornerbacks keep their momentum from the start of padded practices going, Dallas will have the potential to build a significant differential in big pass plays generated on offense versus allowed on defense. Dak Prescott has of an offense that returns all of its starters from 2025, as well as the play-calling head coach and offensive coordinator. With Prescott in full command, and the defense not pulling any punches when it comes to throwing the kitchen sink at opponents and embracing all of their depth, this could create the most important difference. We already know Prescott hasn’t needed much help when it comes to outplaying the other quarterbacks in the NFC East, but if the Cowboys defense is ready to regularly stress all of the opposing QBs on their schedule and make Dak the far-and-away better passer in more matchups, the sky will be the limit for this team. Caleb Downs with a great fill in the run game here #Cowboys pic.twitter.com/dk4t96F8nv — Tommy Yarrish (@tommy_yarrish) August 3, 2026 Even if Downs settles into a true nickel role for the majority of his snaps, and the amount of moving around he does settles down at some point in his rookie campaign, the Cowboys are showing they have enough other exciting depth at safety to still be versatile on the back end and give offenses fits. In the competitive nature of this camp so far, look for the Cowboys offense to come out with man-coverage beaters that get after the cornerback group that won the day Monday, but put a spotlight on Dallas’ safeties to disrupt this even more and continue making a name for themselves as a unit.

title: Cowboys defense dominates the day in first padded practice
summary: The Dallas Cowboys have one of the top offenses in the NFL.
