Tyler Guyton seems to be trending upward, and they’ve also seen some positive things from Javonte Williams, Jaydon Blue, […]
full_text: The Dallas Cowboys have one of the top offenses in the NFL. Quarterback Dak Prescott has been wheeling and dealing to his top two targets CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens, plus Ryan Flournoy continues to ascend. Tyler Guyton seems to be trending upward, and they’ve also seen some positive things from Javonte Williams, Jaydon Blue, and Phile Mafah in running game. That was in shorts and helmets. On Monday, the Cowboys put the pads on for the first time, and things got spicy. One thing was clear during practice, and it was that the defensive unit came out on a mission, because they were making plays left and right during team drills. Let’s start with first-round safety Caleb Downs. What else is there to say? He’s quickly showing why he was such a sought-after draft pick back in April. Downs looked like he was shoot out of a cannon as he did a great job with run fits and making plays against the pass. Look for Downs to keep being lined up in the box, in the deep middle of the field, and close the edge. He’s going to be the chess piece of this defense under Christian Parker, and he’s only going to get better. Caleb Downs … WHOA. #Cowboys #trainingcamp pic.twitter.com/XWBdfdJ43F — Patrik [No C] Walker (@VoiceOfTheStar) August 3, 2026 DaRon Bland and Caleb Downs with tight coverage here for the PBU. pic.twitter.com/QvcfgaRiQ1 — Joseph Hoyt (@JoeJHoyt) August 3, 2026 DeMarvion Overshown had to be salivating to get the pads on after another injury-plagued year in 2025. Much like Downs, Overshown was flying around and roaming on the second level on Monday, and he even had the biggest hit of the day on running back Hunter Luepke on a toss play. He even showed his prowess against the pass some, which isn’t surprising as a former safety. The skill set is undeniable when it comes to Overshown, and as long he remains healthy, this will be more of the same. DeMarvion Overshown 👀 pic.twitter.com/drO3CamM7v — Jon Machota (@jonmachota) August 3, 2026 Rookie linebacker Jaishawn Barham had already been turning heads with his play in shorts and helmets during the first several practices. That continued on Monday as he and Overshown held down first-team reps at the linebacker spot. He looked very fluid and comfortable as he filled gaps against the run, and even beat All-Pro Tyler Smith on a rep that would have been a sack in a real game. He is undoubtedly making a huge statement early in camp that he will be on the field quite a bit in 2026. In fact, it could be more than people think. Jaishawn Barham vs Tyler Smith https://t.co/1VPRHBtrwX — Mauricio Rodríguez (@MauNFL) August 3, 2026 Not to be forgotten, the Cowboys’ cornerbacks were the stars of the day . Shavon Revel had some very nice battles against Lamb, and even did a great job jamming him at the line of scrimmage once. Cobie Durant keeps making plays, and he snagged an interception on Prescott in the end zone. DaRon Bland, who is looking to prove he’s still worth the investment the Cowboys have in him, had a solid day as well, which included some very sticky coverage against George Pickens which led to a pass breakup. Also, rookie Devin Moore got a nice pass breakup versus Lamb, and had some words for him after the play. Cobie Durant INT pic.twitter.com/uUbF9wN64M — Jon Machota (@jonmachota) August 3, 2026 Ceedee Lamb Got Jammed Up By Revel Jr #sheeeesh pic.twitter.com/W5D27EekES — JESSE (With No “i”) (@Mr4thAndLong) August 3, 2026 It’ll be interesting to see what transpires on Tuesday in the second padded practice.

title: Here is what happened to last year’s final Cowboys roster cuts
summary: As training camp kicks off for real this week with padded practices, many a player on the Cowboys’ 90-man offseason roster is beginning to wonder what his chances are of making the roster. Realistically, for most of the UDFAs and street free agents brought in during the offseason, just making the practice squad must be […]
full_text: As training camp kicks off for real this week with padded practices, many a player on the Cowboys’ 90-man offseason roster is beginning to wonder what his chances are of making the roster. Realistically, for most of the UDFAs and street free agents brought in during the offseason, just making the practice squad must be considered a success. But even those up to 16 practice squad spots are highly contested. Out of the standard 16 players, at least 10 must be rookies or second-year players, while up to six can be veterans with unlimited accrued experience. And with teams reducing rosters in one fell swoop from 90 to 53 players, there’ll be a lot of players scrambling for jobs. But what happens to the players who don’t get a spot on the practice squad after final cuts? Do they automatically become the proverbial grocery packers at WalMart or Target? Well, not if they made it through camp with the Dallas Cowboys, at least if last year is anything to go by. On August 25 & 26 last year, the Cowboys released 37 players to get to the final 53. Where are those 37 players now? I’m glad you asked. Here’s an overview of all 37 players, showing what happened to each player in 2025 and where he is today: body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table th, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table { border: 1px solid #000 !important; border-collapse: collapse !important; } body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table th { padding: 0px 6px !important; } 2025 final Cowboys roster cuts Name POS Status 2025 Status 2026 Still on Cowboys Roster Justin Barron* LB Cowboys Cowboys Alijah Clark* S Cowboys Cowboys Malik Davis* RB Cowboys Cowboys Princeton Fant* TE Cowboys PS Cowboys Traeshon Holden* WR Cowboys PS Cowboys DeMarvion Overshown (Reserve/PUP) LB Cowboys Cowboys Jonathan Mingo (Reserve/Injured) WR Cowboys Cowboys Shavon Revel (Reserve/NFI) CB Cowboys Cowboys Josh Butler (Reserve/PUP) CB Cowboys Cowboys Tyrus Wheat DE Lions Cowboys Still In NFL Jalen Cropper* WR Cowboys PS Saints Rivaldo Fairweather* TE Cowboys PS Cardinals Earnest Brown* DE Cowboys PS Titans Geron Christian* OT Denver Denver Robert Rochell* CB Panthers Panthers Kemon Hall* CB Titans Buccaneers Buddy Johnson* LB Colts Raiders Saahdiq Charles* OG Panthers PS Panthers Josh Kelly WR Texans PS Texans Nick Broeker OT Bills PS Bills Tommy Akingbesote DT Bills PS Bills Hakeem Adeniji OT Cowboys Ravens Payton Turner (Reserve/Injured) DE Cowboys IR Lions UFL/CFL Israel Mukuamu S Panthers UFL Deuce Vaughn RB Broncos PS UFL Denzel Daxon DE Cardinals PS CFL Tyler Neville TE — UFL Michael Ojemudia CB — UFL Currently out of football Will Grier* QB Cowboys PS Retired C.J. Goodwin ST Cowboys Retired John Stephens TE Cowboys IR Injury settlement Jalen Brooks* WR Cardinals — Troy Pride CB Colts PS — Darius Harris LB Patriots PS — Mike Smith S — — La’el Collins OT — — Christian Matthew CB — — Couple of topline thoughts: 62% of the final cuts (23 of 37) are still on NFL rosters 76% (28/37) are still playing organized football in the NFL, UFL, or CFL Only 19% may still be looking for a team (which excludes the two retirees) Whatever else you think of the Cowboys’ roster-building, these numbers suggest their scouting department is finding players who remain viable NFL prospects even when Dallas doesn’t have room for them. Of course, I didn’t go through the numbers of the remaining 31 NFL teams to see how the Cowboys’ numbers stack up, but I’m confident that having 23 out of 37 “surplus” players still in the NFL today is a pretty good rate. The players marked with an (*) were the initial 15 players the Cowboys signed to their 2025 practice squad, and the data here suggests that making the Cowboys’ practice squad is a pretty good indicator that a player will remain in the NFL. Five of the initial 15 are still with the Cowboys today, and eight were eventually signed by another NFL team either in 2025 or 2026. Will Grier retired, so he shouldn’t count against the total, which leaves WR Jalen Brooks as the only initial practice squad signing without a team this year. That is a “success rate” of 93% for the Cowboys practice squad. Looks like having the Cowboys on your résumé doesn’t hurt. So if you’re a down-roster guy on the Cowboys’ training camp roster, focus on making the practice squad. Last year’s numbers suggest that getting to 53 isn’t the only way to stay in the NFL. Make the practice squad, and you’ve given yourself a pretty good chance to keep the dream alive. And that’s really all anybody can ask for.

title: Cowboys news: Secondary steals the show in 1st padded practice
summary: Practice Points: Takeaways from first padded practice – Staff, DallasCowboys.com The Cowboys secondary looked pretty good once the pads came on. The Land Shark Cometh – Cobie Durant’s momentum over the first three practices ramped up even more on Monday, when the pads came on. His coverage is some of the best on the Cowboys’ defense […]
full_text: Jul 29, 2026; Oxnard, CA, USA; Dallas Cowboys cornerback Cobie Durant (2) at training camp at River Ridge Playing Fields. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Practice Points: Takeaways from first padded practice – Staff, DallasCowboys.com The Cowboys secondary looked pretty good once the pads came on. The Land Shark Cometh – Cobie Durant’s momentum over the first three practices ramped up even more on Monday, when the pads came on. His coverage is some of the best on the Cowboys’ defense and, on one play in particular, he showed Dak Prescott what he can do. Prescott dropped back in the red zone and threw a ball under duress to CeeDee Lamb, who was in good enough position to make the catch after he broke outside; but Durant peeled off of his original coverage, readjusted and jumped the route to make an acrobatic interception that had Christian Parker smiling. – (Patrik Walker) Bringin’ the Wood – On the first day of pads, you wouldn’t expect anything other than someone named “Julius Wood” to have a physical practice. Just an hour before, his head coach Brian Schottenheimer mentioned Wood as being active and making the safety position rather deep. And then in practice, he had several big pops, jarring the ball loose on a pass during the team drills and he also wasn’t afraid to come up in run support. Also, Caleb Downs had a few run stops as well. But Wood is a guy trying to get noticed – and he did that Monday. – (Nick Eatman) Revel In the Moment – What Shavon Revel is experiencing in his second NFL training camp is the definition of iron sharpens iron. Before today, CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens were narrowly inching him out to make big plays but, in the first padded practice, Revel had several PBUs and even wagged his finger at Pickens on one of them. Going against two of the best in the league combines with Revel being fully healthy to make for what might be a return to peak form once witnessed at ECU only two short seasons ago. (Patrik Walker) Downs to Business – Caleb Downs may not always make the flashy, highlight plays all the time for a defensive back, but he makes big plays that the offense feels well afterwards. That was the case today, as Downs had a teach-tape run fill against the first team offense, as he was waiting in the gap when Jaydon Blue was trying to get through it. Downs’ work at the line of scrimmage is one that popped up a lot at Ohio State, and has done so in flashes during his first NFL training camp with the Cowboys too. He’s also been active around the ball in coverage, as Downs had a near interception today off a pass that DaRon Bland deflected into the air. – (Tommy Yarrish) Cowboys cornerbacks get off to a hot start at first padded practice – Matthew Holleran, Blogging The Boys The Cowboys wide receiver versus cornerback battles have been fiery in Oxnard. If today’s practice is any indication of how the group is going to perform during the regular season, Cowboys fans are going to be very pleased. The trio of Bland, Durant, and Revel all had great showings during today’s padded practice. Bland and Durant started the day off by both recording a PBU against the first-team offense. Dallas’ starting cornerback group continued to perform well as practice wore on, highlighted by Durant intercepting Dak Prescott in the red zone. It’s hard to overstate how much Dallas’ postseason hopes rely on their starting cornerback trio not just staying on the field, but playing well while doing so. There’s no way around it; last year was ugly for both Daron Bland and Shavon Revel. The Cowboys showed plenty of support for the duo this offseason, but now it’s time for both players to prove Dallas right for believing in them. Durant will be a true x-factor for Dallas’ defense. If he can play a vital role in Dallas’ defense alongside Bland and Revel, the Cowboys have a chance to have an above-average secondary. Let’s hope Dallas’ cornerback group continues to play like they did on Monday afternoon moving forward. Dak Prescott already noticed a big difference from this year’s Dallas Cowboys defense only a few days into training camp – Mauricio Rodriguez, A to Z Sports A noticeable improvement from the Cowboys defense under Christian Parker, straight from their highest-paid player and starting quarterback. That hasn’t stopped Prescott from noticing a big difference from the Cowboys defense he’s facing every day. And with the Cowboys set to wear pads for the first time on Monday, it’s only fair to say the battle between an elite offense and a rebuilt defense is only beginning. This summer, Prescott is facing the fourth Cowboys defensive coordinator in camp since 2023. What has he noticed from the new-look defense led by 34-year-old defensive coordinator Christian Parker? “A defense that is communicating,” Prescott told reporters last week. “A defense that takes a lot of pride in what they do in each and every one of their calls, taking pride in playing with one another.” For Parker, who wants to run a defense that is multiple and capable to adjust on the fly, communication is crucial. In order to do that, players have to be loud. So far, Prescott is impressed with the decibels coming from the other side of the line of scrimmage. “When we motion, you can hear how loud they are and them getting to the right fits or calls that they need to make, and just challenging us,” Prescott added. Rookie Caleb Downs Sets Lofty Goal for Cowboys’ Defense During NFL Season – Timothy Rapp, Bleacher Report Caleb Downs’ high expectations for himself as a rookie can be found all throughout the Cowboys defense right now. “To be dominant,” he told Jon Machota of The Athletic when asked about his expectations for the defense in the 2026 season. “That’s what I’ve thought about with every defense I’ve been on. And we have the talent to do it, to dominate every offense that we go against.” In 2025, the Cowboys gave up an NFL-worst 251.5 passing yards and 30.1 points per game. Many pointed to the questionable decision to trade superstar edge-rusher Micah Parsons before the season, though the secondary was porous at best. But attempts were made to rectify the pass defense this offseason. The Cowboys traded for edge-rusher Rashan Gary, filling the void left by Parsons a year ago, and drafted pass-rusher Malachi Lawrence at No. 26 overall (one of five defensive players the team drafted in the first four rounds). The secondary was bolstered in free agency with the signings of safety Jalen Thompson and cornerback Cobie Durant. And most importantly, Downs was the No. 11 overall pick and is already being utilized as both a safety and nickelback. Here’s what Cowboys former 5th-round pick must do to earn game snaps – Reid Hanson, The Cowboys Wire With buzz about the passing game and pass defense still dominating all the headlines from Oxnard, how about another check in on the RB2 competition and Jaydon Blue? It’s no secret the Dallas Cowboys hope Jaydon Blue takes over the RB2 spot behind starter Javonte Williams. The former Texas running back has game-changing speed and big-play ability that would complement Williams’ physical style well. He was a complementary back in college, and he’s tabbed to be a complementary back in the NFL. It’s a match made in heaven. Yet, Blue’s first season in Dallas proved to be a total disappointment. Critical aspects of the job fell on deaf ears and aside from a 16-carry performance in Week 18, Blue was basically a nonfactor in his rookie year. Hope springs eternal in Year 2 for Blue. After saying the right things in the offseason and doing the right things early in training camp, Blue is back on track to be that RB2 he was always meant to be. But there’s one task, one unavoidable quality he has to prove before he can officially be given second-fiddle designation in Dallas, and that’s pass protection. The NFL game is one of chess strategization. Offensive coordinators are trying to outsmart defensive…

Players ratchet up the intensity in a big way, and we get our first true look at which guys can separate themselves from the pack. With Dallas’ offense not featuring many new faces, they figured to have the leg up in the first padded practice of camp. Surprisingly, it was the defense that stole the show early on, including an impressive showing from the Cowboys’ cornerback group. You could make a legitimate argument that how Dallas’ cornerback group performs this season (health aside) will have as much of an impact on the team as any other position outside of quarterback and wide receiver. The Cowboys are relying on Daron Bland and Shavon Revel Jr. to bounce back in a big way while also needing a solid year out of free agent acquisition Cobie Durant. title: Cowboys countdown to kickoff: Top 100 iconic games – Day 41
summary: It is Day 41 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff. We are looking back at the 100 most iconic games in Dallas Cowboys history. full_text: (Original Caption) Miami, Florida: Baltimore's Roy Jefferson (87) is dragged to the ground by Dallas' Lee Roy Jordan (55) in the Super Bowl V. It is Day 41 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff. We are looking back at the 100 most iconic games in Dallas Cowboys history. The countdown will leads us right up to the opening game of 2026. Our look back doesn’t depend on just one criteria for our rankings. We take into consideration things like how big the game was for the organization, how memorable the game was, games that had unusual events take place, games that are a part of NFL lore, Cowboys firsts, and games where the Cowboys just plain dominated. Variety is the spice of life and we have all different kind of Cowboys games to review. At the bottom, we’ll link each day of the countdown so you can go back and check out any you missed. Welcome everyone to Day 41 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff, when we revisit one of the most painful and historically significant losses in Cowboys history. It was Dallas’ first Super Bowl appearance and the first Super Bowl staged after the AFL-NFL merger formally created the AFC and NFC. The Cowboys led for almost the entire afternoon, forced seven Baltimore turnovers, but the end result was heartbreaking for all of Cowboys nation. Sunday, January 17, 1971 — 2:00 p.m. ET Miami Orange Bowl, Miami, Florida Final Score: Baltimore Colts 16, Dallas Cowboys 13 Dallas opened the scoring after Chuck Howley intercepted Johnny Unitas and returned the ball into Colts territory. The Cowboys could not reach the end zone, but Mike Clark made a 14-yard field goal for a 3-0 lead. Clark added another field goal from 30 yards early in the second quarter, giving Dallas a 6-0 advantage in a game that had already become physical, disjointed and filled with mistakes. Baltimore’s first touchdown came on one of the strangest scoring plays in Super Bowl history. Unitas threw high and behind Eddie Hinton, the ball glanced off Hinton’s hands and was touched by Cowboys cornerback Mel Renfro before dropping to tight end John Mackey. Mackey caught the ricochet and ran 75 yards for a touchdown. Dallas blocked O’Brien’s extra point, keeping the score tied at 6-6. The Cowboys reclaimed the lead before halftime. Craig Morton completed a seven-yard touchdown pass to Duane Thomas, and Clark’s extra point put Dallas ahead 13-6. Baltimore then drove to the Cowboys’ goal line in the final minutes of the half, but the Doomsday Defense stopped Norm Bulaich three times near the end zone before forcing an incompletion on fourth down. Dallas carried its seven-point lead into halftime. Neither team scored in the third quarter, but the turnovers continued. Dallas’ defense repeatedly gave the offense chances to extend the lead, while the Cowboys failed to take advantage. Howley intercepted replacement quarterback Earl Morrall in the end zone on the opening play of the fourth quarter, preserving the 13-6 advantage and giving him his second interception of the afternoon. Baltimore then produced another bizarre sequence. Sam Havrilak took a handoff on a planned flea-flicker but was unable to lateral the ball back to Morrall, so he threw downfield instead. Hinton caught it and headed toward the end zone, only for Cornell Green to strip him from behind. The loose ball bounced through the end zone for a touchback, seemingly giving Dallas another escape. The relief lasted only three plays. Morton’s pass was deflected and intercepted by Colts safety Rick Volk, who returned it to the Dallas three-yard line. Tom Nowatzke scored from two yards out shortly afterward, and O’Brien’s extra point tied the game at 13 with 7:35 remaining. The Cowboys still had an opportunity to win. They took possession near midfield with less than two minutes remaining, but a holding penalty against Ralph Neely pushed Dallas backward. Facing second-and-35, Morton threw toward Dan Reeves. The pass went off Reeves’ hands and into the arms of Baltimore linebacker Mike Curtis, who returned the interception to the Dallas 28 with 1:09 left. Baltimore ran two plays to improve the position, and O’Brien came on for a 32-yard field goal. The rookie kicker made it with five seconds remaining, giving the Colts their first lead of the entire game. Dallas’ final desperation pass was intercepted, and Baltimore completed a 16-13 comeback that left Cowboys defensive tackle Bob Lilly so frustrated that he threw his helmet far downfield after the final whistle. This game belongs on the countdown because it represents the deepest pain of the Cowboys’ rise from expansion team to NFL power. Dallas had been close before, but Super Bowl V put the franchise within seconds of its first championship before another late mistake took it away. The defeat also strengthened the perception that the Cowboys could reach the biggest stage but could not finish. But that was soon to change. #Cowboys vs #Colts 1971 Super Bowl V Final Score: Baltimore Colts 16, Dallas Cowboys 13 #DallasCowboys #NFL (📽️: @nfl ) pic.twitter.com/lO6goWZJME — Mike Poland (@kenfigkowboy) August 3, 2026 Interesting Facts About the Game Super Bowl V became known as the “Blunder Bowl” because the teams combined for 11 turnovers. Baltimore committed seven, while Dallas turned it over four times. title: Which Broncos wide receiver will earn the third spot in the rotation?
summary: As training camp rolls along, the position group battle at wide receiver continues to heat up. The Denver Broncos will showcase Courtland Sutton and Jaylen Waddle as their dynamic duo for the 2026 season. However, who will fight their way to the third option in the Broncos’ aerial attack is yet to be determined. Denver […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - DECEMBER 28: Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos celebrates with Marvin Mims Jr. #19 after a touchdown during the fourth quarter against the Cincinnati Bengals at Paycor Stadium on December 28, 2024 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) | Getty Images As training camp rolls along, the position group battle at wide receiver continues to heat up. The Denver Broncos will showcase Courtland Sutton and Jaylen Waddle as their dynamic duo for the 2026 season. However, who will fight their way to the third option in the Broncos’ aerial attack is yet to be determined. Denver had quarterback Bo Nix throw more than any other quarterback in 2025. The acquisition of Waddle will undoubtedly amplify their aerial production. Alas, there are only so many targets to go around and this receiver group is a strong five deep. Behind Sutton and Waddle, Marvin Mims Jr., Troy Franklin, and Pat Bryant all have unique talents and skillsets. From early camp reports , Mims and Bryant appear to be making the most plays of the trio. Though there is still a lot of time left before the regular season to decipher who will rise to the top. Marvin Mims Jr. A second-round selection in 2023, Mims has made a lot of big plays in the Mile High City. Touting two All-Pro and Pro-Bowl nods for his return skills, fans know his impact on special teams. Yet many have always wondered when—if ever—will Mims take flight as a receiver. After an impressive 2024 season, I was convinced Mims would be featured more in ’25. I couldn’t have been more wrong. In fact, he ranked behind Sutton, Franklin, and Bryant in snap count. Mims had a high catch rate, but not nearly as many explosive plays down the field compared to his second-year efforts. Mims has been a highlight reel during camp thus far. His penchant for hauling in deep passes has been on display. For several years now, Head Coach Sean Payton has often been asked about Mims’ involvement in the offense. And virtually every time he acknowledges they need to get him the ball more. Will this finally be the year that happens? Troy Franklin In his second season, Franklin was big part of Denver’s passing plans. In ‘25, he was targeted 104 times and came down with 65 receptions for 709 yards and 6 touchdowns. All those marks ranked second on the Broncos behind only Sutton who led every category. Nearly half of those catches resulted in first downs. His odds of being that involved this season? Personally, I think zero. That’s just being brutally honest. The former Oregon Duck lined up at wideout 670 times last year. One can’t help but acknowledge Waddle’s presence on the team will cut his snaps drastically. In 11 personnel packages, the team may prefer Bryant in many scenarios, especially due to his run blocking ability. When it comes to ball tracking down the field, I feel Mims’ ability in that respect is quite a bit better. Is there any particular area Franklin stands out at more than the others? Pat Bryant Picked in the third round of the 2025 NFL Draft, Bryant earned a lot of reps as a rookie. Appearing in fifteen games with seven starts, the former Illini standout carved himself a nice role in Denver’s rotation. He logged 475 offensive snaps—the third most at the position. Overall, Bryant reeled in 31 passes on 49 targets for 378 yards and 1 touchdown. An impressive 22 of those receptions resulted in a first down. Unfortunately, he suffered two concussions and a hamstring injury that limited his participation and impact down the final stretch of games. Nevertheless, Bryant’s toughness, attitude, and inside-out flexibility have all been praised by Payton since being drafted. Yesterday, he noted crafting a role for the second-year wideout will be easy. Just how large of a roll may that be, perhaps top three in the wide receiver pecking order? What do you think, Broncos Country? I’m not so sure there is a clear consensus on this one. Which player seems poised to earn the third spot in the Broncos’ receiving rotation? Let me hear all your thoughts in the comments section.
author: Christopher Hart

title: Depth and development have played key role in Broncos quick turnaround
summary: The Denver Broncos have swung big trades, reeled in top notch free agents, and drafted several quality contributors throughout the Sean Payton era. Boasting quality starters across the board, the Broncos have transformed from annual underperformers to touting the ability and talent to compete with any team in the National Football League. Securing back-to-back playoff […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MO - DECEMBER 25: Jahdae Barron #23 of the Denver Broncos runs out of the tunnel prior to an NFL football game against the Kansas City Chiefs at GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium on December 25, 2025 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Denver Broncos have swung big trades, reeled in top notch free agents, and drafted several quality contributors throughout the Sean Payton era. Boasting quality starters across the board, the Broncos have transformed from annual underperformers to touting the ability and talent to compete with any team in the National Football League. Securing back-to-back playoff berths and their first division title in a decade, the Broncos’ outlook looks the brightest it has in ages. Overlooked, but equally as important, Payton and his staff have assembled a roster loaded with depth in many areas. That has been critical for Denver’s three-year evolution and franchise turnaround. One position group in particular is the offensive line. Their success is a big reason why the Broncos can contend for a Super Bowl title. Early on, it appears that depth may be tested. In their first pads practice of camp, starting center Luke Wattenberg exited yesterday’s first pads practice session with an apparent arm injury and did not return. After practice, Payton expressed confidence Wattenberg wouldn’t miss much time. However, the extent of the injury and his timetable of return is unknown If he misses time, fourth year pro Alex Forsyth would take over. Forsyth was seventh-round draft selection out of Oregon and part of Payton’s first draft class with the team. A practice squad player for his rookie year, Forsyth has appeared in every game the past two seasons with six starts. Payton took a moment to praise the backup pivot’s intelligence and noted he was wise beyond his years. “Yes, he’s super savvy and smart. He’s one of the smarter guys in that room. You don’t feel a young player. You feel like, if you interviewed him, you’d feel like you’re talking to a seven-year vet,” stated Payton. “He’s a little bit of an old soul that way and much appreciated though. He’s really talented.” Speaking of talent, the Broncos defense has a lot of it. Especially in their secondary. Yesterday, reports acknowledged they were a key reason why the defense won the day against the offense. Sitting atop the depth of Broncos’ defensive backfield is second-year cornerback Jahdae Barron. With the high-profile trio of Patrick Surtain II, Riley Moss, and Ja’Quan McMillian scheduled to start once again, Barron is on the hunt for an increased role in 2026. Selected with their first-round pick in the 2025 NFL Draft, the former Jim Thorpe Award winner appeared in every game and notched five starts as a rookie. He posted 35 tackles, 7 pass breaks ups, 1 forced fumble, and 1 interception. Overall, he saw 334 snaps, roughly 30-percent of the defense’s total in ‘25. Some fans have been critical of Barron’s lack of immediate impact, but the former Longhorns standout fared well and made a positive impact in his snap share. During his post-practice presser, Payton dismissed rumors stating Barron had moved to safety and clarified his role with the defense. “He’s playing nickel, he’s playing corner and then when we get into dime, he replaces a linebacker. He’s doing really good. There’s been no position change.” Another spot where the competition is hot is wide receiver. The Broncos aerial attack is ready for liftoff. The have a batch of talented wideouts vying for the next big role after Courtland Sutton and Jaylen Waddle. Second-year wide receiver Pat Bryant is among them and has been turning heads at camp. A third-round pick alongside Barron in the ‘25 NFL Draft, Bryant’s physicality, run blocking, and ability to snag tough catches were a big part of his rookie campaign successes. He hauled in 31 receptions on 49 targets for 378 yards and 1 touchdown—22 of those catches resulting in first downs. Yesterday, Payton gave Bryant a glowing review for his efforts to date. It’s too early to tell who will earn the third spot battle at wideout, but the former Illini standout is making a tough run for it. “I think his weight is at a good spot. He has some of the better hands in traffic with his feet on the ground. He’s really good at run after the catch. I said this to you guys a year ago, he’s real smart. Someone that can move from ‘X’ to the slot. It’ll be easy creating his role.”
author: Christopher Hart

title: Horse Tracks: ‘Right pieces, right team,’ says Surtain
summary: Good morning, Broncos Country! It was inevitable someone would ask the “Super Bowl or bust?” question. Pat Surtain II didn’t take the bait. After all, it’s August. But he didn’t shy away from it, either. Because it’s August with some high expectations. “Our expectations are pretty high, but we are just going to take it […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - SEPTEMBER 7: Pat Surtain II (2), Ja'Quan McMillian (29) and Talanoa Hufanga (9) of the Denver Broncos prepare for Cam Ward (1) and the Tennessee Titans during the fourth quarter of the Broncos' 20-12 win at Empower Field at Mile High on Sunday, September 7, 2025. (Photo by AAron Ontiveroz/MediaNews Group/The Denver Post via Getty Images) Good morning, Broncos Country! It was inevitable someone would ask the “Super Bowl or bust?” question. Pat Surtain II didn’t take the bait. After all, it’s August. But he didn’t shy away from it, either. Because it’s August with some high expectations. “Our expectations are pretty high, but we are just going to take it week-by-week,” he said, as well-coached in PR as in coverage. “Obviously, that’s the main goal, but it starts right here in training camp and it starts early on in the season. Our main focus is to start out fast and start out hot early. That way we can prepare ourselves to get to that stage.” And the All-Pro corner believes the set-up is perfect for that. “We have all of the right pieces and the right team … the right guys with the right mentality to start things off the right way. This team is great all across the board.” Pat Surtain II “We have all of the right pieces and the right team,” Surtain said. “We have the right guys with the right mentality to start things off the right way. This team is great all across the board.” And a big part of that is the guy calling the defense. Having Vance Joseph back another year is not an insignificant piece of the Super Bowl puzzle. “It does a lot,” Surtain said. “Having ‘VJ’ on our side, a guy that’s been in this league for a long time and knows the ins and outs of this game. When you talk to him, everything about him speaks volumes, but he’s an even better person. Having a guy like that on the defensive side of the ball just translates to success.” Losing players like John Franklin Myers and PJ Locke means there is a void to fill, but Surtain is confident the coaches and veterans can bring the young guys along to do just that. “That’s part of the business, as they say,” Surtain noted about losing Myers and Locke. “Obviously when great players leave, you have to count on other guys to step up.” Between Sai’vion Jones and Eyioma Uwazurike working to replace Myers’ spot, or JL Skinner and Devon Key filling in for Locke, Surtain is not worried about that happening. There are always young guys stepping up. 🔒’d in at #BroncosCamp @R_moss5 x @PatSurtainll pic.twitter.com/KIop5m5aji — Denver Broncos (@Broncos) August 3, 2026 Ja’Quan McMillian, for example, is primed to be an impact player, says Surtain. “His mindset is off the charts. The way that he carries himself on and off the field and his work ethic… There are only a few that quite work like him,” he said. “Being undrafted and coming in, nobody knew about him. Now, he’s a hot commodity. It goes to show the work that he’s put in and how much he values and hones in on his craft. I’m excited for ‘J-Mac.’ He’s a big-time player.” And it was Riley Moss who stole the show yesterday when pads came on. It was cornerback Riley Moss, however, who stole the show with the play of the day. During the final 11-on-11 team period, Courtland Sutton appeared to catch the ball for a big gain, but Moss wrestled the ball away at the last second for the INT. “It’s fantastic,” Sean Payton said of the play. “… The ability to be able to catch it as a defensive back, it’s tough if you don’t have decent enough hands because they’ll just throw at you. So, it was a good play.” In fact, takeaways will be one major emphasis of improvement over last year’s success — something the defense struggled to get last season. “That’s true,” Surtain acknowledged. “We can do that when the ball is in the air, capitalize on more opportunities of taking the ball away. Obviously, those game-changing plays are very vital in NFL games. Taking the ball away and just doing that would definitely help us a lot, too.” But right now, in training camp, it’s mostly about trusting the process, and the wins will come, Surtain says. “I feel like every year, everyone has new goals. …I mentioned before starting out fast early on and not allowing anything to go by. I feel like that is our next step and just staying committed to the process,” Surtain added. “Trusting what ‘VJ’ has for us, and trusting us and our defense as a unit. We have the right pieces at the right places. It just feels right right now.” Even for the six-year veteran, training camp brings a new buzz for the upcoming season, and the buzz this year is good. “I mean, honestly man, it doesn’t even feel like Year 6. It feels like when I was a rookie just starting to come in, starting to come [out of] my shell, but yes, time is flying” he added. “Just seeing how far this team has come has been quite surreal honestly, to say the least. So yes, I’m excited to enter Year 6 and to get it going again.” But first training camp. “It’s going to be a fun camp,” Surtain added.

Pads 🔛, energy 🆙 pic.twitter.com/w5fdW3PuSp — Denver Broncos (@Broncos) August 3, 2026 In today’s piece, we have more on the Broncos defense and Riley Moss winning the day, Pat Bryant looking good, a positive update on Luke Wattenberg’s injury, injury updates, news and notes, tweets from camp, and more! Defense, pass rush, and Riley Moss win the day The pads came on today, and the Denver Broncos defense stepped up. Riley Moss was excellent in coverage and showed off his elite athleticism, making an incredible interception; the Broncos pass rush got after the quarterbacks while Jonah Elliss is beginning to look like an early training camp star. Riley Moss just won a 1-on-1 battle vs Sutton on a deep pass down the left sideline. Great coverage and fought for the ball for a McMillian-esque INT A couple plays later, Pat Bryant was able to adjust and high point it over Moss for 15+ yards — Ryan Edwards (@redwardsradio) August 3, 2026 Riley Moss stole the day with his Ja’Quan McMillian-ish interception in practice where he fought the ball away from veteran wide receiver Courtland Sutton. He showcased his athleticism throughout practice, and showed why he’s a very good number two cornerback in the NFL. After practice, Head Coach Sean Payton was asked how Moss has grown throughout his career, and he told reporters Moss competes his tail off and that he is moving around really well right now. He knows obviously what type of attention he’s going to get relative to the routes, the route tree. I think learning to play with his feet, really working on reducing some of those fouls. He competes his tail off. I love that about him. He has those traits where it’s a short mindset, short memory. He’s moving around really well right now.” He was later asked about his interception vs. Sutton during practice, and Payton told reporters it was “fantastic to watch”. “It’s fantastic to watch because look, there are two things that can happen. You’re either deflecting it, but the ability to be able to catch it as a defensive back, it’s tough if you don’t have decent enough hands because they’ll just throw at you. So it was a good play.” As we know, Moss is in the final year of his deal with the team, and we assume that the Broncos will need to decide who to re-sign between him and McMillian. So, it will be interesting to see how that goes, but it’s great to see he’s doing well in camp. As for Jonah Elliss, he continues to stand out. We’ll see what the future holds for Jonathon Cooper, but it appears that the team has an ascending player here in Elliss. Pat Bryant makes plays The Denver Broncos battle for the WR3 job and/or snaps/targets behind starters Jaylen Waddle and Courtland Sutton continues to be one of the top stories in camp. For the first few practices, Marvin Mims was the standout pass catcher who had multiple explosive plays, and today, second-year wide receiver Pat Bryant took his turn at being the standout wide receiver. Riley Moss and the Broncos defense stole the show, but with Moss in coverage, Bryant caught a beautiful back-shoulder 25-yard pass from quarterback Bo Nix. He followed that with a top-tapping catch from backup quarterback Jarrett Stidham. Sean Payton sees a clear path for Pat Bryant in Denver's offense “It’ll be easy to create his role” pic.twitter.com/f9LrAQD7yq — DNVR Broncos (@DNVR_Broncos) August 3, 2026 After practice, Payton was asked where he thinks Bryant can still grow in year two. He told reporters that Bryant has some of the better hands in traffic, he’s really smart, and can play all over the field, which will make it easy to create his role in this offense. “I think his weight’s at a good spot. He has some of the better hands in traffic with his feet on the ground, he’s really good [at] run after the catch. I said this to you guys a year ago, he’s real smart. So he’s someone that can move from ‘X’ to the slot. It’ll be easy creating his role.” Bryant is my favorite to win the WR3 job simply because of all the things he can do. We saw his role grow at the end of last year; he has great hands, runs good routes, can block, and simply made plays. I think he can thrive in this role, and I believe we see a second-year jump this season. Luke Wattenberg injury Early during today’s practice, Denver Broncos starting center Luke Wattenberg went down hard and was seen holding his arm and talking with trainers. He never returned to practice, and backup center Alex Forsyth handled the starting center duties for the rest of the practice. We’ll go ahead and evaluate. I think he’ll be fine.” So, while we don’t know exactly, it’s good to hear that he thinks he will be fine. However, if he were to miss time, Alex Forsyth stepped in for him nicely at the end of last year, so I believe he can do that in the short-term. If he does miss time, hopefully it’s not for an extended period of time, and he can be ready for Week 1 vs. the Chiefs. title: Lions say Bijan Robinson extension ‘can’t hurt’ Jahmyr Gibbs contract talks
summary: On Tuesday morning, news broke that Atlanta Falcons running back Bijan Robinson had agreed to a three-year extension worth an average of $22.25 million per year, including $51 million guaranteed. That deal resets the running back market and turns eyes to Detroit Lions Jahmyr Gibbs, who is currently holding in from training camp while he […]
full_text: Detroit Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs (0) on field after practice during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Monday, August 3, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co On Tuesday morning, news broke that Atlanta Falcons running back Bijan Robinson had agreed to a three-year extension worth an average of $22.25 million per year, including $51 million guaranteed. That deal resets the running back market and turns eyes to Detroit Lions Jahmyr Gibbs, who is currently holding in from training camp while he awaits a new deal. Minutes after the Robinson news broke, Lions coach Dan Campbell took the lectern for his daily training camp press conference and was asked if the Robinson development could help speed up the process for Gibbs. “I think it certainly’s not going to hurt,” Campbell said. “It’s not going to hurt, but we’ll see. I’m anxious to get Gibbs back out there. Every day that goes by, that’s another day that you feel like you miss with him and getting him out there with the guys and him doing his part. But, there again, it’ll get done when it gets done.” Gibbs spoke extremely briefly with reporters on Monday after practice and simply told them “time will tell” when a deal is done. Gibbs and Robinson were drafted in the same draft class, with Robinson being selected eighth overall while Gibbs was taken 12th. Here’s a side-by-side comparison of stats for both players through three seasons: Bijan Robinson: 805 rushes 3,910 rushing yards 4.9 YPC 25 rush TDs 198 catches 1,738 receiving yards 9 receiving TDs Jahmyr Gibbs: 675 rushes 3,580 rushing yards 5.3 YPC 39 rush TDs 181 catches 1,449 receiving yards 10 receiving TDs At this point, there haven’t been any hard reports on how close a Gibbs deal is to getting done, but some NFL insiders have speculated that it could get done within the next couple of weeks.

title: Tracking the Detroit Lions’ defensive roster bubble: Arise, Ahmed Hassanein
summary: Every week, we are tracking the Detroit Lions players on the roster bubble and offering our predictions for who is in and who is out. The Lions defensive roster bubble continues to grow with questions about injuries and a ton of moving parts in the secondary. Some situations are becoming a little clearer, while others […]
full_text: Detroit Lions edge Ahmed Hassanein(99) during OTAs at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Friday, May 29, 2026. | Junfu Han / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images Every week, we are tracking the Detroit Lions players on the roster bubble and offering our predictions for who is in and who is out. The Lions defensive roster bubble continues to grow with questions about injuries and a ton of moving parts in the secondary. Some situations are becoming a little clearer, while others only seem to be getting more confusing. Here are the Pride of Detroit staff’s current predictions about the players on the defensive roster bubble. We’ll break down each position below the chart to explain the shifts in the depth chart. View Link Defensive end : Assumed in: Aidan Hutchinson, DJ Wonnum, Derrick Moore Ahmed Hassanein: 10 “IN” votes (up 7) Payton Turner: 1 vote (down 5) Anthony Lucas: 0 votes Arise, Ahmed Hassanein believers. The love for Hassanein’s attitude and potential has come together this camp for a very, very strong early performance for the second-year edge defender. He’s making plays on special teams, and has worked his way up to consistent second-team defensive reps. This can’t be a bad look, either: Saw Brad Holmes and Ahmed Hassanein talking after practice today and asked Hassanein about it. “I’m gonna do whatever it takes to prove you right,” Hassanein said he told Holmes. “You prove me right by doing what you’re doing. You’re a football player,” Holmes said to him. https://t.co/1Nx0KxI5ov pic.twitter.com/vd5v6Vgb3L — Colton Pouncy (@colton_pouncy) August 4, 2026 And with Payton Turner struggling to shake his reputation as injury-prone, this decision is starting to look easier and easier. Defensive tackle: Assumed in: Alim McNeill, Tyleik Williams, Levi Onwuzurike OFF BUBBLE WATCH: Jay Tufele (cut) Tyler Lacy: 11 “IN” votes (no change) Skyle Gill-Howard: 8 votes (down 1) Mekhi Wingo: 6 votes (up 3) Chris Smith: 4 votes (up 3) Tyre West: 0 votes (no change) Aidan Keanaaina: 0 votes (no change) Most of the movement here is in regard to the nose tackle position. Essentially, all of Jay Tufele’s votes prior to the start of training camp shifted to Chris Smith and Mekhi Wingo. Smith looks like the next guy up at nose tackle, but hasn’t stuck out early in camp. Wingo, however, continues to rep with the first and second-team defenses when Alim McNeill needs a break. The fact that he is repping ahead of a guy like Levi Onwuzurike is notable, but we’re not yet ready to put Onwuzurike on the roster bubble. Linebacker: Assumed in: Jack Campbell, Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez NEW TO ROSTER BUBBLE: Jimmy Rolder (injury) NEW TO ROSTER BUBBLE: Joe Bachie NEW TO ROSTER BUBBLE: Devin White (signed) Trevor Nowaske: 10 “IN” votes ( up 1) Damone Clark: 10 votes (up 1) Devin White: 6 votes Troy Reeder: 4 votes (up 4) Jimmy Rolder: 3 votes Erick Hunter: 1 vote (no change) The Jimmy Rolder injury has caused some massive shifts here. Campbell said the injury wasn’t significant, but he’ll be out for “a while.” Seems like the most likely scenario is he goes on injured reserve when the cutdowns start, meaning he’ll be OUT and miss at least the first four games. Still, three staffers are holding out hope he avoids IR. Rolder’s votes from last week have been spread across the room, with newly signed Devin White getting the biggest jump. About half of the staff thinks he’s in, but Troy Reeder and Damone Clark have a little more belief, as well. Cornerback: Assumed in: DJ Reed, Rock Ya-Sin, Ennis Rakestraw, Roger McCreary, Keith Abney Khalil Dorsey: 8 “IN” votes (down 2) Nick Whiteside: 6 votes (up 5) I’m dangerously close to putting Roger McCreary on the roster bubble due to the rise in Nick Whiteside. Whiteside’s play has been undeniable, but it’s really challenging to find a way to put him on the roster. Reed, Ya-Sin, Rakestraw, and Abney all feel pretty safe. Khalil Dorsey may be the best special teamer on the roster, which makes it hard to put Whiteside above him. Meanwhile, McCreary is on a one-year, minimum salary contract with just $800,000 guaranteed. I’ve still got him as an assumed in, but with the growing support around Whiteside, I think next week we may need to pull him down to the bubble. As Dan Campbell said on Monday, the cornerback room is about to get interesting. Safety Assumed in: Christian Izien NEW TO BUBBLE WATCH: Kerby Joseph NEW TO BUBBLE WATCH: Brian Branch Avonte Maddox: 11 “IN” votes (no change) Thomas Harper: 11 votes (no change) Chuck Clark: 11 votes (no change) Kerby Joseph: 4 votes Brian Branch: 4 votes Dan Jackson: 1 vote (up 1) Loren Strickland: 0 votes (no change) We are no longer assuming that Kerby Joseph is “IN” nor that Brian Branch is “OUT.” Dan Campbell dropped the bombshell last week that Branch could return to the practice field as early as the end of training camp, which would lead to him avoiding the PUP to start the season. But Campbell also said that they are not expecting Joseph to be ready by Week 1, which was just as big of a surprise. Detroit is going to face a very difficult decision with both players on whether they should start the season on PUP, and as you can see, the POD staff is split on what they’re going to do. Oddly, that hasn’t changed much about the rest of the room, as staffers have used the extra votes elsewhere on the roster. That said, Clark and Maddox are getting very close to moving off the roster bubble. Given that they’ve taken nearly every first-team rep in camp, it seems unlikely Detroit will change course. But we’ll see as camp continues.

title: Who will be in the Detroit Lions’ starting secondary in Week 1?
summary: Going into Detroit Lions training camp, one of the biggest questions was: how will the secondary shake itself out? There were—and still are—a ton of questions among the defensive backs that have left people both curious and concerned. The sudden fall of Terrion Arnold left the outside cornerback position thin and questionable. The unclear injury […]
full_text: Detroit Lions cornerback D.J. Reed (4), center, practices next to cornerback Rock Ya-Sin (23) and cornerback Ennis Rakestraw Jr. (2) during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Thursday, July 30, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Going into Detroit Lions training camp, one of the biggest questions was: how will the secondary shake itself out? There were—and still are—a ton of questions among the defensive backs that have left people both curious and concerned. The sudden fall of Terrion Arnold left the outside cornerback position thin and questionable. The unclear injury timelines for Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph made predicting the Week 1 starters challenging. Detroit also added a handful of new pieces—Roger McCreary, Keith Abney, Christian Izien, and Chuck Clark—who could all challenge for a significant role on this defense. But we now have about a week’s worth of information from training camp. Be it the play on the field or comments from coaches and players, we’ve got a somewhat better picture of what Detroit’s secondary may look like when they kick off the season against the New Orleans Saints. So today’s Question of the Day is: Who will be part of the Lions’ starting secondary in Week 1? My answer: Let’s start at the safety position. At this point, I think it’s fair to say that Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph are unlikely to be ready at the start of the season. Don’t get me wrong, there are seriously promising signs that Branch will return earlier than initially expected , and Joseph is going through some pretty intense workouts with trainers. However, coach Dan Campbell said they aren’t expecting Joseph to be out there in Week 1 , and he said Branch is on a very similar timeline. So while I think those players could be ready by Week 2-4, I remain doubtful for the season opener. In training camp, the Lions haven’t wavered in their replacements for the two. It’s been Chuck Clark and Avonte Maddox almost exclusively. It’s clear Detroit likes having experienced, trustworthy veterans on the backend, and defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard explained why: “As far as bringing in veteran guys, who understand what we’re looking for as far as disguising. That’s where we’re trying to get to now as a defense. I told them it’s time to go to the next level guys. The quarterbacks in thisleague are too good now. So, it’s all about lying to them. You have got to be liars on defense. You have got a lot of that guy with the green dot on offense. Pre-snap, he has to see something and then post-snap, that picture has to change or else you’re sitting duck. And, these guys have done these things. They understand the why behind it.” So, injuries pending, I think Clark and Maddox are the Lions’ starting safeties in Week 1. As for the cornerback situation, it’s a little more muddled. While I do think D.J. Reed and Rock Ya-Sin have separated themselves early in training camp, things get a lot more complicated when you start talking about the nickel spot. Ennis Rakestraw has seen plenty of first-team reps at outside corner and nickel, but I don’t think he’s exactly stood out yet. Roger McCreary has also gotten a ton of reps as the first-team nickel. But the wild card here is Christian Izien. He missed the first three practices, but then Campbell revealed the original plan was for him to start as the No. 1 nickel. He’s just now getting started in camp, and he’s already starting to command some first-team nickel reps. If he wins that job, do McCreary and/or Rakestraw move more predominantly to the outside corner position and contend for a starting job there? Of course, I can’t completely count out Nick Whiteside, either. He’s made more plays than anyone in training camp, albeit with the second and third-team defenses. He got extremely high praise from Dan Campbell on Monday, and Detroit has a history of being a meritocracy. Doesn’t matter when you were drafted. Doesn’t matter how much you’re getting paid. If you produce, you’ll play. And if Whiteside can continue this crazy start to camp—and do so against starting-level competition—he could win this job. Ultimately, though, I think the starting secondary looks like this in Week 1: CB1: D.J. Reed CB2: Rock Ya-Sin NB: Christian Izien S: Chuck Clark S: Avonte Maddox Now, it’s time for you to make your predictions. title: How Week 1 of training camp impacts Detroit Lions roster bubble: Offense
summary: The Detroit Lions aren’t even a full week into 2026 training camp, but we’ve already seen some surprises when it comes to the roster. The depth chart may not be exactly what we expected, and injuries have forced some roster reshuffling. For Week 2 of our Roster Bubble series, it’s not surprising that there have […]
full_text: Detroit Lions wide receiver Dominic Lovett (19) walks off the field after practice during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Thursday, July 30, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions aren’t even a full week into 2026 training camp, but we’ve already seen some surprises when it comes to the roster. The depth chart may not be exactly what we expected, and injuries have forced some roster reshuffling. For Week 2 of our Roster Bubble series, it’s not surprising that there have been some significant shifts—although most are on defense. Today, let’s re-examine the players on the roster bubble on offense. View Link Quarterback: Assumed in: Jared Goff, Teddy Bridgewater Luke Altmyer: 0 “IN” vote ( down 1 ) I don’t think there’s anything in particular that has caused the one vote drop in Altmyer. Based on my personal observations, Altmyer has displayed a strong arm and decent accuracy. However, his progression and defense reading is taking time… like most rookies. That’s enough for him to keep the QB3 a conversation, but I think his camp will make or break with the preseason games. Running back: Assumed in: Jahmyr Gibbs, Isiah Pacheco, Sione Vaki Jacob Saylors: 9 “IN” votes ( no change ) No change for Saylors here, as he still needs to convince a couple of staffers that he’s worth keeping an RB4. Obviously, this outlook could change after Sione Vaki suffered an injury on Monday morning , but hopefully the poking of the eye isn’t too serious. Wide receiver: Assumed in: Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jameson Williams, Isaac TeSlaa, Greg Dortch Cedrick Wilson Jr.: 10 “IN” votes (up 2) Dominic Lovett: 2 votes (down 6) Tom Kennedy: 0 vote (down 1) Cedrick Wilson’s stock is reasonably up after a strong start to camp and some praise from Dan Campbell. “He just gets it. There’s nothing better than freaking vets, man, true pros that get it. They know how to go about their business, man. They come in here, they compete. They’re not entitled, they just go work, man and that’s what he does. And by the way, his special teams reps are pretty good, too. I mean, for a receiver, he can do some stuff and his tape says that too.” Wilson’s gain is Lovett’s pain. The second-year receiver had a sluggish start to camp, but he’s admittedly stacked a few good days here recently. Tight end: Assumed in: Sam LaPorta, Brock Wright OFF BUBBLE WATCH: Zach Horton (cut) NEW TO BUBBLE WATCH: Anthony Firkser (0 votes) Tyler Conklin: 11 “IN” votes (no change) Miles Kitselman: 2 votes (up 1) NOTE: SOME VOTES WERE MADE BEFORE NEWS THAT MILES KITSELMAN WILL BE OUT FOR “A WHILE.” Despite not playing yet due to injury, Conklin remains the unanimous pick for the TE3 spot. And with Conklin looking like he’s nearing a return that makes sense. Unfortunately for Detroit, the main competition keeps getting injured. Kitselman was getting a lot of early reps with the first and second team, but he’s now expected to miss serious time . Anthony Firkser came in and immediately put together two strong practices with some first-team reps sprinkled in, and now he suffered an injury on Monday that caused him to get carted off . It will be interesting to see if Jackson Meeks starts to get some early reps now and if he can rise to the occasion. Offensive tackle: Assumed in: Penei Sewell, Blake Miller, Larry Borom OFF BUBBLE WATCH: Giovanni Manu (injured) Colby Sorsdal: 0 votes Devin Cochran: 0 votes With Manu out an estimated three months , the tackle room just isn’t very interesting right now. Sorsdal and Cochran seem a far way from making a case for the 53-man roster. Plus, with Miles Frazier now taking a significant amount of reps at tackle, he could very well be the team’s OT4 going into the regular season without taking up an additional roster spot. Interior offensive line: Assumed in: Tate Ratledge, Cade Mays, Christian Mahogany, Miles Frazier Ben Bartch: 11 votes (no change) Juice Scruggs: 10 votes (down 1) Seth McLaughlin: 0 votes Michael Niese: 0 votes Bartch still has yet to see the field in any team drills, and his health appears to be heading in the wrong direction with two straight absences from practice. Nevertheless, the staff still has him in based on his strong reputation with Campbell. Additionally, there haven’t been a ton of standouts among the depth—although Scruggs still continues to get the majority of first-team reps with Christian Mahogany still being eased back in.

title: Detroit Lions 2026 training camp observations, Day 5: Offensive line shines in pads
summary: The Detroit Lions donned pads for the first time during their 2026 training camp, and while they spent a bit less time on the field than in previous practices, the intensity was ramped up. Monday’s practice was roughly only an hour and a half, but according to coach Dan Campbell, this was just a precursor […]
full_text: Detroit Lions center Cade Mays (64), left, talks to offensive tackle Penei Sewell (58) as they walk off the field after practice during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Wednesday, July 29, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions donned pads for the first time during their 2026 training camp, and while they spent a bit less time on the field than in previous practices, the intensity was ramped up. Monday’s practice was roughly only an hour and a half, but according to coach Dan Campbell, this was just a precursor for what should be a week of intensity that will separate players between those hoping to make an NFL roster and the ones who are ready. “I told the players last night that by the end of this week, this roster will begin to separate itself. So, this is where we’ll find out. We’re about to get four really, really good days of pads. And this is day one just to kind of break them in for the other three.” Injury updates Campbell gave injury updates on rookies Blake Miller, Derrick Moore, Jimmy Rolder, and Miles Kitselman in his morning press conference, and then Jeremy Reisman followed up practice with a second update, including a participation report, along with notes on the three players who left practice on Monday . “Time will tell” Star running back Jahmyr Gibbs, who is still not participating in practices due to a presumed contract holdout, watched his teammates from the sideline of the practice field on Sunday and was back again on Monday. While he was able to avoid the media over the weekend, Gibbs walked through the media on Monday but did not shed any light on his situation. When he was asked when he expected to return to the field to practice, his response was simply: “Time will tell.” Campbell, at his morning presser, made sure to emphasize that Gibbs is in the building, attending meetings, getting some work inside the training facility, and is “still part of us; and the guys, our players, love him. We love him. And he’s a part of what we do.” Opening with 1 vs. 1, but with a twist As has become tradition under Campbell, the first practice in pads opens with a one-on-one tackling drill, where the team gathers in a large semi-circle, and two players square up in the middle. At the whistle, the player with the ball needs to get past the defender, while the defender needs to make a stop. While this drill is typically full go and a way to increase intensity, the Lions scaled back this year’s opening drill and eliminated the tackling portion, instead asking the defenders to two-hand touch the offensive player. The Lions have been criticized for their practices in the past, and this is the drill Ennis Rakestraw was injured in in 2025, so it appears as if the Lions are being more cautious with their players this year. However, as Campbell mentioned previously, this practice is part of the ramp-up period, so it’s possible this drill could add tackling back in the coming days. As for the drill itself, the defense got the majority of the wins (two-hand touch certainly helps them), but I did award some offensive wins: RB Jabari Small was the only player to earn two wins, utilizing a cutback on the first and a speed-to-the-edge move on the second. WR Dominic Lovett got past his defender on a slick cutback. WR Lawrence Keys used a hesitation move to catch his defender throttling down. WR Tay Martin won with speed-to-the-edge. DB Aamaris Brown switched to offense for a snap and executed a juke move on his defender Offensive linemen impress in pads Whether in team drills or one-on-ones with defensive linemen, the offensive line showed fans a lot of optimism on Monday. On Monday, the Lions offense spent a fair amount of time working on their rushing offense, and that meant a variety of blocking schemes on display. While it can be challenging to sift through the bodies to see which individual players are standing out in the trenches, it gets much easier when they end up out in space, either by pulling or running their blocks out of the play. We saw Cade Mays and Christian Mahogany stand out on pulls during this practice, with the center walling off a hole for the back to run through, while Mahogany—fresh off returning from injury—pulled from his left guard spot and overpowered Aidan Hutchinson, a difficult thing to do. Mahogany’s power has been evident since his return, and now that he has flashed on pulls the last few days, it’s easy to see why I believe he’ll fit into Drew Petzing’s blocking scheme. The most impressive offensive lineman in camp has to be second-year utility lineman Miles Frazier, who continues to not only show off ridiculous range and endurance, but also execute at a strong level. After starting camp in the battle for the left guard position, he’s since shifted to right tackle on the second unit, while also contributing on the third team at both guard spots and sometimes left tackle as well. The offensive line also showed well on 1-0n-1s with the defensive line, showing nice patience and the ability to anchor versus power. OL vs. DL 1 vs. 1 recap: Starters Penei Sewell and Hutchinson split their two reps Mahogany bested Alim McNeill twice Tyleik Williams overpowered Mays, but Mays rebounded by taking down Chris Smith Tate Ratledge got wins against Mekhi Wingo and Levi Onwuzurike Blake Miller took care of Tyler Lacy, but DJ Wonnum caught him with a snatch-and-pull Reserves Larry Borom beat Wonnum and Ahmed Hassanein Miles Frazier (at RT) stallmated with Anthony Lucas, beat Eric O’Neill, then shifted inside to RG and beat Wingo Juice Scruggs locked down Skyler Gill-Howard, but lost to Lacy Melvin Priestly beat Gill-Howard and Tyre West Seth McLaughlin beat Myles Adams and Aidan Keanaaina Jacob Saylors stepping up With Gibbs holding out and Sion Vaki leaving practice early after getting poked in the eye, Jacob Saylors stepped into a larger role behind Isiah Pacheco. Saylors made the most of his opportunity, bursting through a right side gap for a 20+ yard gain during 11-on-11s, then closing out practice with a 40+ yard wheel route that he took untouched for a touchdown. Saylors has quietly had a solid camp, and depending on Gibbs and Vaki’s situations, could suddenly be in line for more touches and a chance to prove his worth. The Christian Izien domino effect Christian Izien has worked past the flu bug that kept him from practicing the first three days of camp, and while he returned to the field on Sunday, Monday was a truer representation of how his presence can create a domino effect on the secondary depth chart. At practice, Izien opened as the starting nickelback, working inside of D.J. Reed and Rock Ya-Sin or Ennis Rakestraw. However, when the second team took the field, Izien shifted back to safety alongside Thomas Harper. As a result of Izien’s presence, Roger McCreary shifted to the second team, operating on the outside opposite Khalil Dorsey when only two corners were on the field, then kicking inside when they went to nickel. When Izien took a breather from second-team safety, it was UDFA rookie Aamaris Brown who stepped in as his replacement, who appears to have possibly jumped Dan Jackson and Loren Strickland on the depth chart. With McCreary on the second team, rookie Keith Abney was bumped to the third team. Like McCreary, Abney worked as an outside corner in two CB sets (opposite Nick Whiteside), then kicking inside in nickel sets. Quick hitters The Tyler Lacy hype looks deserved and is gaining momentum. On Monday, during 11-on-11s at big end, he burst into the backfield and forced Jared Goff to throw the ball away. A few plays later, he kicked inside to defensive tackle and overpowered a second-team guard right into Teddy Bridgewater. DJ Wonnum sets a mean edge. Ahmed Hassanein delivered a powerful double-swipe and swim move to beat Colby Sorsdal in 1-on-1s. Hassanein’s intensity is ramping up on the field. After beating Thomas Gordon on a special teams drill, he stared…

title: Detroit Lions training camp Day 5 injury news: Optimism for Brian Branch’s return
summary: While the Detroit Lions’ injury list continues to grow, there is some potential good news on the horizon. It begins with Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph, who continue to show signs of progress toward returning to the field, but there are also a few players whose injuries may not be as serious as they look. […]
full_text: Detroit Lions safety Brian Branch (32) walks off the field after practice during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Wednesday, July 29, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co While the Detroit Lions’ injury list continues to grow, there is some potential good news on the horizon. It begins with Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph, who continue to show signs of progress toward returning to the field, but there are also a few players whose injuries may not be as serious as they look. We break it all down below with our Day 5 training camp injury report. Note: All injury designations are unofficial based on my own observations unless otherwise stated. Returned to practice: RT Blake Miller (unknown) Miller didn’t miss Sunday’s practice, but he was limited to individual drills. Dan Campbell said on Monday that they were being precautious and he would be a full go during Monday’s practice. He was taking every visible right tackle first-team rep during the first padded practice of camp. While the job seems safely his over veteran Larry Borom, Campbell continued to preach caution until we see everyone in pads. “We like where Blake (is), we feel like has gotten a little bit better every day, and that’s a good thing,” Campbell said Monday. “Larry’s played in this league. But now here we go, now it’s real. So, we can talk about how good somebody looks, how much better they get without pads on. Well, now the pads are on. So yeah, anybody’s got a shot. So, we’ll see what it looks like. My gut tells me that Blake’s going to continue to grow, but we’ll see.” Not practicing: RB Jahmyr Gibbs ( not-injury related ) TE Milles Kitselman (leg) OT Giovanni Manu (NFI) EDGE Derrick Moore (groin) EDGE Payton Turner (back) LB Jimmy Rolder (leg) Campbell gave full injury updates on Miles Kitselman and Derrick Moore . Kitselman is expected to miss significant time, while Moore’s timetable is more optimistic with a minor strain that should sideline him 7-10 days. Still no sign of Payton Turner, who only lasted a day in training camp before a back injury. It’s worth noting, at the time, Campbell did not believe it was serious. “He’s got a little bit of a stiff back, so just got that, but we don’t think that’ll be anything serious,” Campbell said last Thursay. Out, but working with trainers G Ben Bartch (undisclosed) TE Tyler Conklin (PUP, calf) S Kerby Joseph (PUP, knee) S Brian Branch (PUP, Achilles) Conklin continues to put in serious work with trainers and appears to be one of the players closer to returning from injury. Bartch missed a second straight day of practice with an undisclosed injury. But the significant news here comes from Brian Branch getting his first on-field work during training camp. It was just a relatively short session with a trainer (15-20 minutes, by my estimate), but he was moving at a good speed and doing some change of direction things. Remember that early in camp, Campbell broke the news that Branch could return to practice as soon as the end of training camp. “Branch is doing well. His will be—obviously PUP, there’s no setbacks,” Campbell said. “Take it as it comes and we’ll see. I’m sure late training camp, maybe early September he can start practicing. We’ll see.” If he returns to practice and avoids the regular season PUP, it would mean he would not have to sit the first four games of the season, although it still seems unlikely he’ll be ready for Week 1. Kerby Joseph’s trainer work lasted significantly longer than Branch’s, and he continues to work up a good sweat. Left practice early RB Sione Vaki (eye) TE Anthony Firkser (leg) WR Lawrence Keys (leg) On the second play of full team padded practice, Vaki took a carry and stayed down for a considerable amount of time, forcing the team to move further down field to continue the drills. Eventually, he exited the field and did not return to practice. The team reported that he got poked in the eye. Jacob Saylors bumped to RB2 for the rest of the day with Gibbs and Vaki out. On the final play of an early 11-on-11 session, Firkser limped off the field with a leg injury. He was not able to make his way to the building on his own, so he was carted inside the facility. I did not see Lawrence Keys’ injury and can only go off the team report of a “leg” injury.

title: Tuesday Cheese Curds: Chris McClellan makes an early push
summary: The Packers’ defensive line is facing a lot of questions this season. How will they answer them? If it comes down to a single player, the answer might have to be Chris McClellan. We’ve written quite a bit about McClellan in the months since he was drafted, but it’s been a waiting game to see […]
full_text: Chris McClellan #55 of the Green Bay Packers rides a bicycle while pointing toward the crowd during the Green Bay Packers Training Camp at Ray Nitschke Field in Ashwaubenon, Wisconsin, on August 2, 2026. (Photo by Ross Harried/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images The Packers’ defensive line is facing a lot of questions this season. How will they answer them? If it comes down to a single player, the answer might have to be Chris McClellan. We’ve written quite a bit about McClellan in the months since he was drafted , but it’s been a waiting game to see if any of our analysis would find the mark. So far, it looks like the Packers were on the money with their faith in the rookie defensive tackle. The Missouri product has been running with the first team early in camp as other defensive linemen work their way back from injury. What does that really mean when most of camp has been un-padded and McClellan’s contributions have come against his own teammates? Well, pretty much nothing, but we also can’t just flat out ignore it, either. If the Packers’ defense is going to rise to its full potential, the Packers are going to need McClellan to play well throughout this season, but especially early. With Micah Parsons on the mend, the Packers will need all the help they can get, and with the defensive line still vulnerable, an early push from McClellan could go a long way.
