title: Vikings Training Camp Notes: 8/3 Edition
summary: Since my last training camp notes, there have been three practices- the rained out practice on Friday that was moved indoors and turned into a walk-through practice, so nothing significant to report on that one. Saturday’s practice was significant in the quarterback competition and also positive when it comes to contributions from this year’s draft […]
full_text: Since my last training camp notes, there have been three practices- the rained out practice on Friday that was moved indoors and turned into a walk-through practice, so nothing significant to report on that one. Saturday’s practice was significant in the quarterback competition and also positive when it comes to contributions from this year’s draft class. Today’s practice, which I attended, has also been significant as the first padded practice of training camp. Quarterback Competition Trends For J.J. McCarthy, the first few practices featured competent short passing, with a high completion percentage and shorter depth of target. Perhaps that was McCarthy being more conservative in his decision making and avoiding more difficult passes that could lead to mistakes, perhaps that was McCarthy simply trying to build a rhythm with a focus on completions. Perhaps those were simply the best options on a given play, or perhaps those were the best options McCarthy processed on a given play. Whatever the case, this was largely the McCarthy we saw last year in training camp. Last year, the overall impression of McCarthy in training camp was that he was fine, as in some degree of okay or solid. He was not spectacular overall, although each practice he managed a deep ball or two that was completed, and seemed to have developed a good rapport with Jordan Addison (Justin Jefferson didn’t participate in training camp last year). But McCarthy’s targets were largely short targets with occasional intermediate ones. He was trying to gain a comfort level with the offense and in reading defenses, which led to some understandable indecision and more difficulty connecting downfield or really attempting much downfield. Brian Flores’ defense often won the day, which was understandable as well as defenses often have the upper hand early, and the first-team offense was missing some keys pieces in Jefferson and Christian Darrisaw. So, McCarthy’s performance was seen as basically fine under the circumstances. He was still developing and this was his first training camp with significant reps and Brian Flores’ defense was throwing a lot at him and led to a number of would-be sacks if defensive players were allowed to hit the quarterback. McCarthy showed he had a strong arm (some questioned his arm strength coming out) and he often drilled wide receivers with his fast ball, especially on shorter routes. I remember one time McCarthy hit Josh Oliver in the back of the end zone in a red zone drill and the ball went off Oliver’s outstretched hand and hit the crossbar so hard it rang like a bell and caused the it to shake back and forth afterward. That led to a brief discussion with Kevin O’Connell- presumably regarding managing velocity. So, while McCarthy might have been said to be doing fine under the circumstances last year in training camp, there were some hints of issues that were to come in the regular season. And with that being McCarthy’s first season playing, the expectation was for some growing pains but also that he could have one of the better first seasons for a quarterback given the strength of the team around him. Most said McCarthy had the best landing spot of any of the quarterbacks selected in the first round in 2024. I mention all that because it provides more context and history in examining McCarthy’s career development path as a pro- in addition to his performance during the regular season last year. Most agree that McCarthy struggled the first half of his starts, except the fourth quarter of the week one Bears game, but showed some improvement over the last half of the season, although some point out that came against bottom tier passing defenses (Commanders ranked 27th is pass defense DVOA, the Cowboys 31st, and the Packers played their second-string in McCarthy’s last start). So both are true. Fast forward to this year’s training camp, and we largely see a repeat of the McCarthy we saw in last year’s training camp. I don’t think we’ve seen the over-amped velocity issues to the extent of last year, and many commented on his improved mechanics/footwork over the offseason program, but we really haven’t seen much of the layering/touch passes that were missing last season. We’ve seen completions, but are we really seeing improvement? The answer so far is probably not much. Saturday’s practice was also a setback for McCarthy as he struggled with accuracy and processing that led to his worst practice of training camp this year. An example: Looks like McCarthy with 1st team vs. 2nd team defense. McCarthy holds the ball too long… would’ve been a sack but slightly off with the throw as well. https://t.co/0u5jo5EEI2 — Warren Ludford (@wludford) August 2, 2026 Here McCarthy holds the ball too long and would’ve been sacked by Ivan Pace but still missed on the late checkdown to Jordan Mason. His footwork was problematic, demonstrating he hasn’t mastered that after reportedly spending the offseason working on it. Of course this is just one snap (and the only one I’ve seen of McCarthy on Saturday) but it is an extension of issues we saw with McCarthy last season. I have not read any comments to date of observers reporting McCarthy processing faster in training camp. There haven’t been reports from beat writers of his layering passes or throwing with anticipation either. There have been reports from the offseason program saying McCarthy’s footwork/mechanics looked improved/smoother/changed, but based on the video above it appears that improvement is not consistent. After viewing McCarthy for the first time in person in training camp this year, in today’s first padded practice, my overriding impression is that 2026 training camp McCarthy looks very similar to 2025 training camp McCarthy. In fact, he looked worse today than he was overall last year in training camp. But taking a longer view of McCarthy’s development arc up to now, I’m not really seeing improvement from last year. He still looks a bit skittish in the pocket with mainly short targets- dump offs, check downs, or short over-the-middle routes. It doesn’t appear that things have really slowed down for him, as the saying goes for quarterbacks after gaining some experience and getting used to the speed and competition and complexity of the NFL. So, bottom line on J.J. McCarthy at this point is that I’m not seeing any noticeable or significant improvement. I don’t think that’s really a controversial assessment at this point. It’s disappointing to be sure, and I would be surprised if the Vikings’ coaching staff didn’t have a similar viewpoint. Kyler Murray, since the start of training camp and even toward the end of the offseason program, looked to be working through some mishaps and difficulties learning what other veteran quarterbacks like Kirk Cousins and Sam Darnold have described as a complex offensive scheme. Murray appeared to be working the ball downfield with his pass attempts with some impressive throws alongside some misfires. He had some interceptions and some miscommunications with receivers, fumbled snaps, and also some long passes that hit receivers in stride. As a veteran starting quarterback with seven years of experience, Kyler Murray has developed the core skills required for the job. Namely the ability to process quickly and deliver the ball accurately, make all the throws, pocket poise/management, and good decision making. His issues are more with consistency with these core skills, rather than still needing to develop them. Murray also demonstrates advanced skills like throwing with anticipation and his off-schedule scramble/run ability. In more recent years as a starting quarterback Murray has thrown more shorter passes than in his early years, and has done very well with those in terms of accuracy and completions, but hasn’t been as successful with deeper passes since he led the league in PFF deep pass grade (99.2) in 2021. Some say the changes to his receiver group since 2021 and the team overall…

title: Patriots training camp primer: Day 9 practice preview, schedule, more
summary: The New England Patriots are in the middle of a challenging training camp stretch, with Tuesday’s session the second in a string of five straight. The expectation is that the team will once again be in full pads, which suggests that the level of competition and physicality will remain high. With that said, here is […]
full_text: Foxborough, MA - August 1: New England Patriots linebacker Gabe Jacas runs during training camp at Gillette Stadium on August 1, 2026. (Photo by Jonathan Wiggs/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images The New England Patriots are in the middle of a challenging training camp stretch, with Tuesday’s session the second in a string of five straight. The expectation is that the team will once again be in full pads, which suggests that the level of competition and physicality will remain high. With that said, here is what you need to know about camp practice No. 9. Schedule After Monday’s session was moved indoors due to inclement weather, practice will be taking place on the fields behind Gillette Stadium on Tuesday. This, in turn, means that fans will be able to attend the session again. 9:30 a.m. ET: Mike Vrabel press conference 10:15 a.m. ET: Practice ca. 12:15 p.m. ET: Player availability (RB TreVeyon Henderson, WR DeMario Douglas, C Jared Wilson, ED Dre’Mont Jones, ED Gabe Jacas, LB Namdi Obiazor) As always, of course, the schedule is tentative and subject to change. For more information, please visit our Pats Pulpit Training Camp Guide . Story of the day How is A.J. Brown looking one day after dislocating his thumb ? The Patriots’ star offseason addition admitted after Monday’s session that he hurt his thumb, but that it was popped back in. He finished practice with four catches, including three during 11-on-11s, and no visible limitations. However, it remains to be seen whether or not his status changes heading into another fully-padded practice. Injuries to monitor NFI: S Brenden Schooler PUP: TE C.J. Dippre, ED Harold Landry III Practice absentees: OL Caedan Wallace, DT David Blay Jr, CB Carlton Davis III New injuries: WR A.J. Brown Monday’s practice saw running back Terrell Jennings return from the non-football injury list, adding a new dimension to the competition for the third running back spot. In the meantime, Carlton Davis has now missed a week’s worth of practices, with Caedan Wallace also out after getting banged up on Saturday. David Blay Jr’s absence could be related to the signing of fellow defensive tackle Casey Rogers , who took his jersey number in what might be an ominous sign for the undrafted rookie. Players to watch OL James Hudson III: A reserve offensive tackle entering camp, Hudson saw some action at guard on Monday. For the offseason signing, who has had his issues throughout the summer, adding a second position might be the difference between a spot on the roster or practice squad and being cut for good. ED Gabe Jacas: The Patriots’ second-round draft pick managed to up his participation level on Monday, but he remains limited. Will Tuesday see him further add to his workload? And if so, will he begin challenging Elijah Ponder for starter reps on the edge? LB Chad Muma: The linebacker depth chart behind Robert Spillane and Christian Elliss remains unsettled, but Muma looks like the current frontrunner for the third spot. He spent some time with the starters on Monday and looked good particularly as a run defender. Him playing a similar role again on Tuesday might be a sign that he has taken the lead in the LB3 competition. The backup cornerbacks: Speaking of competitions, the one for the fifth and possible sixth cornerback spots is heating up. On Monday, rookies Channing Canada and Karon Prunty were among the standout performers , while Marcella Dial Jr. also remains part of the mix. Kindle Vildor and Kobee Minor, meanwhile, have seemingly slipped over the last few sessions. Pats Pulpit will have you covered throughout the day, so please make sure to regularly check back to patspulpit.com for all the latest news from camp. Credentialed Patriots beat writers Brian Hines ( @iambrianhines ), Andrew Guindon ( @NestPgs ) and Taylor Kyles ( @tkyles39 ) will bring you live updates from camp on their Twitter/X feeds, so please make sure to give them a follow.

title: Patriots secondary emphasizing takeaways as practice intensity heats up
summary: The New England Patriots’ secondary is looking to generate more takeaways during training camp. After Monday’s practice moved indoors due to heavy rainfall, increased verbal banter from both the offense and defense fuels friendly competition between the two sides. New England’s third-year safety Dell Pettus helped spark that competitive energy for the defensive backs after […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - JUNE 02: Dell Pettus #24 of the New England Patriots walks on to the field during New England Patriots OTA on June 2, 2026, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Summer Lamont/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New England Patriots’ secondary is looking to generate more takeaways during training camp. After Monday’s practice moved indoors due to heavy rainfall, increased verbal banter from both the offense and defense fuels friendly competition between the two sides. New England’s third-year safety Dell Pettus helped spark that competitive energy for the defensive backs after picking off a Drake Maye deep pass on Saturday . That turnover marked just the defense’s second interception this summer through the first seven sessions. “It was definitely a great feeling,” Pettus said of the pick following Monday’s practice. “Just trusting the process, the scheme and the technique. It’s something that we talk about all the time — it’s just like, do your job. You can do your job one million times, be in a good spot, and never get the ball your way. But we have a really good quarterback, so he rarely makes bad decisions.” After the play concluded, Pettus ran toward the end zone and punted the ball over the fence in celebration of securing the first defensive takeaway since day two of summer camp. That energy stems from a conversation the safeties had before that practice. “In that situation, I just think I was able to be in a good spot, get rewarded and make a good play,” Pettus added. “The defense needed that. We were talking about getting more takeaways at practice and getting more turnovers. And I think [the pick] was just like an energizer at practice.” Veteran Kevin Byard led that conversation. The Patriots’ free-agency signing spent six seasons with the Tennessee Titans under Mike Vrabel, and he’s carrying the same edge and competitive mindset as his head coach does in the safety’s first year in New England. “After those first few practices, [Byard] brought us up, and he was like, ‘We need takeaways today,’” Pettus shared. “Before we went to any competitive team activity, he said, ‘We need more takeaways; we’re going to go out here and go get the football. Forget what everybody else is talking about; forget what the coaches talk about. This is our team. This is our defensive backfield.’ And like, it’s up to us to go get it, because the coaches can’t play for us. And I told him I thought that was great to hear just because he set the tone for us that day.” Byard acknowledged that the intensity in training camp is “heating up,” and that’s what this time of the offseason is for. A frequent matchup this summer has been between A.J. Brown and Christian Gonzalez. Brown secured a pass from Maye under smothering coverage from Gonzalez during Monday’s seven-on-seven period and turned to the cornerback with friendly banter. “I think it was competitive. You know, a heavy emphasis on [the] red zone,” Byard said about Monday’s session. “We got some really competitive periods, whether it was one-on-ones or team … Obviously it’s still early in training camp, so it’s a lot of back and forth. But it’s been fun. I think it’s just the competitive spirit of this team at every position and level. Offense and defense [are] just trying to get better, and I think we’re pushing each other.” Entering his 11th year in the NFL, Byard is coming off a First-Team All-Pro selection, leading the league with seven interceptions for a new career total of 36. Adding a ball hawk like Byard not only elevates outcomes on the field for New England in 2026 but also impacts the development of the safety corps. “How to get the football,” Pettus said of what he’s learned from Byard thus far. “He’s such an impressive guy … But he came in week one, and he’s asking our coaches and challenging them about why we’re doing things and how that’s going to help us get the football. As a young defensive back, you always want the football, but hearing that’s his process no matter what he’s doing, it’s, ‘How am I going to get the football? What can I do to get myself in a better position to get the football?’ “I took a step back, and I was like, I don’t think I ever really thought like that … He’s really breaking it down in a science-type of way of where am I going to be and how am I putting myself in a position to get the football? Because if I can’t get the football, I’m not doing my job. You can tell he’s a veteran and why he led this league in interceptions last season. I look forward to working with him this season because I feel like all he’s going to do is help me and everybody around him be a better player.”
author: Andrew Guindon

title: Drake Maye breaks down the Patriots wide receiver room
summary: The New England Patriots wide receiver room is one of the deepest position groups on the roster. Following the additions of A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs this offseason, New England’s top seven now features Brown, Doubs, DeMario Douglas, Mack Hollins, Kayshon Boutte, Kyle Williams, and Efton Chism III. Rather than viewing the room as crowded, […]
full_text: Foxborough, MA - July 28: New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye and wide receiver Mack Hollins shake hands at training camp on July 28, 2026. (Photo by Danielle Parhizkaran/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images The New England Patriots wide receiver room is one of the deepest position groups on the roster. Following the additions of A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs this offseason, New England’s top seven now features Brown, Doubs, DeMario Douglas, Mack Hollins, Kayshon Boutte, Kyle Williams, and Efton Chism III. Rather than viewing the room as crowded, Drake Maye sees it as competitive. Appearing on SiriusXM NFL Radio on Monday, the quarterback broke down the group, starting with his two newest targets. “Start off the bat with A.J., having him coming in and kind of set the tone for the room. I think him and Romeo — the guys in there, they’ve really enjoyed the competitive drive in that room. People say it’s a crowded room but, as you know as receivers go, you’re going to need everybody. “With A.J., the ability for him to not only make me look good, but go out there and make plays and catch the football; we were watching some of his ‘target tape’ the other day, and him being able to take a slant, take an under, and take it to the house. But at the same time he has route craft and he knows you can’t just win everything physically. At some point, you have to use routes, use his technique, and he does a great job. “I think Romeo has done a great job coming in here and learning the offense. He hasn’t been in an offense like this that has some decision-making [for receivers]. I think he’s getting better and better as he’s gotten through OTAs and even in camp, he’s making some great plays for us. He’s kind of shifty and has a little wiggle to him that I didn’t really expect throwing to him in camp.” Through eight training camp practices, Maye’s chemistry with both Brown and Doubs has progressed nicely. When the offense breaks the huddle in 11 personnel, those two are stapled on Maye’s sides. In the slot, however, has primarily been DeMario Douglas. “Next up, we have Pop in the slot,” Maye said. “I think Pop’s the one from last year that’s just continuing to get better and better. You see it every year. From my rookie year being with him to Year 3 now, just kind of the connection and knowing how he runs routes. I think he does a great job in man; it’s hard to cover him. So he’s going to be a big piece of what we do when we’re in ‘11’ personnel. I’m looking forward to seeing how he continues to grow and make more plays this year. I think he definitely will.” Last season, veteran free agent addition Mack Hollins led all Patriots wide receivers playing 68 percent of the offensive snaps. Hollins turned in a productive season catching 46 passes for 550 yards while being a strong veteran presence in the locker room. “Mack is kind of the Swiss-Army knife. He does it all,” Maye explained. “He’s obviously big in the run game, but I think Coach [McDaniels] rewards him with play-action off it. So he always says, ‘Just throw it to me on the in-cuts.’ He loves [that]. He’s big and has that demeanor to him that people feed off, that energy about him.” New England’s wide receiver room then features a pair of second-year players in Kyle Williams and Efton Chism III, who are both pushing for larger roles this season. “Kyle, last year, was kind of a big-play guy,” Maye said. “I think he’s worked hard to be able to [run] different routes and be able to build his route-arsenal coming into his second year. I’m looking forward to seeing how that goes. And obviously he’s a deep threat, he’s fast, can run by people – which is always something the defense has to think about. “Then Chis, you can’t forget about Efton Chism. He kind of became one of those guys late in the season when Mack got hurt, he had a role where we tried to replace what Mack does. I think the biggest thing with Chis is he’s just doing the right things and making a lot of plays. He was a big preseason guy last year and so he’ll probably continue to make plays.” Last but not least, Maye mentioned wide receiver Kayshon Boutte. The twos chemistry has been apparent over their two seasons together, but the 24-year old has been in the middle of trade talks this offseason as he enters the last year of his rookie contract and has been pushed down the depth chart. “Probably the last one is Boutte,” Maye said. “He’s a comforting receiver to throw to. You get to know him – same thing as Pop, this is my third year with Boutte and I was throwing to him on scout team when I was a rookie. Now we’re making plays; I threw my first touchdown to him. He’s just one of those guys that is quiet, does everything the right way, cares about his teammates, and he just puts his head down and works. There’s a lot of talk about whatever you want to say with Boutte, but he just continues to make plays. He’s going to be in the right spot and make a play on the football.” Whether there is any significance to Maye mentioning Boutte last is unknown. It is notable, however, that the quarterback also did not mention Boutte when discussing his pass catchers last week, instead highlighting Brown, Doubs, Douglas, tight end Hunter Henry, and running backs Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson. How the logjam at wide receiver resolves itself is a question that will be answered later this summer. But for now, it is a good problem to have with all seven off to a strong start this training camp.
author: Brian Hines

title: Patriots 2026 scouting report for TE Tanner Arkin
summary: The New England Patriots made some significant investments in their tight end group this offseason. However, at the end of the day, it might not be a surprise if the most impactful player of the bunch ends up being one who flew largely under the radar: undrafted rookie Tanner Arkin. One of the pleasant surprises […]
full_text: Jul 28, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots tight end Tanner Arkin (84) dose a drill during training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New England Patriots made some significant investments in their tight end group this offseason. However, at the end of the day, it might not be a surprise if the most impactful player of the bunch ends up being one who flew largely under the radar: undrafted rookie Tanner Arkin. One of the pleasant surprises of this year’s training camp, Arkin currently looks like the Patriots’ top blocking tight end. It is a role he is well-suited to fill. Hard facts Name: Tanner Arkin Position: Tight end Jersey number: 84 Opening day age: 23 (7/7/2003) Measurements : 6’3 5/8”, 262 lbs, 10 1/8” hand size, 32 1/4” arm length, 77 5/8” wingspan, 4.88s 40-yard dash, 7.44s 3-cone drill, 4.50s short shuttle, 33 1/2” vertical jump, 9’5” broad jump, 21 bench press reps, 5.45 Relative Athletic Score Experience NFL: New England Patriots (2026-) | College: Colorado State (2021-22), Illinois (2023-25) A three-star recruit coming out of Fossil Ridge in Fort Collins, CO, Arkin started his college career less than six miles from his high school field: he joined Colorado State in 2021, and in two season as a Ram played 15 games with eight starts. Catching 15 passes for 125 yards along the way, he decided to enter the transfer portal shortly after his redshirt freshman campaign. Arkin took his talents to Illinois, where he saw prominent action right out of the gate before becoming a fixture in 2024 and 2025. A team captain both seasons, he finished his tenure in Champaign with the second-most career starts by a tight end in school history (29 of 38 games). He also hauled in 30 catches for 226 yards and six touchdowns before leaving school in 2026. Primarily a blocking tight end in college, Arkin received limited hype entering the NFL. He eventually went undrafted and joined the Patriots as a rookie free agent. Scouting report Strengths: From his build to his tenacity and physical play style, Arkin is a blocking tight end through and through. Checking in at just under 6-foot-4 and 262 pounds, he is able to hunker down as a pass protector and take the battle to the defense as a run blocker. He uses his big hands and natural grip strength well to latch onto defenders, and keeps his feet churning to drive them off the ball. He also has the core strength and raw power to hold his own 1-on-1 against defensive edges, as well as a natural feel for leverage and balance. In addition, he operates well when asked to block on the move and can execute down and reach blocks from his alignment on the edge. #Patriots TE Tanner Arkin (#85) run blocking pic.twitter.com/HmbZyOKI35 — Taylor Kyles (@tkyles39) April 27, 2026 Weaknesses: Arkin catching only 45 passes during his college career did not happen by accident. He simply lacks the foot speed and agility to function as anything but a rudimentary part of a passing game, while also not having the length to be used as a consistent contested-catch target. Even when he was thrown the ball, he has been unable to do a lot with it as far as picking up yards after the catch or breaking tackles is concerned. Even as a blocker, he is not a finished product. He oftentimes forces his way to success, winning by brute strength rather than an advanced technical setup particularly in regards to his hand usage. 2025 review Stats : 13 games (13 starts) | 684 offensive snaps, 156 special teams snaps | 17 targets, 13 catches (76.5%), 114 receiving yards (8.8/catch), 2 TDs, 1 drop | 8 QB pressures surrendered (2 sacks, 2 hits, 4 hurries) | 2 penalties (incl. 0 declined/offsetting) Season recap: Arkin earned a starting role in the Illinois offense in 2024, and he retained it heading into his final season in college. That was not the only continuation between those two years: he also was once again voted a team captain and ended up seeing a majority of his snaps as a blocker: either run blocking or pass protecting on 72.5% of his offensive snaps, he set new career highs in terms of usage in both categories. Arkin blocked the run on 368 snaps, and the pass on 128. He was at his best in the running game and helped Illinois average 4.6 yards per carry and score 11 touchdowns when running outside the tackles. Those numbers are naturally not only a byproduct of his presence on the field. That said, his steady usage is an illustration of his success and the trust head coach Bret Bielema and his staff had in him. As a pass protector, meanwhile, Arkin surrendered a career-worst eight pressures, including two sacks. His 6.6% pressure rate allowed, however, on par with his 2024 season. In the receiving department, Arkin was again somewhat quiet and went catch-less in five of 13 games. The others saw him post career-highs in yards (114) and yards per catch (8.8), but his impact was still relatively inconsequential — a result of both his role as well as his comparatively uninspiring abilities as a receiver. After the season, Arkin did participate in the American Bowl. He was neither invited to any of the premier college showcases nor the Scouting Combine. 2026 preview Position: Y-tight end | Ability: Depth player/Role player | Contract: Signed through 2028 (2029 RFA) What will be his role? Arkin is the prototypical blocking tight end and will be used accordingly as a Patriot. His first eight training camp practices already show what this means: he mostly lines up inline as a Y-tight end to help create a push in the run game and occasionally provide an extra body in pass protection. Unsurprisingly, he has been employed in a limited fashion as a receiver. The 23-year-old projects as a second or third tight end. What is his growth potential? It would be easy to say that Arkin has room for growth as a receiver, but the expectations in that regard should still be tempered; his abilities and athletic skill are simply not at the level of a regular pass game contributor outside of helping shore up the protection. When it comes to his blocking, he already is looking like an NFL player but should still improve with more time and experience. He therefore has the potential to become a starter-level TE2 and one of the league’s better blocking specialists at the position. Does he have positional versatility? Arkin’s versatility manifests itself differently that for other players. He won’t move all around the formation as a receiver, even though he does have some experience in that regard. He also should not be expected to see a high number of snaps as a receiving outlet. He is mostly a blocker, but one who can perform his duties from various alignments inline or in the backfield. He additionally brings extensive special teams experience to New England, having seen most of his action on kickoff return as well as a protector on punts, field goals and extra points. What is his salary cap situation? Arkin’s salary cap number of $890,833 consists of an $885,000 base salary as well as a fully-guaranteed signing bonus proration of $5,833. In addition, the deal includes $145,000 in salary guarantees. At the moment and with the NFL’s Top 51 rule in place, only the signing bonus counts against New England’s cap. How safe is his roster spot? Typically, undrafted rookies are longshots to make a team’s roster. Arkin, however, does not look like your typical UDFA. He did not particularly stand out during open offseason workouts, but has regularly repped with the starters since the beginning of training camp and at this point can be regarded the team’s top run-blocking tight end. If there is one rookie free agent to make the team this year, it very well could be him. Summary: The season-ending injury suffered by free agency acquisition Julian Hill changed the Patriots’ tight end room and robbed them of their designated blocking tight end. Arkin, however, appears to have picked up the slack and…

title: What signing Casey Rogers means for the Patriots
summary: After releasing linebacker Otis Reese, the New England Patriots headed into the weekend with one open spot on their roster. They filled it on Monday: the team of head coach Mike Vrabel signed defensive tackle Casey Rogers following a successful workout. Let’s asses what the move means. Defensive line TBD Besides filling out their 90-man […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - AUGUST 08: Casey Rogers #91 of the New York Giants warms up prior to an NFL football game against the Detroit Lions at MetLife Stadium on August 8, 2024 in East Rutherford, NJ. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images After releasing linebacker Otis Reese , the New England Patriots headed into the weekend with one open spot on their roster. They filled it on Monday: the team of head coach Mike Vrabel signed defensive tackle Casey Rogers following a successful workout. Let’s asses what the move means. Defensive line TBD Besides filling out their 90-man roster, the Patriots now also have 10 defensive tackles on their roster; the team effectively replaced Otis Reese’s roster spot with an interior defensive lineman. However, as a seemingly trivial look at the jersey numbers shows, more change might be afoot: Interior defensive line (10): Milton Williams (97), Christian Barmore (90), Cory Durden (94), Joshua Farmer (92), Leonard Taylor III (93), Eric Gregory (95), Jeremiah Pharms Jr. (98), Isaiah Iton (62), David Blay Jr. (96), Casey Rogers (96) At the moment, the team has assigned both Rogers and undrafted rookie David Blay Jr. the No. 96 jersey. That might in itself not mean much, but with the latter ominously absent from practice on Monday , it appears another move could very well be on the horizon. For now, all we know is that Rogers is on the team and that Blay Jr’s status is unclear. Immense athleticism Rogers projects as a rotational member of the Patriots’ interior defensive line who is best suited to attack from a 3-technique position. More of a pass rusher than a run stopper, he brings an intriguing athletic profile to the table: his 9.82 Relative Athletic Score had him ranked 34th out of 1,809 DTs coming out of college between 1987 and 2024, the year he entered the league as a rookie free agent. The Patriots signed an impressive athlete today. — Bernd Buchmasser (@berndbuchmasser.bsky.social) 2026-08-03T22:01:21.852Z So far in his career, Rogers has not been able to make use of his athletic skills. He has played just 35 defensive snaps over three career games and has no statistics to his name. Maybe another change of scenery — he also had a brief stint in Buffalo last summer — will help him properly get his career started. Familiarity The Patriots coaching staff has some familiarity with Rogers. Defensive coordinator Zak Kuhr, for example, was a defensive assistant with the Giants when they signed the Oregon product as a UDFA in 2024. Also part of the New York staff were Shane Bowen, the former Giants DC who came to New England as a defensive analyst earlier this offseason, as well as vice president of player personnel Ryan Cowden. That familiarity might not have been the ultimate deciding factor in hiring Rogers over fellow workout participant Jared Penning, but it certainly did not hurt either. The 27-year-old having some experience in a similar system should make for an easier transition. No cap changes Rogers is entering his third season in the NFL, but his addition as the 91st player on the team — including roster-exempt offensive tackle Lorenz Metz — does not have an impact on New England’s salary cap. His expected $960,000 minimum salary pact does not qualify for Top 51 status, and no guarantees will be part of the pact he signed to come to Foxborough. As of Monday afternoon, cap expert Miguel Benzan’s calculations have the Patriots $33.7 million under the salary cap.

title: 6 performances of note from the Patriots’ eighth training camp practice
summary: The New England Patriots practiced behind semi-closed doors on Monday, moving their session into their Field House due to inclement weather. The conditions may have prevented fans from attending, but they did nothing to stop the competitiveness. To recap the eighth practice of the summer, please visit our Patriots training camp notebook. In the meantime, […]
full_text: Jul 28, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots wide receiver Mack Hollins (13) catches the ball during training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New England Patriots practiced behind semi-closed doors on Monday, moving their session into their Field House due to inclement weather. The conditions may have prevented fans from attending, but they did nothing to stop the competitiveness. To recap the eighth practice of the summer, please visit our Patriots training camp notebook . In the meantime, here is who caught our eye during the two-hour session. Standout of the day WR Mack Hollins: With other wide receivers drawing most of the attention early in training camp, Hollins had a relatively quiet start to his second summer in Foxborough. That changed on Monday, with the veteran taking center stage and leading all receivers in catches and touchdowns during 11-on-11s. Working as a second-string option behind the starting trio of A.J. Brown, Romeo Doubs and DeMario Douglas, he hauled in five passes including three scores. It wasn’t just the numbers but more so the fashion in which the ever-flamboyant wideout produced: he caught the pass all over the field and won his matchups regardless of the route he was asked to run. He failed to haul in his lone end zone target from Drake Maye, but that was the only blemish on an otherwise solid day. Other performances of note WR Efton Chism III: Mack Hollins’ workout buddy made the most of his opportunities on Monday, including seeing some time with Drake Maye and the top offense in lieu of an injured Kyle Williams. He finished with three receptions in team drills, including an impressive high-point touchdown over Marcellas Dial, and also was part of the first kickoff returners duo alongside Terrell Jennings. LB Chad Muma: With undrafted rookie Khalil Jacobs putting some pressure on veteran backups K.J. Britt and Chad Muma, the latter delivered a good performance on Monday. Not only did he see some action with the starters, he also had a pass breakup against Rhamondre Stevenson and looked good as a run defender, including on one quick stuff. CB Channing Canada & CB Karon Prunty: With Carlton Davis remaining sidelined, the Patriots opted to give a pair of rookie cornerbacks some opportunities with the starters. Canada was particularly impressive, allowing just one catch on three targets and also winning a 1-on-1 against Romeo Doubs. Prunty, meanwhile, provided some good coverage on a fade intended for A.J. Brown. CB Kindle Vildor: Entering training camp, Vildor looked like a candidate to challenge for the CB4 spot. However, not only does Charles Woods seem fairly secure in that position, the youngsters have also started taking some reps from him. To make matters worse, he also was beat by Mack Hollins on a fade touchdown. Not the best day for the veteran. Other players worth mentioning include A.J. Brown, who was competitive despite dislocating his thumb during a 1-on-1 drill. Furthermore, Kayshon Boutte had some positive moments again, as did rookies Dametrious Crownover and Quintayvious Hutchins. The Patriots will hold their ninth practice of training camp on Tuesday. If the conditions allow for spectators, the gates will open at 9:15 p.m. ET. Practice is scheduled to kick off at 10:15.

title: Will Campbell entering Year 2 with confidence after strong start to camp
summary: One year into his NFL career, Patriots left tackle Will Campbell no longer feels like a rookie. After starting 17 games, making a run to Super Bowl 60 and playing through a knee injury late in the season, Campbell entered Year 2 with a much better understanding of what it takes to succeed in the […]
full_text: Jul 28, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots offensive tackle Will Campbell (66) works with a member of the coaching staff during training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect One year into his NFL career, Patriots left tackle Will Campbell no longer feels like a rookie. After starting 17 games, making a run to Super Bowl 60 and playing through a knee injury late in the season, Campbell entered Year 2 with a much better understanding of what it takes to succeed in the NFL. “I know what to expect now. I know what it takes to win and play at a high level in this league, and then what stuff can get you hurt,” Campbell said. “Just trying to be more consistent, not make rookie mistakes… Try to be a guy up front that they can count on and help lead the team.” Through the first several padded practices of training camp, Campbell has backed up those words. The offensive tackle has protected Drake Maye’s blindside at a high level and added two more wins to his impressive 1-on-1 record Monday. Campbell has also looked fully healthy after last year’s knee injury and appears to have expanded his pass-set toolbox. “I feel good. My body feels good,” Campbell said. “I’m just trying to be consistent as I possibly can be every single day and get better. And find something that I might not being doing well out at practice and try to attack that the next day. “Getting some great opportunities to go against really good guys. Dre’[Mont Jones] is a guy I played in a game and he’s a really good player. It’s good work for both of us because we’re familiar with each other. It’s kind of like a little chess match out there. So, it’s been fun and I’m excited to keep going.” After being selected fourth overall in the 2025 NFL Draft, Campbell started the Patriots’ first 12 games at left tackle before suffering an MCL injury. He returned for the regular-season finale and remained on Drake Maye’s blindside throughout the Patriots’ four-game playoff run, but struggled as he was not 100 percent healthy. Now healthy entering his second season, Campbell believes the continuity around him has allowed him to play faster and with more confidence. “I think the confidence comes knowing that the guys that we have on this team, everybody believes in each other. Also we’re in the same system for the second year,” Campbell said. “It’s a lot less thinking. OTAs last year when I got here was a lot of installing and taking more time. This year, we were kind of just able to hit the ground running from where we left off. “We added a few new guys, so we had to teach them, but for the most part, we just hit the ground. That’s how we’ve been doing it and that gives you a sense of confidence, just the familiarity and what we’re trying to get done.” Campbell’s new left guard, Alijah Vera-Tucker, believes the differences can help the 22-year old take the next step. “I think that he’s a very smart two-year guy,” Vera-Tucker said. “And I can see him making that very big two-year jump. But I only say that because he is a competitor. I know what kind of talent he has.”

title: Patriots training camp recap: Gabe Jacas increases participation level
summary: After a day off on Sunday the New England Patriots were back to work on Monday. While the rain pushed the team inside the FieldHouse, the pads stayed on as work was inside the red zone with a focus on the run game. Here’s what went down throughout the competitive session. Attendance Absent: CB Carlton […]
full_text: Foxborough, MA - August 1: New England Patriots linebacker Gabe Jacas arrives for training camp at Gillette Stadium on August 1, 2026. (Photo by Jonathan Wiggs/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images After a day off on Sunday the New England Patriots were back to work on Monday. While the rain pushed the team inside the FieldHouse, the pads stayed on as work was inside the red zone with a focus on the run game. Here’s what went down throughout the competitive session. Attendance Absent: CB Carlton Davis III, OL Caedan Wallace (new), DT David Blay Jr. (new) Returnee: RB Terrell Jennings (NFI) Limited: WR Kyle Williams PUP/NFI: TE C.J. Dippre, ED Harold Landry III, S Brenden Schooler Patriots second-year wide receiver Kyle Williams joined practice late on Monday and did not participate after appearing to be banged up on Saturday. Offensive guard Caedan Wallace, who also suffered an injury on Saturday, was then a new absence. The Patriots did activate running back Terrell Jennings off the NFI list. Jennings took a handful of reps in full-team work and worked as a kick returner in his first practice of the summer. Meanwhile, newly-signed defensive tackle Casey Rogers was present. Undrafted rookie David Blay Jr, on the other hand, was not. Takeaways Jacas’ participation: After making his practice debut on Saturday, rookie pass rusher Gabe Jacas upped his participation level on Monday. Jacas took a handful of reps in full-team work and a lone 1-on-1 rep — where he beat depth tackle Lorenz Metz along the edge. OLB coach Mike Smith did get his revenge, however, after Jacas bullrushed the coach over in drills last practice. Smith pretended to give his group instruction with Jacas next in line before tackling him down onto a pad before added some playful punches. Best friends: With Kyle Williams sidelined, best friends Mack Hollins and Efton Chism III were active throughout the day. Hollins hauled in five passes from Tommy DeVito including three touchdowns on a slant, play-action crosser and goal line fade. The big bodied receiver was not able to pull in his lone target from Drake Maye in the end zone. As for Chism, the slot receiver took a handful of reps with Maye’s offense in run packages but caught three passes from DeVito — including another high-point touchdown grab over Marcellas Dial in the back of the end zone. For the rest of the wide receivers, A.J. Brown suffered a dislocated thumb after getting pressed by Christian Gonzalez in a 1-on-1 rep. Brown spent time with the trainers and put on a brace but did not miss any time as he caught three passes from Maye in full-team work. Kayshon Boutte then added two touchdown receptions from DeVito, including a fade in the end zone to end practice. Depth corners: As veteran Carlton Davis remained sidelined, cornerback Charles Woods continued to serve as the top option opposite of Christian Gonzalez and had an impressive breakup along the goal line guarding Romeo Doubs. New England then got a pair of younger cornerbacks increased reps as UDFA Channing Canada received a late first-team rep after a competitive day that featured a pass breakup on Hollins, while rookie Karon Prunty continued to stack positive days by forcing an incompletion on a go-ball against A.J. Brown and nearly hauling in an interception on Behren Morton. 1-on-1s: Work transitioning inside the bubble gave a good look at the offensive and defensive lines for 1-on-1 work. Rookie tackle Caleb Lomu appeared to split his six reps, but overset and was beat inside by both Quintayvious Hutchins and Bradyn Swinson. Hutchins also had an impressive victory over Marcus Bryant as the seventh-round speed rush continues to impress. It was also a strong day for rookie offensive tackle Dametrious Crownover, who used his length to beat Elijah Ponder while also recording a win over Swinson. Other notes: After a slow start to the summer, the Patriots run game had their most competitive day of training camp on Monday. The group also had a pair of positive plays off screens. With the focus on the ground, Drake Maye threw just 14 passes with plenty of play-action and screen work. On 3rd-and-short situations, the Patriots introduced loud sirens on the speakers instead of the usual music to amplify noise. Rookie tight ends Eli Raridon and Tanner Arkin continued to be used with the first-team offense. Raridon had a drop in the end zone on his lone target from DeVito, but appeared to help pave the way in-line next to Morgan Moses for a long touchdown run by Rhamondre Stevenson. Veteran offensive lineman James Hudson got some work at guard on Monday. He won a 1-on-1 rep there with an impressive anchor vs. Jeremiah Pharms. Chad Muma had an impressive pass breakup while guarding Stevenson out of the backfield and was active on run defense with a quick stuff. Kick returners: Terrell Jennings and Efton Chism was the first duo up followed by Lan Larison, Channing Canada, Kobe Prentice, Jam Miller, and Myles Montgomery. The Patriots will be back on the practice fields on Tuesday, which is set to begin at 10:15 a.m. ET where the expectation is to be back in full pads.

title: Jonas Sanker on developing at the Star position
summary: During his media availability after Monday’s training camp, New Orleans Saints safety Jonas Sanker was asked about watching players like Jalen Ramsey play in the slot. It was a great question because Ramsey played the position while Brandon Staley was his defensive coordinator with the Los Angeles Rams. Sanker went on to explain that Ramsey […]
full_text: METAIRIE, LOUISIANA - JULY 30: Jonas Sanker #33 of the New Orleans Saints participates in drills during training camp at Ochsner Sports Performance Center on July 30, 2026 in Metairie, Louisiana. (Photo by Tyler Kaufman/Getty Images) | Getty Images During his media availability after Monday’s training camp, New Orleans Saints safety Jonas Sanker was asked about watching players like Jalen Ramsey play in the slot. It was a great question because Ramsey played the position while Brandon Staley was his defensive coordinator with the Los Angeles Rams. Sanker went on to explain that Ramsey wasn’t the only player he has studied because Ramsey possesses such a unique skill set that you can’t, and really shouldn’t, try to play exactly like him. Instead, Sanker said he has leaned on the resources available to him within the building. Justin Reid, Julian Blackmon, and Terrell Burgess have all played in the slot as well. Burgess, specifically, played the position under Staley, making him a valuable resource. You can already see the growth Sanker is making early in camp. The extra work and veteran leadership appear to be paying off, as he has consistently been making plays throughout camp. Sanker also praised Blackmon, mentioning how he has been able to make plays for the defense as well. Sanker was also asked if his experience playing safety has helped him now that he’s lining up closer to the line of scrimmage. He said that his background at safety has definitely benefited him. At safety, you’re taught to be patient because if you make a mistake, the other safety has to clean it up and make you right. Now that he’s playing closer to the line, he understands exactly what the safeties behind him are seeing because he has played that position himself. That experience allows him to fit his assignments properly and avoid putting the safety in a position where they have to compensate for his mistakes. Sanker appears to have a firm grasp on the star position and is showing early signs of success.

title: Julian Blackmon embracing fresh start after injury-shortened first season with Saints
summary: After signing with the New Orleans Saints as a free agent last offseason, veteran safety Julian Blackmon appeared in just one game before suffering a season-ending shoulder injury that sidelined him for the remaining 16 games. Now healthy, Blackmon says the experience has changed the way he approaches football. “I feel like that’s exactly how […]
full_text: After signing with the New Orleans Saints as a free agent last offseason, veteran safety Julian Blackmon appeared in just one game before suffering a season-ending shoulder injury that sidelined him for the remaining 16 games. Now healthy, Blackmon says the experience has changed the way he approaches football. “I feel like that’s exactly how I approached the offseason—just humbly,” Blackmon said after practice. “Because something that’s given to you can be just as quickly taken away.” Blackmon’s 2025 season came to a disappointing end in the Saints’ season opening loss to the Arizona Cardinals. Despite suffering what was later diagnosed as a posterior labrum tear in his right shoulder, he finished the game, playing every defensive snap while recording seven tackles and a pass breakup. It wasn’t until the following day that the severity of the injury became clear, ultimately landing him on injured reserve for the rest of the season. Looking back, Blackmon said the setback was a reality check of just how quickly things can change in the NFL. “For me, obviously, my career has been trials and errors. A lot of hardships, but at the same time, a lot of gratitude,” he said. “So just being out there with my guys again, remembering what it feels like to be in pads again, it’s a blessing. That’s how I approached the offseason and how I approach the season coming up.” Although his regular season lasted just one game, Blackmon believes he left enough of an impression during last year’s training camp to earn the coaching staff’s confidence heading into 2026. “I felt like I was doing really well in training camp last year,” Blackmon said. “The coaches felt like I did enough and they saw enough to know that if I came back and was able to get a full season, things would be really good. It’d benefit the whole team.” That confidence has only fueled his excitement entering his second year in The Big Easy. “We like to say, ‘Together we eat,’ and I’m excited for my opportunity this year because I feel like we can do that with me on the field,” he said. Blackmon is also optimistic about what the Saints’ safety tandem can become alongside veteran Justin Reid. With both players entering their second season under defensive coordinator Brandon Staley, the Blackmon believes their familiarity with the system has put them in position to take a significant step forward. “It’s a possibility,” Blackmon said when asked if he and Reid can become one of the league’s top safety duos. “I feel like both of us have a good understanding of what we want to get done. Year two under Staley helps a lot. We feel a lot more comfortable.” Blackmon added that communication has been one of the biggest reasons for their growing chemistry during their time in New Orleans. “There’s a lot of different caveats that we have in each coverage, but because we are very communicative with each other, it makes it a lot easier,” he said. “That’s something that I don’t see too out of reach for us to go for.” After losing almost an entire season to injury, Blackmon is no longer taking the opportunity to play for granted. If he can stay healthy, the Saints believe they’ll finally get the player they signed a year ago.

title: Saints’ new guard explains why the run game is coming together early in camp
summary: The New Orleans Saints are still in the early stages of training camp, but one of the team’s newest additions, former Buffalo Bills guard David Edwards, believes the offense is already beginning to establish its identity on the ground. Speaking with the media after practice, the veteran offensive lineman said the biggest strength of the […]
full_text: Jul 30, 2026; Metairie, LA, USA; New Orleans Saints guard David Edwards (76) during training camp at Ochsner Sports Performance Center. Mandatory Credit: Stephen Lew-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New Orleans Saints are still in the early stages of training camp, but one of the team’s newest additions, former Buffalo Bills guard David Edwards, believes the offense is already beginning to establish its identity on the ground. Speaking with the media after practice, the veteran offensive lineman said the biggest strength of the Saints’ backfield is that every running back brings something different, giving the coaching staff plenty of options when building the rushing attack. He pointed to new Saints running back Travis Etienne Jr. as a player whose patience separates him. “I think the beauty of Travis is his ability to start and stop and kind of have this patience behind the line of scrimmage as well as at the line of scrimmage,” he said. “Then make a decision and go is really special and unique.” He also praised Alvin Kamara’s ability to change a game with one touch. “What’s really special and unique about AK is I feel like that guy can hit a home run at any second,” he said. “His twitchiness, athleticism and burst is really unique.” Rather than asking every running back to do the same thing, Kellen Moore and the coaching staff are working to put each player in positions that fit his skill set. “You’ve got to find a certain balance between, ‘This guy does this well. This guy does that well,’ and then ultimately letting the guy cut it loose and play free and have fun,” he said. That approach also refers to the blocking schemes up front. The veteran said New Orleans has been installing both zone and gap concepts throughout camp, giving the offense multiple ways to attack defenses while emphasizing the details behind every play. “I think there’s been some great zone schemes that we’ve been activating, there’s great gap stuff,” he said. “It’s all the same stuff that I’ve kind of been accustomed to, but it’s been really cool to have the nuance and the detail.” He added that the Saints’ coaching staff has done a good job making sure everyone on offense understands not only their own job, but how every position works together. “I really believe our coaches have done a great job of incorporating the entire unit, 11 players working as one, to accomplish a great play. The best part is we’re still installing,” he said. “Once that full package is in, and you can activate a gap scheme, a zone scheme, a keeper, a play action, out of all these different formations, I just feel like that’s going to serve you well as an offense.” Like every offensive line around the league this time of year, much of the focus has been on fundamentals. The emphasis has been on technique, footwork and building good habits before the physical work ramps up as the Saints had their first practice in pads on Monday. “There are certainly clips and reps that we’ve had where you can reference and say, ‘Hey guys, this is exactly how we want to do it,'” he said. “There’s a lot of good things that we’ve done so far, and there’s a lot of stuff that we’ve got to clean up and be better at, but there are a lot of things we can point to right now and say, ‘Hey guys, this is what we’re hunting up.'” The Saints still have plenty of work ahead before their season opener against the Detroit Lions on the road, but the early signs indicate the offensive line and running backs are beginning to develop the chemistry needed to make the ground game a reliable part of the offense.
author: Nic Jennings

title: Offense wins the day, but defense is winning Saints training camp
summary: With the second week of training camp underway, the New Orleans Saints offense finally found its rhythm. The defense has looked very good, and that’s a positive for a unit that finished last season strong under first-year defensive coordinator Brandon Staley. The addition of LB Kaden Elliss following the departure of Demario Davis is already […]
full_text: METAIRIE, LOUISIANA - JULY 30: Tyler Shough #6 of the New Orleans Saints participates in drills during training camp at Ochsner Sports Performance Center on July 30, 2026 in Metairie, Louisiana. (Photo by Tyler Kaufman/Getty Images) | Getty Images With the second week of training camp underway, the New Orleans Saints offense finally found its rhythm. The defense has looked very good, and that’s a positive for a unit that finished last season strong under first-year defensive coordinator Brandon Staley. The addition of LB Kaden Elliss following the departure of Demario Davis is already paying dividends. Staley has been moving Elliss all over the defense, utilizing him in multiple roles within the scheme. The pass rush has also been effective early in camp. It’s not as if the offensive line has been struggling in one particular area—the defense has simply been making the right plays. The coverage on the back end has been very strong as well. Jonas Sanker is making significant strides at the star position, and it’s helping elevate the entire defense. This is how the flow of camp should go. A defense with a great deal of returning experience should naturally be a little ahead of an offense that is young and breaking in several new players at key positions. Today, however, belonged to the offense. Nick Underhill of NewOrleans.Football reported that the offense had a huge bounce-back performance . This was the first padded practice of camp, and that proved to be a major benefit for the offensive line. With pads on, the line of scrimmage can finally play the way it’s intended to—with maximum physicality. The offensive line was able to establish true run fits and lean on that physicality to help slow down an aggressive pass rush. That, in turn, opened things up for Tyler Shough, who put together his best practice of training camp so far. Underhill noted that Shough finished team periods completing 11 of 14 passes, with one throwaway and no turnovers. It’s also important to note that Shough’s average depth of target was more than 10 yards, meaning the offense was pushing the ball downfield rather than relying on short, safe throws. It was an outstanding response considering how uncomfortable both Shough and the offense looked on Sunday, when he reportedly finished team periods just 3 of 13. A practice like this is one the team can build upon. The defense now has some film to evaluate and make adjustments, while a young offense can gain confidence, continue to develop chemistry, and grow together.

summary: There may be an unsuspecting star rising for the New Orleans Saints as the first day of pads ended. Rookie wide receiver Barion Brown has been stacking good days and performed well again on Monday. Brown, a sixth-round pick by the Saints, was making plays left and right. Despite being announced as a return specialist […]
full_text: Aug 02, 2026; Metairie, LA, USA; New Orleans Saints wide receiver Barion Brown (19) during training camp at Ochsner Sports Performance Center. Mandatory Credit: Stephen Lew-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect There may be an unsuspecting star rising for the New Orleans Saints as the first day of pads ended. Rookie wide receiver Barion Brown has been stacking good days and performed well again on Monday. Brown, a sixth-round pick by the Saints, was making plays left and right. Despite being announced as a return specialist during the draft, Brown has been a favorite target among quarterbacks through the first week of camp. Ironically, the first comment by the commentators when the LSU wideout was drafted was “Look how they announced it…so don’t come in here thinking you gonna be catching a whole bunch of passes.” At 5-foot-11, Brown has game-breaking speed, but his ability to make contested catches is better than many expect. He won’t be the same red zone target as Devaughn Vele, but he is a willing playmaker and has a wide catch radius. Barion Brown 🔥 pic.twitter.com/Oq1zNQ6bvK — New Orleans Saints (@Saints) August 3, 2026 The Saints wide receiver room is a lot different than what it was just a year ago. From entering the season saying “who’s going to help Chris Olave” to wondering how New Orleans will get all their playmakers on the field at the same time. With Olave, Vele, and first-round pick Jordyn Tyson, Tyler Shough will have plenty of weapons to spread the ball to. Brown was also the third and last wide receiver the Saints drafted in the 2026 NFL Draft, making his road to seeing playing time with the offense even further. Despite this, he has taken advantage of his opportunities and shown the ability to make plays. Monday saints training camp 1-on-1 Barion Brown making the catch deep down the sideline @wdsu https://t.co/pH3cV0GrPd pic.twitter.com/pmdfqlct4y — Sharief Ishaq (@ShariefWDSU) August 3, 2026 Brown’s versatility as a kick returner already made his chances of making the roster high, but the display of his speed and effort during training camp has only elevated his chances. This is only emphasized with the recent and surprise retirement of wideout Ja’Lynn Polk, who was placed on the reserve/retired list on Saturday. With his continuous playmaking and one less player to beat out, Brown is looking like a lock to be on the Saints’ 2026-27 roster.

title: The Giants’ salary cap situation for 2026 and beyond
summary: During training camp, most of what we as fans think about is which players are going to start or provide valuable backup and what that suggests about the team’s chances of success in the upcoming season. I’m pretty sure, though, that the New York Giants’ brain trust is also thinking about the team through a […]
full_text: During training camp, most of what we as fans think about is which players are going to start or provide valuable backup and what that suggests about the team’s chances of success in the upcoming season. I’m pretty sure, though, that the New York Giants’ brain trust is also thinking about the team through a financial lens. That means three things: How much flexibility the team’s current financial situation gives them to make moves during camp if a dire need arises, whether because of a major injury (heaven forbid) or underperformance of the players at a specific position. Which players with significant contracts may be “on the block” in head coach John Harbaugh’s mind as targets to be cut, or to be traded in-season if the team does not perform well. Which players might be targets for contract extensions during the season to lock them up for additional years while creating 2027 cap space. Let’s look at the Giants’ financial situation from each of these perspectives. Current cap space The Giants at the moment have $10.1 million in cap space, ninth-lowest in the NFL, per Over The Cap . That’s not a good look for a team coming off a 4-13 season. The teams in worse cap position were all either playoff teams (Steelers, Packers, Bears, Jaguars, Bills) or playoff wannabees who didn’t get there (Chiefs, Cowboys, Buccaneers). In other respects the Giants’ cap situation looks better. The Giants are middle of the pack in active cap spending (i.e., top 51 players on the roster) at $262.9M. It’s not more because the Giants carry $28.6M in dead money into the 2026 season. If that sounds bad, consider the Dolphins ($179.2M dead money), the Browns ($116.8M), the Saints ($112.1M), and the Jets ($111.5M). Miami is only spending $112.6 million on players actually on the roster and only has $16.1 million in cap space left to add more. Half the Giants’ dead money is from the unavoidable Dexter Lawrence breakup, $5 million more from the release of Bobby Okereke, which I think everyone agrees was the right move, and the rest from the releases of (in decreasing order of cost) James Hudson, Jamie Gillan, Chris Board, Graham Gano, Jason Sanders, and Cam Jones. Veterans at risk The Giants whose cap hits are the highest for the 2026 season are: Paulson Adebo ($24.2M) Brian Burns ($21.4M) Jevon Holland ($18.5M) Darius Slayton ($15.9M) Kayvon Thibodeaux ($14.5M) Andrew Thomas ($13.0M) Jon Runyan Jr. ($11.8M) Abdul Carter ($10.3M) Arvell Reese ($8.7M) Greg Newsome II ($8M) Malik Nabers ($8.0M) Chauncey Golston ($6.9M) Of those, Burns, Thomas, Carter, Reese, and Nabers are surely not going anywhere, strictly from the standpoint of value to the team. As for the rest, from the financial standpoint, all of them would incur a significant dead money hit in 2027 if released this season. The only ones who would actually save money against the 2026 cap if released are Runyan ($9.25M) and Newsome ($5M). Runyan and Newsome are also the players in the group above with the smallest dead money hits in 2027 if cut ($2.5M and $3.0M respectively). Thus, these two seem to be the players most at risk of being released if they do not perform up to Harbaugh’s standards in camp, or if they are simply beaten out by other players. Creating cap space with contract extensions As I have complained several times on these pages, general manager Joe Schoen doesn’t like to use void years to create cap space. He has been one of only a few GMs not to take advantage of the void year loophole to add talent. That said, what Schoen does like to do – a lot – is to convert salary to a signing bonus whose cap accounting is spread out over the life of the contract. It’s the equivalent of tiptoeing right up to the void year line but not crossing it. The player doesn’t care because the signing bonus cash is paid up front. Among current Giants: Andrew Thomas signed a five-year, $117.5 million contract extension in 2023. Thus far his contract has incurred cap charges of only $9.3M, $19.9M, and $9.3M in 2023, 2024, and 2025 because the cap charge for his $15 million signing bonus was spread over several years. This year, for the third consecutive season, Schoen converted part of Thomas’ salary ($14.8M) into a signing bonus to free up $11.0 million in cap space. The good news is that Thomas’ 2026 cap hit is now only $13 million. The bad news is that by deferring the cap hits, Thomas’ cap hits for 2027-2029 will now be $29.95M, $29.95M, and $29.62M. Schoen is paying those amounts in cheaper dollars since the NFL salary cap has risen every year except after the pandemic, but the you-know-what will hit the fan starting next season. That’s the price Schoen pays for eschewing void years. Thomas has had a troubling injury history, having played in only 10, 6, and 13 games the past three seasons. When healthy, though, he is one of the top few left tackles in the NFL. He’s also still only 27 years old. Don’t be surprised if Schoen tries to sign Thomas to a contract extension in mid-season to alleviate those $29M+ cap hits that are coming via further signing bonus cap sleight-of-hand. Brian Burns’ story is almost identical to Thomas’. Burns signed a 5-year, $141 million contract with the Giants as part of the trade that brought him here. He incurred cap hits of only $15.5M and $17.8M his first two seasons as a Giant. In 2025, though, Schoen converted $16 million of Burns’ salary into a prorated signing bonus to free up up $12 million of cap space. In 2026, once again Schoen played the same game, converting $22.75M of salary into a signing bonus for cap purposes. The bad news is that in 2027 and 2028, Burns’ cap hit will now be $44.1 million. That type of cap hit can’t be swallowed easily. Burns isn’t quite at Thomas’ level of excellence, but he is probably in no worse than the second tier of edge defenders behind players such as Myles Garrtt, Micah Parsons, Maxx Crosby, etc. Thus, look for Schoen to also try to sign Burns to a contract extension during the season and use the same signing bonus strategy to lessen those $44.1 million cap hits. Adebo’s contract is tied for 14th-highest among NFL cornerbacks. It’s only for three years, but it carries the largest cap hit of any Giant ($24.2 million) this season, and next season’s $20.3 million cap hit is nothing to sneeze at. Unlike Thomas and Burns, Adebo has really only had one excellent NFL season (2023). He was all right as the Giants’ CB1 last year, but with one interception and five pass breakups, he wasn’t an impact player. There is little the Giants can do with his contract situation this year. His play has not earned him an extension, and the Giants would lose $5.7M by cutting him while incurring $29.9M of dead money. The Giants just have to hope that Adebo returns to his 2023 form in Dennard Wilson’s defense, which might convince them to offer a contract extension. If not, then the Giants will probably swallow $6.3 million of dead money in 2027 to release him and save $14 million of cap space. Jevon Holland is in a somewhat similar situation. He had two elite seasons in Miami but two mediocre ones as well, and his first Giants season was also nondescript. He carries an $18.5 million cap hit this year and $18.9 million next year, and the Giants can save $13.8 million by cutting him in 2027, swallowing $5 million in dead money to do so. But if he bounces back, an extension is a possibility. Darius Slayton is probably in the most precarious future situation of anyone on the list. His $15.9 million 2026 cap hit is unavoidable, because almost all of it would be dead money if he is released. In 2027 the Giants could save $10 million against the cap, with only $3M in dead money, by releasing him. Add to that the plethora of wide receivers in training camp this summer. If Slayton falls on the depth chart and sees much less playing time, he’s surely a goner in 2027. On the other hand, if his recently revealed 2025 sports hernia is fully healed and he becomes entrenched as WR2, an…
