title: Pittsburgh Steelers roster 2026: Zach Frazier, Jamel Dean, Eli Heidenreich are underrated
summary: Reunions can be splashy things, but they don’t always work out. For every Led Zeppelin, Soundgarden, or Eagles, there’s a Van Hagar, Sex Pistols, or Velvet Underground. Just because you worked well together once upon a time doesn’t mean that you can recreate the magic. Obviously, Mike McCarthy and Aaron Rodgers are hoping to wind […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - JANUARY 4: Zach Frazier #54 of the Pittsburgh Steelers in action during the game against the Baltimore Ravens at Acrisure Stadium on January 4, 2026 in Pittsburgh, United States. (Photo by Joe Sargent/Getty Images) | Getty Images Reunions can be splashy things, but they don’t always work out. For every Led Zeppelin, Soundgarden, or Eagles, there’s a Van Hagar, Sex Pistols, or Velvet Underground. Just because you worked well together once upon a time doesn’t mean that you can recreate the magic. Obviously, Mike McCarthy and Aaron Rodgers are hoping to wind up on the positive side of the ledger in their own reunion. They worked together in Green Bay from 2006 through 2018, and while McCarthy helped develop Rodgers as an NFL quarterback, he also benefited from Rodgers at his best in the early 2010s, when Rodgers may have been the best pure thrower of the football we’ve ever seen. Now, as Rodgers winds his career down, the whole thing is about getting the Steelers past the recent spate of mediocre seasons we’ve seen as of late. Mike Tomlin will have a bust in Canton someday, and the fact that he never had a losing record over 19 years is ridiculous, but stringing together a bunch of 10-7 seasons with Wild Card playoff losses isn’t really the point in the Steel City. “ I felt last year might be it ,” Rodgers recently said of his future. “And then Mike [McCarthy] got hired. I talked to the wife, and she said, ‘You can do one more year.’” If Rodgers is to go out on a high note, and if McCarthy is to match the successes of his predecessors, everybody on the roster will want to step up — especially the guys whose names aren’t as familiar to the nation. To that end, I’ve identified three Hidden Gems for the 2026 Steelers — one underrated veteran, one underrated free-agent signing, and one underrated draft pick. Underrated veteran: Center Zach Frazier The Steelers already have more than their share of Pro Football Hall of Famers, and former center Maurkice Pouncey could find himself on that list someday. The nine-time Pro Bowler, two-time First-Team All-Pro, and member of the Hall of Fame All-2010s team retired after the 2020 season, and for a while, the center position was in flux without him. But in 2024, the team was smart enough to select West Virginia’s Zach Frazier with the 51st overall pick in the second round of the draft. Since then, center has not been a problem, no matter the quarterback. Over his two NFL seasons, Frazier has allowed two sacks and 23 total pressures in 1,258 pass-blocking snaps, he’s become a true force as a run-blocker at 6’3” and 310 pounds, and he’s perfectly capable of sorting out line calls and protections pre-snap. Something that impressed a certain Aaron Rodgers right away. “Well, it starts with Zach,” Rodgers said before the 2025 season. “Zach is a highly intelligent player. It helps, because as much as I have a good feel for the offense, I’m not what I would call an expert yet. I become an expert when you break the huddle, and you can see the picture in your mind. Every now and then the picture’s a little fuzzy still, so I’m still working some things out, but Zach is so freaking smart. He’s making some calls for me. I told him, ‘Don’t get used to that.’ I said, ‘At some point, I’m going to be making the calls for you.’ He’s got a real good disposition for a center. He’s obviously a talented player, and I think his leadership is what I’d like to see most continue to grow, because the leadership often grows at the same rate as a performance, and everybody knows what kind of player he is. He’s going to have more opportunities to lead.” Those leadership opportunities will continue as the Steelers’ offensive line shuffles everywhere but Frazier’s position in 2026. Tackle Troy Fautanu and guard Mason McCormick are moving to the left side from the right, and that right side is up for grabs with any number of options (including rookie guard Gennings Dunker and rookie tackle Max Iheanachor) in play. However that shakes out, the Steelers have the right man in the middle, and you should expect Frazier to continue his ascent as one of the NFL’s best centers… because he’s there already. 2025 was Year 2 for Zach Frazier. He has all the technique and protection smarts in the world, but what I love is the instinct to dominate. Get ready to see "First-Team All-Pro" before his name. @steelers pic.twitter.com/yusgxgZZYg — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) August 2, 2026 Underrated free agent: CB Jamel Dean Last season, the Steelers’ defenders lined up at either slot or outside cornerback allowed 140 completions on 249 attempts for 1,792 yards, 16 touchdowns, seven interceptions, 39 pass deflections, and an opponent passer rating of 88.6. Not one of the worst situations in the NFL, but not in the top five, either — and certainly not what Steelers fans are used to expecting when it comes to defensive excellence. New defensive coordinator Patrick Graham is in charge of making things better in 2026, and the front office helped Graham out by signing former Tampa Bay Buccaneers cornerback Jamel Dean to a three-year, $36.75 million contract with $12 million guaranteed. That puts Dean pretty far down the list of average annual salaries for the position , and it could turn out to be an amazing bargain. Because when he’s allowed to do what he does, both in press and off coverage, the 30-year-old Dean still has it all together when it comes to coverage. Last season for the Bucs, Dean allowed 25 catches on 54 targets for 311 yards, 105 yards after the catch, one touchdown, three interceptions, five pass breakups, and an opponent passer rating of 47.7 — the NFL’s lowest among corners who played at least 50% of their teams’ snaps. “You guys know this better than I do, but first it starts with your division,” Graham recently said when asked what it means to have two cornerbacks in Dean and Joey Porter Jr. who can be physical players and press corners as well. “If you’re talking about a division where teams run the ball and have big receivers, it’s good business. Whether you’re talking about Cincinnati, you’re talking about Baltimore, or you’re talking about Cleveland, in terms of whether I’m talking about the receivers, the run game, that’s what our division is all about. So, I think it’s good business. “It’s a highway-speed league. So, if you’ve got length, you’ve got speed, and then the fact that there’s some physicality to it, that’s always going to be good for us. Because no matter what we talk about, the spread, run game, the spread pass game, when it gets down to January, and in this division every week, it comes down to the physicality of the game, and you have to establish that. “So, when you have corners that can tackle, that’s a bonus.” Well, Dean also had 38 solo tackles, 10 stops, and two forced fumbles last season, so the 6’1”, 206-pound veteran has no issue getting grimy in the paint. Most importantly though, Dean’s tape shows a player conversant with breaking down any passing game concepts, and blowing it up. Dean’s value to the Steelers will be the perfect blend of acumen and athleticism, and that will show up right away. Jamel Dean is the NFL's best cornerback nobody talks about nearly enough. @steelers pic.twitter.com/KvTjmnKuGs — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) August 2, 2026 Underrated draft pick: RB/FB/WR Eli Heidenreich When we talk about versatile players in football, we are generally focusing on defensive linemen who can win from multiple gaps, linebackers who can also rush the passer at the line of scrimmage, or defensive backs who can credibly play multiple positions without embarrassing themselves. In this case, we’re talking about a running back and a receiver in the person of Navy’s Eli Heidenreich, who was one of the more interesting prospects in this class, regardless of position. Frankly, I was shocked that the Steelers were able to steal him with the 230th overall pick in the seventh round.…

(Photo by Maria Lysaker/UFL/Getty Images) | Getty Images With training camp comes roster shuffling, and the Seattle Seahawks made a minor rearrangement to the deck on Tuesday. Garrett Nelson, an EDGE who went undrafted after the 2023 NFL Draft, was signed to the Seahawks’ 90-man roster, the team announced on Tuesday morning . Nelson was among four Seattle tryouts listed in Monday’s transaction wire. To make room for Nelson’s addition, rookie UDFA wide receiver Kyre Duplessis was waived just a week after he himself joined the team. Since going undrafted, Nelson has spent time with the Miami Dolphins, Cincinnati Bengals, Denver Broncos, and New Orleans Saints, with his second stint in Denver taking him through most of the 2025 season before he was waived in May, though he is yet to appear in a regular season game. He also made a two-season cameo in the UFL with the San Antonio Brahmas, where he totaled 2.5 sacks and three tackles for loss. In four seasons at Nebraska, the 6-foot-3, 240-pound pass rusher registered 12 sacks and 26 TFLs. Duplessis, waived after a short stint in Seattle, had previously spent time with the Detroit Lions this offseason.

title: HBO ‘Hard Knocks’ director Pat Harris: Mike Macdonald ‘has embraced us being here’
summary: HBO’s critically acclaimed ‘Hard Knocks’ series premiered 25 years ago, when the defending Super Bowl champion Baltimore Ravens were chronicled throughout training camp and preseason. It was a groundbreaking behind-the-scenes look at the inner workings of an NFL locker room, the off-field lives of coaches, players, and other staff, the tough world of roster cuts, […]
full_text: RENTON, WASHINGTON - JUNE 12: A sign at the entrance to the Seattle Seahawks headquarters and training facility at the Virginia Mason Athletic Center on June 12, 2024, in Renton, Washington. (Photo by Kirby Lee/Getty Images) | Getty Images HBO’s critically acclaimed ‘Hard Knocks’ series premiered 25 years ago, when the defending Super Bowl champion Baltimore Ravens were chronicled throughout training camp and preseason. It was a groundbreaking behind-the-scenes look at the inner workings of an NFL locker room, the off-field lives of coaches, players, and other staff, the tough world of roster cuts, and countless other aspects of the sport the average fan previously had limited or no access to. At long last, after previous resistance over a decade ago , the Seattle Seahawks are finally on board. Furthermore, they’re the first reigning Super Bowl champion since the Ravens to be ‘Hard Knocks’ headliners. On Monday, Field Gulls had the opportunity to interview Pat Harris, lead director of ‘Hard Knocks’, who provided some insight into the filming process and how the Seahawks have taken to their first appearance. A former high school quarterback, Harris has been with the program in some capacity for over a decade, and this year he’s tasked with directing a season centered around the Super Bowl champions. This was a 20-minute interview, so some questions were omitted for length reasons and may be used another article, while some answers were condensed for clarity. You’ve been around ‘Hard Knocks’ for over a decade, but this is your second season as the lead director, last year you got to chronicle your childhood team, the Buffalo Bills? Looking back on it now, what was that experience like for you personally? Pat Harris : “It’s very surreal even hearing you say that I’ve been doing this a decade, uh, is still kind of crazy to me. I don’t really see myself as having been doing it that long, but that is factually correct. Last year was surreal. I think even getting to see some of those random phone memories that pop up, even knowing I got to spend time with my family during the month of July and August, which, unfortunately I have not been able to do in the last decade. I think those are just cool memories that I’ll always have with me and always kind of cherish. So I’m very happy to just [have] good memories.” Did you have any standout moments from last season? I know Buffalo Joe, Joe Andressen, him making the roster again last year was great just for the local rooting interest. Harris: “Yeah, so I actually personally love the Josh Allen, [biometric expert] Chris Hess stuff we did . That was a piece, actually, tried to… I read some stuff on Chris Hess years prior and pitched a piece at NFL Films, and it didn’t ever come together. So then it was kind of a full circle moment when we found out Chris was going to be coming to camp. I got to do some of the biometric stuff and the super high speed throwing mechanic stuff. So that was kind of a cool, personal project, getting to see how that all came together and then, kind of letting our camera people,flex their muscles a little bit. That’s always a cool one that still sticks out in my head.” This is the first time a reigning Super Bowl champion has been featured in a traditional training camp Hard Knocks since the very first edition 25 years ago with the Baltimore Ravens. Do you think, in a way, that this actually can garner even more general viewer interest knowing you’re chronicling the champs? Harris: “I would hope so. I think that’s our plan. You know, it was kind of similar to the Bills last year, picking some of the best teams in the league and trying to showcase the stories a little different than it might be with a team coming off the first overall pick, like we’ve done in the past. So I think the hope is that, yeah, we want to obviously showcase the Seahawks more, if those East Coast fans just don’t know as much about this team. We want to be able to take this opportunity to do that, but I’m hoping that, yeah, I mean, it doesn’t get any better than the Super Bowl champs.” “ I think [Mike Macdonald] has just been incredible. He has welcomed us with open arms. He’s embraced us being here.” HBO Hard Knocks director Pat Harris It’s interesting you bring that up with the East Coasters because it seems like the Seahawks have generally been perceived as this sort of afterthought champion, just like those Ravens were, kind of like an out of nowhere team to win it all. Do you see this as also an opportunity for non-Seahawks fans not just to get to know the team better, but some of the players and their personalities and also just help viewers get a better sense of ‘Ah, this is why Seattle was able to win the Super Bowl’ ? Harris : “No question. I think that was kind of our thought coming in and it’s exceeded expectations, I think, since we’ve been here, starting with Coach [Mike] Macdonald. I think he’s just been incredible. He has welcomed us with open arms. He’s embraced us being here. And then there’s just so many personalities. I think it’s fun to see the players getting comfortable with us after a couple days and really just trying to, you know, being able to showcase their true selves, they’re not nervous, having us around or anything. So I’m hoping that that’s kind of the two-pronged effect that obviously makes for great TV, but then the random fans can just kind of fall in love with players and people and ideally an organization.” If you could take a time machine and go back to, say, the 2013-2014 era, back when the Seahawks actually turned down hard knock, do you think it would have been an amazing experience to have ‘Hard Knocks’ be there during the Legion of Boom years? Harris : “From what everybody’s told us here, yes, they said that was like the cliche ‘made for TV’ team. I think it would have almost been too perfect looking back. You know, I wish we could have. It’s been fun seeing some of those guys pop around training camp, even the clip we posted with Richard Sherman coming by [to see Bud Clark]. So I think it’s fun to see them show up, but I think that would have been probably a pretty iconic one as well to document that team.” . @Seahawks rookie safety Bud Clark was so psyched to meet @RSherman_25 💚 Hard Knocks: Training Camp with the @Seahawks premieres Aug 4 on @hbomax pic.twitter.com/TqkiAVmjxq — NFL (@NFL) July 31, 2026 Some teams kind of run away from ‘Hard Knocks,’ some teams welcome with open arms. So what can you say so far about how the Seahawks organization has taken to the ‘Hard Knocks’ crew being there and just being a part of this whole process for the first time? Harris: “They’ve embraced it right off the bat, I think we had a very good first conversation. We came down here when the Seahawks were first announced. Met with [Mike Macdonald], GM [John Schneider], front office, and it was amazing to see their—I think they were excited for this opportunity from the beginning and that’s held true all throughout. “And I think that’s, you know, kind of been a trickle-down effect for all players and staff and coaches and the fact that everyone’s embraced it, has been great for us. Our crew, you know, we say countlessly, that everyone top to bottom has been so friendly and really welcomed us here. So I think it’s been great for that perspective. And I think the players just feel comfortable knowing their coach is being himself. They’re not seeing anything change. I think they’re just operating the exact same way.” And it also has helped that the weather has just been lovely at this time of year. It dispels the myth that it rains in Seattle all the time. Harris: “It’s amazing. I think a lot of smiles from our crew—we’re definitely used to camp, you know, usually being pretty hot and humid and uncomfortable and that has been far from it. We preemptively had to get crew sweatshirts this year for the first time because thought it might be a little chilly in the mornings, which it might be to…

It was another non-padded practice, with fans not permitted for attendance until ( likely very smoky, low air quality ) Tuesday. Probably the biggest storyline(s) from Monday is the team’s injury situation, which isn’t hitting the absolute top of the depth chart, but there was an injury suffered in practice and a new concern regarding fullback Robbie Ouzts. Here’s a recap of the notable events and news. Robbie Ouzts injured again, clarity coming soon “We’re going to try to find out more information with Robbie’s situation. More @thenewstribune pic.twitter.com/qcLczzVhOO — Gregg Bell (@gbellseattle) August 3, 2026 Seattle’s rookie cornerback and fan favorite wide receiver have missed several practices in a row due to injury. Defensive lineman Mike Morris has also sat out a couple of practices with his own injury. Mike Macdonald has not raised any concerns regarding long-term injuries for any of those players. He said that Neal is a “shorter term” return, at this point. Noah Igbinoghene has been getting more nickel reps while Neal has been out. Jacardia Wright suffers leg injury Seattle’s second-year undrafted running back did not finish practice after injuring his leg, per the Seattle Times’ Bob Condotta. We’re still unsure of the severity, but if it was super terrible I imagine there would’ve been stronger noise about it. It’s still nevertheless unfortunate for Wright, who missed almost all of last year on practice squad IR after hurting his ankle against the New Orleans Saints. That also means there will be some growing pains and lumps to take even through any successes. “Bud’s one of those rookies that we’re asking a lot of them right now and I’m really impressed with how he’s handling it,” Mike Macdonald said. “There’s things where it’s not perfect, but how he goes about his business is what we’re looking for. And I think he needs to trust that he’s going to come out of the the fog, and take it from there. But I think I it’s important to start building a relationship with those guys and having a feel for, you know, the speed of the game with the ones and how we communicate and how we play and and he’s doing a good job.“ NBA Finals head coach shows up to training camp Mitch Johnson and some other Spurs coaches here today. pic.twitter.com/fUCOH47ZRe — Bob Condotta (@bcondotta) August 3, 2026 San Antonio Spurs head coach Mitch Johnson, a Seattle native and high school graduate, was a special guest at Seahawks camp. Shaheed came over in a midseason trade from the New Orleans Saints last year, and while he had flashes of effectiveness as a receiver, his best moments were generally on special teams. With a full offseason to work with Darnold, the early returns in camp are positive. full_text: A Pro Bowl, All-Pro votes, 72 tackles, 0.5 sacks and an interception. These are all statistics that Seattle Seahawks star cornerback Devon Witherspoon totaled in the 2025 season while leading a defense to a Super Bowl victory. However, he is not one of the NFL’s Top 100 players, at least not according to a survey completed by his peers. No, the third-year man out of Illinois narrowly missed making the list, being ranked at 107 behind several stars, according to the NFL. Witherspoon fell behind players like Detroit Lions wide receiver Jameson Williams, Houston Texans quarterback CJ Stroud and new San Francisco 49ers wideout Mike Evans. Not to mention the players who actually made the list, like Seahawks’ legend Bobby Wagner (81), who is currently a free agent, and Eagles corner Quinyon Mitchell (47). Players who just missed the NFL Top 100… 110: Tyler Warren 109: Tee Higgins 108: Brian Branch 107: Devon Witherspoon 106: Jameson Williams 105: Dexter Lawrence 104: Chris Lindstrom 103: CJ Stroud 102: Lane Johnson 101: Mike Evans pic.twitter.com/bjfSYLDg0V — NFL (@NFL) August 3, 2026 For whatever reason, NFL Top 100 survey ballots start after Thanksgiving of the previous season and players often submit them after the Super Bowl . Witherspoon has proven to be an x-factor in Mike Macdonald’s defense, with his speed and tackling ability elevating the Seahawks anytime he’s on the field. This game-changing ability was on full display in the Seahawks’ Super Bowl against the New England Patriots, in which he recorded one sack, one pass defensed, four tackles and a strip of Drake Maye, which was caught by Uchenna Nwosu for the game-sealing touchdown in the fourth. With Witherspoon’s snub, there remains only one Seahawks player on the NFL Top 100 list after over half the list has been revealed. Ernest Jones IV, the team’s impeccable linebacker, just barely cracked the list at No. 97 after a 126-tackle and five-interception season There are only 39 players on the list yet to be revealed, and it’s safe to assume at least a few more of Seattle’s stars will make the list, including Leonard Williams and Jaxon Smith-Njigba. The list will continue to be revealed weekly until Sept. 4, when undoubtedly we will have far more to complain about than this list.

title: Seahawks 2026 training camp: 3 things we’re looking for during Week 2 of practice
summary: The Seattle Seahawks resume training camp practice on Monday. It’s their last full week of practice before preseason begins on Aug. 15 versus the Dallas Cowboys. There will be more padded practices than non-padded practices, and the competition for roster spots will really start to heat up in the days to come. Field Gulls will […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks resume training camp practice on Monday. It’s their last full week of practice before preseason begins on Aug. 15 versus the Dallas Cowboys. There will be more padded practices than non-padded practices, and the competition for roster spots will really start to heat up in the days to come. Field Gulls will once again be at Seahawks this week, providing written and video content over the next several days. Yours truly and Bryce Coutts are set to attend Aug. 5 and Aug. 7 practices at VMAC, and on Aug. 8 we’ll be joined by Josh Hite to make it a Field Gulls trio for Football Fan Fest at Lumen Field. All of this, of course, is pending the air quality not being completely unhealthy due to the incoming smoke from the horrifying Spokane wildfires . To get prepped for camp, the three of us each listed three things we’ll be paying attention to throughout the practices. Have a look below! Mookie Alexander First thing I’ll be paying attention to is the straight dropback passing game. Obviously, you don’t show your whole playbook in camp, but last year when Klint Kubiak was spamming under-center play-action and getting Tory Horton increased work with the first-team offense, that proved relevant when the games actually happened. An area where I think Brian Fleury can and arguably must improve from Kubiak’s offense is the passing attack without play-action. Seattle’s efficiency wasn’t terrible in non-PA but it wasn’t amazing, and less so when Jaxon Smith-Njigba wasn’t targeted. I’m curious to see if we’ll get a glimpse of more running back targets, three-step quick game, slants, and shallow crossers with YAC potential. Second on my “What/Who to watch for” list is the young’uns in the secondary, more specifically Julian Neal (who’s injured, so it may be moot on his part), Andre Fuller, Michael Dansby, and Bud Clark. Dansby has been heralded throughout camp, so I’m intrigued to see if he can go from afterthought to a real roster candidate. Clark has had a few splash plays and worked with the starters over the weekend, and he has that nose for the ball that will make him an intriguing and exciting watch. The last thing I’m looking forward to seeing is how Rylie Mills performs. He excited everyone with his sack in the Super Bowl, and he’s drawn rave reviews in camp already. Mills could be a major part of Seattle’s interior pass rush. I’m curious to see how often he lines up as a 3-tech vs. 5-tech. Josh Hite The Seahawks generally keep five cornerbacks on the roster, and Devon Witherspoon and Josh Jobe are solidly locked in, but the remaining three spots are open for grabs. Will the rookies step up and claim them, or will the veterans like Noah Igbinoghene fight off the rookies? Another area I will be watching is the pass rushers. With the rumors that the Seahawks have interest in another veteran pass rusher, I believe a lot of that will depend on how the younger pass rushers are producing in camp and the preseason games. Can these younger players show the coaching staff that they can take that next step? Finally, I will be watching the interior offensive line. The Seahawks generally keep 10 offensive linemen on the active roster, Grey Zabel, Jalen Sundell, and Anthony Bradford seem to have the staring gigs locked up, but the backup spots remain in contention. Will Olu Oluwatimi and Christian Haynes make the team once again, or will Mason Richman, Bryce Cabeldue, and Beau Stephens show the coaches that they can step up? These are things I will be looking out for while I am there. Bryce Coutts When I’m on location at Seahawks training camp this week, there are three things I’ll be watching especially closely through my coaching lens. The first is the continued evolution of Seattle’s offense and what it looks like with Sam Darnold running the show. We talk about this constantly: quarterback play is about much more than completion percentage or whether a throw ends up on a highlight reel. I want to watch Darnold’s feet, timing, eye discipline, command of the offense and how quickly he is processing when the picture changes after the snap. I’ll also be paying close attention to how Brian Fleury is putting this offense together the formations, motions, play-action concepts, RPO elements and how Seattle is creating answers for the quarterback before the ball is even snapped. Connected to all of that is my second major focus: the offensive line and protection. I want to see communication, how they handle movement and pressure, whether the run game is creating displacement and how consistently the five-man unit is giving Darnold a clean platform. The Seahawks can have all the weapons they want, but everything offensively still starts with winning up front. The third thing I’ll be studying is Mike Macdonald’s defense and how much further Seattle can take what has already become one of the defining identities of this team. I’m going to be watching the details that don’t always show up on a camp highlight: pre-snap disguise, safety rotations, communication, leverage, how defenders pass routes off in coverage and whether Seattle can create pressure with its front without constantly having to add bodies to the rush. I’ll also be watching the competition throughout the roster because camp isn’t simply about which player makes the biggest play on a given afternoon it’s about consistency. As a coach, I want to see what happens on the rep after a mistake. Does the player correct it? Does his technique hold up when he gets tired? Does he understand the assignment or is he simply relying on athletic ability? Those are the details I try to bring to my analysis, and being on the ground in Seattle this week gives me the opportunity to evaluate this team beyond the highlights and really see how ready the Seahawks are for what comes next. And as a final reminder… The Seahawks Syndicate quartet of myself, Bryce Coutts, Dan Viens, and Brandon Cain (who will be joining our podcasts virtually this year) are back for more training camp podcasts! Our live shows will broadcast from our special recording area at Fast Fashion Brewing in SoDo! Emerald City Spectrum ’s Corbin Smith will be a special guest on Aug. 5 at 7:30 pm PT . You’re all invited to all three recordings, but especially our Town Hall style show on Aug. 7 at 7:30 pm, in which there will be a ticket giveaway by Dan for the Seahawks-Cowboys preseason game. Our last show is 2:30 pm PT before Fan Fest on Saturday. Come hang with us at Fast Fashion and/or meet us at the berm on those two VMAC days. What are you looking forward to the most in this week’s training camp? Let us know in the comments section below! Join the conversation! title: 49ers’ new return man? Deebo Samuel was among the league leaders in 2025
summary: Special teams coordinator Brant Boyer spoke with the media on Monday. When asked how the competition for returners was going, he said, “I think [Jacob] Cowing, [Will] Pauling, and [Jordan] Watkins, all those guys are back there. Junior Bergen. There’s a big handful of guys, and hopefully they can make great decisions and catch the […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 05: Deebo Samuel Sr. #1 of the Washington Commanders in action against the Los Angeles Chargers at SoFi Stadium on October 05, 2025 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images) | Getty Images Special teams coordinator Brant Boyer spoke with the media on Monday. When asked how the competition for returners was going, he said, “I think [Jacob] Cowing, [Will] Pauling, and [Jordan] Watkins, all those guys are back there. Junior Bergen. There’s a big handful of guys, and hopefully they can make great decisions and catch the ball first and foremost. That’s important. Boyer stressed decision-making. He continued, saying, “It’s a matter of, can they make the right decisions? Can they block a gunner when they’re supposed to? Can they let a ball hit the ground when they’re supposed to? Can they go up and catch a fair catch when they’re supposed to? There’s a lot more that goes into it than just returning the ball. We’re trying to find the guy that has the whole package, that we can count on every week, that can catch the ball and make great decisions.” There isn’t much experience on the roster. All of Jacob Cowing’s stats came in 2024, when he returned 28 punts and a single kickoff. He’s the only one with returner experience. It seems like the punt return job is Cowing’s to lose. However, the addition of Deebo Samuel might mean Cowing has competition at kick returner. It might also make it more difficult for a player like Cowing to make the roster. Boyer spoke highly of Samuel: “Well, certainly when they told me that he was coming I was like, ‘Hell yeah. Let’s go.’ Because he is a difference maker. He’s obviously proven and he’s done it at a very, very high level. I’m really anxious, we were all talking about it, to get him in our scheme. I’ve watched him and really liked what he’s done throughout his career, liked him coming out of college. He’s a hell of a player and he’s really tough to tackle. He’s got speed to take it to the house all the time. Again, any time you can add a guy like that to the roster, you’re jumping up for joy as a special teams coach.” Samuel hasn’t returned a punt in his career, but does have 41 kickoff returns, with 32 of those coming in the previous two seasons. During his final season with the 49ers, Deebo averaged 31.3 yards per return, including a 60-yarder. Last season with the Commanders, Samuel was still over 30 yards per return and had a 69-yarder. Both of those would have been among the top 5 had Samuel had enough attempts to qualify. If the 49ers used Samuel to return in 2024, when the receiving room was thin, you’d think they’d give him the opportunity in 2026, with Mike Evans and De’Zhaun Stribling on the roster, no? Perhaps the team will see what Watkins, Pauling, and Bergen show in the preseason. If they aren’t up to par or look like they bring anything to the table, the fallback option is Deebo.
author: Kyle Posey

title: Ji’Ayir Brown says the previous 49ers schemes didn’t want football players. Raheem Morris does
summary: Steve Wilks, Nick Sorensen, Robert Saleh. One of those names is not like the others, though all three were the San Francisco 49ers defensive coordinators each of the last three years. Wilks and Sorensen were fired after one year while Saleh left in the offseason to become head coach of the Tennessee Titans. That should […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - JANUARY 11: Ji'Ayir Brown #27 of the San Francisco 49ers celebrates after an NFL wild card playoff football game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field on January 11, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Steve Wilks, Nick Sorensen, Robert Saleh. One of those names is not like the others, though all three were the San Francisco 49ers defensive coordinators each of the last three years. Wilks and Sorensen were fired after one year while Saleh left in the offseason to become head coach of the Tennessee Titans. That should tell you the difference. 49ers safety Ji’Ayir Brown says all three had something in common: schemes lacking football players. The 49ers safety may have found his scheme in Raheem Morris, who succeeded Saleh as defensive coordinator. “Raheem is dope, bro.” Brown said when speaking to the media on Monday. “Super dope. He wants football players. Previous schemes we’ve been in haven’t been that, haven’t wanted that. Raheem wants you to play football. He wants instinctive players. He wants guys who can get out there and play ball and read the quarterback.” It’s no secret the 49ers and their fans had a common issue with Wilks and Sorensen. Saleh has his own criticisms, but there was no comparison between his defenses and the two coaches before him. According to Brown, Saleh’s scheme had some severe issues. “The scheme fits all of us,” Brown continued. “It’s been great to see us transition into this explosive, D-back unit.” Or maybe he has a point. Wilks had one of the most stacked defenses in the league—and somehow it had head-scratching brain farts every game. The less said about Sorensen, the better; he’s simply a guy in over his head. Then there’s Saleh. Did the 49ers defense improve? Oh yeah — even with the injuries. Those injuries really left the 49ers without a next man up of sorts. When a starter went down, things didn’t take a step back; they hit a massive stumbling block. A good example was when Nick Bosa went down with a torn ACL; the 49ers’ pass rush plummeted. Expected when losing a player like Bosa, but they really didn’t have a plan “B” of sorts. Brown isn’t going to point any fingers. “I’m not going to even go there,” Brown said. “What happened last year was what happened last year. Could things have been better? Of course. But I’m not going to hold nobody accountable to that. I’ll just hold myself accountable and take whatever comes with that. But what happened last year was last year.” Brown was seen as a possible starter in 2025, but lost the starting safety job in September to Marques Sigle . Shortly after the demotion, Brown said he was a top-5 player in the NFL. Whether you agree with top-5 or not, Brown did emerge as the season went on. His huge game against the Carolina Panthers in November definitely had everyone chatting. Unfortunately, Brown couldn’t stay consistent, and it led to an offseason where he feuded with former 49ers safety Donte Whitner of all people . The 49ers notched just six interceptions in 2025. Brown was tied with Deommodore Lenoir for having the most with two. He also had one forced fumble. In practice on Monday, Brown notched a pass breakup. On Saturday, Morris spoke of Brown’s rushing potential when there were injuries along the defensive line. Brown will be a player to watch. Not just because of the 49ers’ safety position, but because he may have finally found a scheme he can thrive in. He’s had his moments of excellence, but if Morris can help get some consistency, then he might finally be the top player he claims he is.

There’s a lot of guys that have good skill sets. It’s a matter of, can they make the right decisions? Can they block a gunner when they’re supposed to? Can they let a ball hit the ground when they’re supposed to? Can they go up and catch a fair catch when they’re supposed to? There’s a lot more that goes into it than just returning the ball. We’re trying to find the guy that has the whole package, that we can count on every week, that can catch the ball and make great decisions.” 49ers Camp Notes: I’m all in on Romello Height (paywall) “[Height’s] arms are short, though, which raises a question about whether he actually finishes plays himself. He might end up being more of a guy who creates sacks for someone else than one who racks them up personally — more pressures than finishes. What I’m confident of is his ability as a disruptor, even if it’s a bit role. I do know I saw him cook Colton McKivitz at least once on Monday. Another time, I saw him spin inside violently, forcing Dominick Puni to help. He and McKivitz ultimately drove Height into the ground, but it also meant Puni had to account for him. It was a proactive double team on a rookie. If people are having to double-team Height the way they double Nick Bosa or Osa Odighizuwa, that’s going to result in sacks and meaningful pressure elsewhere on the line. I’m legitimately all in on this kid as a pass rusher. He has a four-move bag I outlined in the draft guide that’s predicated on converting speed and hesitation……Good day for both starting corners. Deommodore Lenoir had at least a couple of breakups, including one on Jake Tonges. Renardo Green looked pretty good. I loved that he, Marques Sigle, and Dre Brown were all communicating together. That communication is fundamental to raising the defense’s ceiling. Green had a full clamp on Jordan Watkins in the red zone….. Tonges looks really good. I think he’s a great No. 2 receiving tight end I’d expect production from him regardless of George Kittle’s status. Jordan Watkins showed up from time to time and looked alright. There was one incredible catch from Brayden Willis: a back-shoulder, one-handed grab, defended by (I think) Patrick McMorris. That was the only time I really noticed Willis. Good stuff from Junior Bergen. Popped up in a lot of different places. Demarcus Robinson also had at least one nice grab early on….Keep an eye on Bryson Eason. He’s a hefty guy who packs some real punch with his hands. I think he has a route to make the team, especially with Gracen Halton not practicing.“ Mike Evans joins 49ers’ growing list of injuries despite team’s dialed-back camp (paywall) “Jaden Dugger was drafted in the fifth round to play linebacker. His versatility, however, was notable after he played linebacker, edge and safety at different points in his college career. Monday was the first time Dugger worked with the defensive line group, which was particularly shorthanded due to injury. Dugger recorded what would’ve been a sack in a live setting from a defensive end’s alignment.” Matt Maiocco’s 53-man 49ers roster projection 1.0 ahead of the 2026 NFL season “Cowing looks the most comfortable among all the candidates when he is fielding punts. Winning that job in the return game will lock him into one of those spots.….The last couple spots [on the defensive line] are wide open, and such players as Sample, Sebastian Valdez, Bryson Eason and James Thompson still have plenty of time to win their spots….There is good competition among the cornerbacks. Veteran Nate Hobbs is definitely right there for one of these spots, as is fourth-round draft pick Ephesians Prysock. Depending on how he looks in the two joint practices and three preseason games, Prysock could be a no-brainer to win a spot on the team. The 49ers might feel that way, anyway, because he was selected in the fourth round and has a lot of promise. But, right now, Luter is looking good as one of the backups behind the top four guys: Lenoir, Green, Stout and Jones.” Do the 49ers finally have a Trent Williams heir? Enrique Cruz Jr. is off to a good start (paywall) “Instead, the least experienced of them all, rookie Enrique Cruz Jr., bounded into the huddle like an eager golden retriever, and the second-team offense didn’t skip a beat. “Coach, who goes in?” Cruz recalled excitedly asking Chris Foerster. The offensive line coach’s quick response: “You! You go in!” The sequence ended up being a good way to get rid of Day 1 jitters, Cruz said. And it offered a glimpse at one of the rookie’s top qualities: He isn’t shy. “He has an infectious personality,” Cruz’s high school coach, Nick Hildreth, said. “He’s fun, he’s so outgoing, he’s so happy to be there. I’ve never seen him where he’s negative toward anybody, ever.”….. and though the two hit it off right away, there were some early obstacles. The first was Cruz fancied himself a basketball player. Even after Hildreth convinced him to give football a try, he informed his coach he was a wideout. “And I’m like, ‘You’re not a wideout,’” Hildreth told Cruz, who grew to 6 feet 5, 252 pounds before his senior season. “We did throw him the ball his senior year. He got the ball in his hands once.” Another problem was Cruz’s GPA, which fell as low as 1.4. His worst subject? Cruz laughs and admits it was Spanish — funny because his family’s from Puerto Rico and he speaks the language. “It was a different version of Spanish,” he said. “I’d be at my grandma’s house doing it, and my grandma would tell me it’s wrong, it’s the wrong term because it’s Puerto Rican Spanish and not Spanish Spanish. So it was pretty hard for me to learn.”….Hildreth also convinced Cruz to drop his beloved basketball for wrestling, a sport he’d never tried before but one that would make him a better offensive lineman. “It’s hard on the ego to be the biggest, baddest kid in the building and then go to the wrestling room and get beat up,” Hildreth said. Cruz truly took off as a junior. He was tall, powerful, long-limbed, and he could pull and wreak havoc on opposing linebackers. During the playoffs that year, Cruz caused a riot of euphoria on the Willowbrook sideline when he blocked a highly touted opponent out of the back of the end zone and into a snowbank. “That was the beginning of his coming-out party,” Hildreth said. By the time he graduated, his GPA was up to 3.0, and he’d gotten a scholarship from Syracuse. Hildreth essentially told Foerster that story when the 49ers assistant flew to Willowbrook to give Cruz a workout before the draft.“ 49ers star Nick Bosa shares why he feels faster after his 3rd ACL injury ”You learn something every time you do it, every year really, injury or not, you kind of learn how to prepare a certain way to be your best. When I came off of the one in 2020, it forced me to..I don’t know how to…

And while he’s currently on the Active/PUP List, […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - FEBRUARY 08: George Kittle #85 and tight ends coach Brian Fleury during San Francisco 49ers practice ahead of Super Bowl LVIII at Fertitta Football Complex on February 08, 2024 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Chris Unger/Getty Images) | Getty Images George Kittle continues to progress from his January surgery that repaired a torn right Achilles tendon. The San Francisco 49ers are kind of caught in limbo with what to do with Kittle, as it sounds like there is uncertainty whether Kittle will be ready for Week 1. And while he’s currently on the Active/PUP List, using the same designation once the season begins would mean Kittle couldn’t play for the first four games of the season. Decisions, decisions. My guess is the team doesn’t rush one of the most important players on the roster, and they start Kittle on the PUP list. See ya in October, George. Mykel Williams is also a candidate to begin the season on the PUP. John Lynch didn’t sound like somebody who was confident in Williams being ready to play by Week 1, despite the second-year pro’s best efforts . According to our weekly FanDuel Sportsbook survey, 49ers fans are convinced we’ll see Kittle on the field before Williams. If that’s the case, how long until we see Mykel? He’s the queen on the chessboard for this 49ers defense. He’s the player — if Mykel is as good as the Niners believe him to be — who can unlock the pass rush and raise the run defense’s floor dramatically. That’s under the assumption he takes a jump in his second season and remains healthy — a dangerous assumption to make.

full_text: SANTA CLARA, CA - JUNE 03: Mike Evans #5 of the San Francisco 49ers speaks with the media after a team OTA practice at SAP Performance Facility on June 3, 2026 in Santa Clara, CA. (Photo by Matthew Huang/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The hits keep coming for the San Francisco 49ers. Wide receiver Mike Evans isn’t practicing on Monday due to a quad strain. Rookie running back Kaelon Black has an adductor injury and will also miss Monday’s session. Depending on the grade of the strain, Evans could miss anywhere from one week to multiple months. If it’s a Grade 1 strain, Evans would be sidelined anywhere from 1-to-3 weeks. The problem there is a strain could feel fine early, but a re-tear of the fibers is possible, just as they begin to knit together. It’s how these kinds of injuries can go from two weeks to two months. Needless to say, expect the 49ers to be overly cautious with Evans. Kyle’s update, 12:32 p.m. PT: Ian Rapoport said Evans’ injury wasn’t serious and that he could return to practice sooner rather than later: Black is the second player in as many practices to suffer a groin injury. Again, depending on the grade, Black could miss anywhere from a week or two to a couple of months, depending on whether it’s a mild strain or a complete rupture. The 49ers have suffered injuries to three of their top four running backs before they made it to the third window of the practice blocks. That explains why they went out and signed Khalil Herbert this weekend. Wide receiver De’Zhaun Stribling will continue to sit out with hamstring tightness. He’s day-to-day. Mikail Kamara suffered a torn ACL. He was waived/injured over the weekend. CJ West and Romello Height will practice on Monday.

title: Do the 49ers still need to improve their defense ahead of the season?
summary: The San Francisco 49ers took multiple steps to improve their defense this offseason, adding key players both via free agency and the draft. San Francisco signed linebacker Dre Greenlaw back to pair with Fred Warner. They traded for Osa Odighizuwa to add a veteran at defensive tackle alongside second-year pros C.J. West and Alfred Collins. […]
full_text: The San Francisco 49ers took multiple steps to improve their defense this offseason, adding key players both via free agency and the draft. San Francisco signed linebacker Dre Greenlaw back to pair with Fred Warner. They traded for Osa Odighizuwa to add a veteran at defensive tackle alongside second-year pros C.J. West and Alfred Collins. They drafted Romello Height to provide more juice for the pass rush from a speed perspective. But are the moves enough to improve a pass rush that ranked 32nd in the NFL last year in sacks? Or do the 49ers need to add more to their defense to return to a top unit this season? Speaking to reporters last week, general manager John Lynch acknowledged the defense wasn’t good enough last year. But he feels confident that they’ve made considerable progress this offseason. “I think when we’ve been successful here, our defensive line has wreaked havoc,” Lynch said. “And I think that’s pretty consistent around the league. We weren’t good enough last year. And there’s a lot of reasons for that. But ultimately, all those reasons are just excuses. So you have to address it. I feel confident with the way that we addressed it. “Yes, Nick [Bosa] being back is a difference maker, but it was bigger than that. And so we’ll do some things schematically without changing. Raheem [Morris]’s background comes from Monte Kiffin, so very similar to what [Robert] Saleh has done for us and who we’ve been. But there will be some expanded things, some more versatility. In addition to the schematic changes, San Francisco is going to trust on its young core to develop and produce. “We’ve kind of turned over this defensive line over the last couple of years with players like Alfred Collins and CJ West and this year, Gracen Halton, Romello Height, Keion White who came in last year. I’m really excited to see that group together and see what they can do because that certainly is a priority. “When we’ve been at our best, we’ve made life miserable on the opposing offense from the defensive front. Everything starts there. I agree. I knew that as a player. I was a better player when I played with Warren Sapp than when I went to Denver and didn’t have that. So I get that, believe me. And we’ve made a concerted effort to improve that. Now we’ve got to go show that we have.” San Francisco’s defense has been dealing with a few injuries and recoveries. Nick Bosa, Mykel Williams, Alfred Collins, and C.J. West are all recovering from offseason procedures or last year’s injuries. In addition, Height has missed some of the early practices as he works through an injury sustained in camp. Collins and West will be crucial for the 49ers, not only in stopping the run, but also in the passing game, as they’ll need to take another step. The big key is obviously Bosa, who is trending well ahead of the season and has even shared he’s felt faster this offseason. Now, the 49ers secondary hasn’t made changes, and that wasn’t necessarily a strong point last season. But San Francisco will hope for another jump from both Upton Stout, who was quite good as a rookie, and Renardo Green, who had his inconsistent moments in 2025. San Francisco hasn’t been against a midseason trade, but we’ll see if they make a veteran addition, potentially even on the defensive line, ahead of the season.

title: 49ers star Nick Bosa shares why he feels faster after his 3rd ACL injury
summary: Sports’s Illustrated’s Albert Breer caught up with San Francisco 49ers edge rusher Nick Bosa, where they discussed surgery, rehab, and why Bosa jokingly could play for a handful more years at an elite level. Bosa said, “I had a little tendinitis from my high school ACL, and he cleaned that up while he fixed my […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - SEPTEMBER 14: Nick Bosa #97 of the San Francisco 49ers celebrates a sack against the New Orleans Saints during the second half in the game at Caesars Superdome on September 14, 2025 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Sean Gardner/Getty Images) | Getty Images Sports’s Illustrated’s Albert Breer caught up with San Francisco 49ers edge rusher Nick Bosa, where they discussed surgery, rehab, and why Bosa jokingly could play for a handful more years at an elite level. Bosa said, “I had a little tendinitis from my high school ACL, and he cleaned that up while he fixed my ACL. That’s gone. So it’s like an improvement. So once I’m through this rehab, I feel like my right knee — because that was kind of a chronic issue that I had a little bit, and he cleaned that up in my quad tendon, and that hasn’t been an issue at all — could feel better when I’m done with this recovery.” Bosa explained why he feels faster after his third ACL injury: “You learn something every time you do it, every year really, injury or not, you kind of learn how to prepare a certain way to be your best. When I came off of the one in 2020, it forced me to..I don’t know how to explain it. Honestly, my legs get so big when I have years built up of training them. And it’s not like I trained to bodybuild my legs. They get big. And I feel like it’s just an observation that I’ve made: coming off that injury in 2020, I was moving better with less mass on my legs.” If you’ve ever seen Bosa in person, he has tree trunks for legs. It’s almost as if he’s waddling from side to side when he’s walking because of it. Good on Bosa for evolving and understanding what his body is telling him. He continued: “This is a speed game. I’m a power rusher, but speed creates power, and the way you can move is everything. So I think there’s something to, ‘I move better when my legs aren’t quite as massive.’ I kind of have that feeling right now.” We’ll see how long it takes until the 49ers clear Bosa to return to practice as a full participant. I bet the offensive line is content doing 11-on-11 drills without Bosa. Bosa also told Breer, “I should play four more years because I tear my ACL every five years.” The 49ers would welcome Bosa with open arms if he could play for another contract.

title: 3 questions for the 49ers at running back
summary: Running back was a revolving door for the San Francisco 49ers in the first few years of the Kyle Shanahan era. But that all changed when the 49ers acquired Christian McCaffrey in the 2022 season. Now, it’s hard for any running back not named McCaffrey to get consistent carries, and for good reason, with McCaffrey […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - JULY 27: Christian McCaffrey #23 of the San Francisco 49ers works out during training camp practice at SAP Performance Facility on July 27, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images Running back was a revolving door for the San Francisco 49ers in the first few years of the Kyle Shanahan era. But that all changed when the 49ers acquired Christian McCaffrey in the 2022 season. Now, it’s hard for any running back not named McCaffrey to get consistent carries, and for good reason, with McCaffrey being one of the best offensive weapons in the league. But with McCaffrey coming off one of his least productive seasons in terms of yards per attempt and him starting to get a little bit longer in the tooth, there might be some serious questions surrounding the position group. Here are three questions that will be answered over the next six months for the 49ers running backs: What does Christian McCaffrey look like as a running back in 2026? Christian McCaffrey was easily the Offensive Player of the Year and the likely MVP for the 49ers during the 2025 season, but that wasn’t because of his effectiveness on the ground but his role as an offensive weapon. But if you take Christian McCaffrey and remove the receiving numbers and look at him just as a running back, it was one of the least productive seasons as a pro. Yes, he surpassed 1,200 yards, but that was more of a product of quantity over quality. McCaffrey eclipsed 300 rushing attempts for the first time in his career. But that number of rushes didn’t produce the results you’d expect from what McCaffrey had shown in his previous seasons with the 49ers. For just the third time in his career, McCaffrey averaged fewer than four yards per rush, the first two instances coming in an injury-riddled 2020 when he averaged 3.8 yards per rush attempt in just three games, and his rookie season in 2017 when he averaged 3.7 yards per attempt on 117 carries. To give some context to McCaffrey’s 2025 production on the ground, he became the 41st running back since 2010 to eclipse 300 rushing attempts in a season. Of those 41 running backs, McCaffrey’s 1,202 rushing yards ranked 39th , only beating out 2021 Najee Harris who had 1,200 yards on 307 attempts and 2010 Cedric Benson who finished 1,111 yards on 321 attempts. McCaffrey was the most important piece to the 49ers’ offense in 2025, but the 49ers would probably prefer him to give more production than a Najee Harris or a Cedric Benson, especially with that heavy of a workload. Will Christian McCaffrey have as heavy of a workload? Now, this is three questions for the running back position, but we will cheat a bit and include McCaffrey as a pass catcher in this next section. Due to injuries and Brandon Aiyuk falling off the face of the earth, McCaffrey stepped into a larger role than expected and not only led the 49ers in rushing, but also receptions and receiving yards. Due to that, McCaffrey finished with a career-high 413 touches, just the second time he’s eclipsed the 400-touch plateau in his career. Not only was the 413 touches the most in his career, but McCaffrey led the league in touches by a healthy margin. Jonathan Taylor finished second in the league with his 369 touches, with Bijan Robinson third at 366 touches (although Robinson finished with 172 more total yards than McCaffrey despite the 47 fewer touches). Now, with the additions of Mike Evans, De’Zhaun Stribling, and now Deebo Samuel, and George Kittle ideally staying healthy, McCaffrey’s role as a pass catcher will likely drop to closer to the 65-70 receptions per season he averaged entering the 2025 season, and in theory, that helps save his legs to improve on his 2025 season as a running back. But all of that doesn’t even factor in that McCaffrey hit the dreaded age of 30 for running backs, which likely won’t affect his workload, but if the production on the ground is like it was in 2025, that ugly word regression might rear its head. How will the other running backs be used? For the third consecutive year, the 49ers used a draft pick to add a running back, using the 90th overall selection in April’s draft on Indiana’s Kaelon Black. Drafting running backs, however, hasn’t meant much usage, with Isaac Guerendo and Jordan James combining for just 84 rush attempts over their combined tenures with San Francisco. The 49ers were so confident in Guerendo and James entering training camp last year, they went out and sent a sixth-round pick to Washington for one season of Brian Robinson, who finished second on the team in rushes with his 92 rushing attempts. I think the short answer to this question is that it really doesn’t matter how the non-McCaffrey running backs will be used, as they will likely only see the field when McCaffrey needs a breather. Since the 49ers acquired McCaffrey, he has been far and away the most used running back on the team. With 2023 being McCaffrey’s first full season with the 49ers, here’s the breakdown year-to-year since 2023 of McCaffrey’s carries versus the other running backs (which removes Deebo Samuel and QB scrambles), throwing out the 2024 season since McCaffrey missed 13 games: 2023: McCaffrey – 272 carries Elijah Mitchell, Jordan Mason, Tyrion Davis-Price combined – 121 carries 2025: McCaffrey – 311 carries Brian Robinson – 92 carries In his two full healthy seasons, McCaffrey has taken 74.5 percent of all carries taken by 49ers running backs. It’s hard to imagine that any of Black, Guerendo, or James will change that in 2026. Maybe the addition of Samuel throws a wrench in things, but even then, it’s hard to imagine McCaffrey not getting around that 75 percent share of the carries we have seen.

title: Titans need to break passing yards curse in 2026
summary: The Tennessee Titans have not fielded an effective passing offense in five seasons. That’s an extremely sad sentence to write, but it’s true. This past campaign, they ranked 30th as an offense in passing yards, averaging 166.1 per contest. They finished the 2024 campaign ranked 26th in passing yards under Brian Callahan and Will Levis, […]
full_text: Tennessee Titans Offensive Coordinator Brian Daboll addresses the media during his first press conference at Ascension Saint Thomas Sports Park in Nashville, Tenn., Wednesday, Feb. 18, 2026. | DENNY SIMMONS / THE TENNESSEAN / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images The Tennessee Titans have not fielded an effective passing offense in five seasons. That’s an extremely sad sentence to write, but it’s true. This past campaign, they ranked 30th as an offense in passing yards, averaging 166.1 per contest. They finished the 2024 campaign ranked 26th in passing yards under Brian Callahan and Will Levis, averaging 195.1 per game. They were 29th in 2023 (180.4/game), 30th in 2022 (171.4), 24th in 2021 (201.1), and 23rd in 2020 (228.3). That’s an unfathomable streak of consistently being a bottom-10 passing offense. The Titans invested significant offseason resources to hopefully change that in 2026. After hiring a defensive minded head coach in Robert Saleh, the Titans hired one of the most sought-after offensive coordinator candidates in Brian Daboll. Coach Daboll loved Cam Ward as a prospect and is legitimately excited to develop him this year. The Titans also invested big at wide receiver. They drafted Carnell Tate with the fourth overall pick and paid Wan’Dale Robinson $70 million in free agency. Both additions were approved by Daboll, and he’s expected to make them the focal point of his passing offense. The Titans are arguably deeper at wide receiver than they’ve ever been. They kept Calvin Ridley via a restructured contract as opposed to making him a salary cap casualty. They also have sophomores Chimere Dike and Elic Ayomanor. At tight end, they have the developing Gunnar Helm, and paid Daniel Bellinger $8 million per year in free agency. The Titans need to field a significantly more impactful aerial attack in 2026 than they have in several seasons. A lot of that will be decided by how Ward develops as a sophomore quarterback. Adding supporting pieces like Daboll, Tate, and Robinson should have a monumental impact. The Titans have the pieces in place to effectively pass the ball in 2026.

full_text: Tuesday marks Day 5 of Washington Commanders training camp in Ashburn, VA. Head coach Dan Quinn spoke to reporters before the start of today’s practice. Javon Kinlaw and Bill Croskey-Merritt are scheduled for Q&As after practice, along with players getting interview on the field. Quinn said this three-day block (Monday-Wednesday) is about powering up, stacking and fixing any issues with what’s been installed. They’ll be running longer drives in practice, putting more stress on the secondary and getting a better look at the wide receivers in space. Quinn was asked about several of the free agents Washington signed this year including Fabian Moreau, who was signed today to replace a retiring Ahkello Witherspoon . The head coach said Washington liked the former third-round pick’s versatility. He’s also familiar with defensive coordinator Daronte Jones from their time together on the Vikings the last two seasons. Quinn also praised LB Leo Chenal’s winning standards and is very high on the Commanders big offseason signing, EDGE Odafe Oweh. The competition at left guard is on, and Quinn said that Chris Paul has dropped 20 pounds since last season. He said the new offense will run more zone and playaction, and Brandon Coleman has “always been quick off the spot”. He also talked about Jayden Daniels’ red-zone touch, and said, “That’s not luck.” Rookie receiver Antonio Williams is further along as a rookie than Luke McCaffrey was, but Quinn noted McCaffrey had recently switched positions from quarterback. full_text: The Daily Slop — August 4, 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles WUSA9 ‘Them boys are coming’ | Washington defenders going after the ball, even after the whistle Early on, you can tell this Daronte Jones defense is not going to make it easy for offenses to hang onto the ball. Several times Monday, Commanders defenders were trying to punch or rip the ball out of the ball carrier’s hands. Sometimes after the whistle. “Yeah, definitely like even after the whistle they’re going at the ball,” said tight end Chig Okonkwo. “I mean one time today, you know, [K’Lavon Chaisson] got me after the whistle. Them boys are coming and it’s just nice to, you know, have that competition that just raises up, raises up another level of competition.” To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Washington Post (paywall) Commanders’ offense gets cooking and other observations from Monday’s practice Overall, it was easily the best practice the offense has had in camp thus far. Daniels was on the money, and the pass catchers did a better job of creating separation. The downside: The offensive line continued to have issues both in pass protection and the run game. As has been the case throughout training camp, the defensive line outperformed its counterpart. The run defense was stout throughout practice, and the running backs didn’t have much room to create. The defensive line did a good job of maintaining gap integrity, while the linebackers were quick to trigger and make plays close to the line of scrimmage. In the passing game, the defensive line was able to win frequently off the edge while also creating a consistent push up the middle of the pocket. Oweh credited defensive coordinator Daronte Jones for making it clear when players can go all-in on the pass rush and giving them freedom to improvise along the way. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders Roundtable Daronte Jones’ brought constant heat, but Jayden Daniels and new-look offense flashed high-end creativity on Day 1 in pads David Blough’s hands-on energy: Offensive Coordinator David Blough is an active, hands-on coach. Throughout practice, you could see him engaged in drills, dropping back into coverage, or pulling a player aside to talk one-on-one. To begin practice, the WRs engaged in light pass-and-catch drills. Blough used what looked like a padded pole to punch at the ball and try to provoke a fumble. He seems like a guy with real attention to detail. Defense wins Day 1: If I were to declare a winner today, I would give it to the defense. On many occasions, they penetrated the gaps and took away any potential for positive yardage on runs. In this same Red Zone series, Javon Kinlaw broke through the line and “sacked” Daniels. The defense provided sticky coverage, and while Daniels tried to buy time, it was to no avail. Personnel wrinkles: The offense will provide fans (and opposing defenses) a lot of eye candy with pre-snap motion. The Commanders ran a lot of 12-personnel sets today and moved both tight ends in pre-snap motion. It’s an interesting wrinkle that wasn’t present last year. On defense, I was surprised to see Frankie Luvu at the Mike position. He spent a good amount of time there, which allowed other LBs, including Styles, to blitz off the edge. Sinnott’s versatile role: Sinnott will be used creatively this season. Today, we saw him as an H-Back and a true fullback in I-formation. I can see why he is excited for a fresh start under Blough. Long after practice wrapped up, Sam Hartman stayed on the field to throw extra routes to Sinnott, Ryan Cracraft, and others. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders.com Training camp notebook | Sonny Styles stands out during first padded practice The first drill was indicative of how the practice went for both sides of the ball. Players were competing on every play, and each unit had some positive moments. Right after Styles’ tackle on Croskey-Merritt, Marcus Mariota connected with the running back for a touchdown. Perhaps the best catch of the day came when the starting offense was on the field, as Jayden Daniels connected with Terry McLaurin in the back corner of the end zone for the score, despite Mike Sainristil providing tight coverage. [R]ookie Joshua Josephs was one of the more entertaining players to watch today. Josephs’ athleticism shone on Monday, as he was all over the field making plays. He batted down a pass from Daniels early in the day, and he showed impressive speed during pass protection drills. It’s still unclear where he fits on the depth chart and how many snaps he’ll get, but there have been signs of his potential. A lot of people were wondering how rookie wide receiver Antonio Williams would look with the pads on after getting open and creating separation in the first three days of camp. The answer is that he looked basically the same and continued to find ways of getting open. He had two touchdowns today, one of which came on the last play of two-minute drills. Williams practiced mostly with the second group today, but that could change soon because of how impressive the rookie has looked against defensive backs. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Sports Illustrated The Good and Not So Good From Commanders’ First Padded Practice The Not So Good Kaliakmanis appearing in this section for another interception after being picked off in each of the previous two open practices is not a good look. Turnovers in three consecutive practices are hard to defend or dismiss for a seventh-round quarterback trying to take reps from Sam Hartman as a developmental quarterback. Rookies are expected to make mistakes, but throwing interceptions every day will never be acceptable and is worth tracking. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders Wire 4 standouts from Commanders’ first padded practice CB Mike Sainristil Sainristil was playing inside and outside on Monday. While he did allow the touchdown to McLaurin early in practice, it was strong coverage. He was beaten by a terrific throw. Sainristil got his revenge later, breaking up a pair of plays in the red zone. It’s been a good camp so far for Sainristil. Confidence is everything. Washington needs a strong bounce-back year from Sainristil, and he seems up to the task . Sam Cosmi , Washington Commanders Cosmi returned from a knee injury midway through last season and brought his trademark stability back to Washington‘s offensive line. Though he appeared in only nine games, his 76.3 PFF grade ranked 10th among qualified guards. Cosmi allowed just 11 pressures and two sacks over those nine games, and his 72.3 PFF run-blocking grade was another strong mark. It’s reasonable to expect an even stronger season in 2026, assuming he stays healthy. title: Commanders EDGE Odafe Oweh details underrated part of his game
summary: Odafe Oweh has built a reputation as an excellent pass rusher. Collecting 17.5 sacks over the last two seasons will establish that. His quarterback pressure rate is way up there, hovering near 16%, illustrating how ferocious he can be getting after the passer.   His usage suggests that as well, with the Baltimore Ravens using […]
full_text: Odafe Oweh has built a reputation as an excellent pass rusher. Collecting 17.5 sacks over the last two seasons will establish that. His quarterback pressure rate is way up there , hovering near 16%, illustrating how ferocious he can be getting after the passer. His usage suggests that as well, with the Baltimore Ravens using him primarily as a situational pass rusher. The Commanders edge rusher would like to remind you that wasn’t always the case. He had zero sacks in his final season at Penn State , even with all the physical tools required to be an excellent NFL pass rusher. Without the pass-rush stats, Oweh had to be a force in another aspect of his game that has gotten a bit lost as he enters his fifth professional season. “My run game,” Oweh said in a press conference following Monday’s training camp practice . “I came in as a run defender. I had zero sacks (his last year at Penn State), and some people forget that. I worked hard, and by the grace of God, he has helped get better as a pass rusher. The run game is what I hung my hat on at first. People forget that, because I was a designated pass rusher in some defenses. I’m really trying to get back to that playing style against the run, attacking the edges and getting TFLs.” He’s right. Go back to his NFL.com draft profile and you’ll find this assessment of his run defense: “He has dominant potential as a run defender with burst and range to upend back-side and play-side runs, turning them into short gains or losses.” Opportunity plays a part in how much run defending Oweh gets to do. He was more of a situational guy in Baltimore, where he was drafted No. 31 overall back in 2021. While pass rushing was key to the Commanders giving him a four-year, $96-million contract in free agency, he’ll be more of a three-down presence in Washington. That will give Oweh a chance to prove he’s a complete player. He’s proud of his development as a pass rusher, which involved refining the technique required to accentuate his elite physical skills. His motivation stems from doubters, from those projecting what he can’t do. “Each obstacle, each moment of adversity is like a test,” Oweh said. “That’s when you’ve got to work. That’s the universe telling you that’s where you’ve got to get better. Even if you’re listening to the fans, you can compartmentalize it and use it as motivation. I think, ‘Alright, I’m going to show you guys.’ That’s why I celebrate so much and point to the naysayers. You have to use that. “We play sports. You can’t hang your hat on the bad reps. You have to work hard for the good ones. I feel like that was the best part for me. I’m glad I went through (tough times), because now y’all know me as a pass rusher, but y’all gonna remember that I’m a run defender, too. That’s a testament to how hard I work and my ability to close out the naysayers and do my job well.” Oweh believes Daronte Jones will give him great opportunities to do that. He has generally been a secondary pass rusher, behind Kyle Van Noy or Justin Houston in Baltimore and Khalil Mack with the Chargers. Washington brought in some serious talent off the edge, Oweh’s the alpha here. New coordinator Daronte Jones is given Oweh some freedom on when to stay disciplined in rush lanes and when to take a big shot. He’ll have plenty, but isn’t putting everything on his shoulders to sack the quarterback. “Rushing well as a group is key,” Oweh said. “I’d rather have that than one dominant pass rusher. A group of pass rushers who know how to play and work well together. That’s what these first few days of training camp are all about…having chemistry with the guys and understanding what they like to do.” A quick reader poll:
